hydraulic-assembly.summary: The hydraulic casing assembly is the stationary, pressure-containing envelope (volute casing, casing cover, wear ring, gasket, fasteners and connections) that guides liquid to and from the impeller.
hydraulic-assembly.function: It contains the pumped liquid at discharge pressure and seals it from the atmosphere. It guides flow from the suction flange to the impeller eye and collects the flow leaving the impeller, converting part of its kinetic energy into static pressure before the discharge flange. It also provides the alignment interfaces for the impeller, the shaft seal and the bearing frame.
hydraulic-assembly.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters axially through the suction nozzle and reaches the impeller eye, where the static pressure is close to its lowest value in the pump. The rotating impeller adds energy, so liquid leaves the impeller periphery with raised static pressure and high absolute velocity. The volute collects this flow around the circumference and, together with the widening discharge nozzle, decelerates it so that velocity energy is recovered as pressure. A close running clearance at the wear ring limits leakage of high-pressure liquid back to the suction side. Gaskets and bolted joints keep the stationary parts pressure-tight.
hydraulic-assembly.construction: The casing is radially split: the volute casing, with integral tongue, suction nozzle, top centreline discharge nozzle and feet, is closed on the drive side by a separate casing cover that also forms the seal chamber or stuffing box. The casing-to-cover joint is sealed by a gasket and clamped by studs and nuts. A renewable casing wear ring sits opposite the impeller eye. Drain, vent and pressure-tapping connections are machined into the casing. Back-pull-out construction allows the cover, impeller, shaft seal and bearing frame to be withdrawn as one unit while the casing stays connected to the piping.

materials.family: Cast iron wetted set (grey or ductile iron casing and cover)
materials.why: Economical, easily cast and machined; adequate for clean water and many non-aggressive liquids.
materials.limitations: Limited corrosion and erosion resistance; grey iron is brittle and sensitive to pipe loads and thermal shock.
materials.typicalService: Water supply, HVAC, cooling water and general industrial service.

materials.family: Stainless or duplex stainless steel wetted set
materials.why: Higher corrosion resistance and (for duplex) higher strength and erosion-corrosion resistance.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; chloride, temperature and pH limits of the chosen alloy must be checked; galling risk at stainless rubbing pairs.
materials.typicalService: Chemical, process, hygienic, seawater or chloride-containing service after verification.

failureModes.mode: External leakage at joints or connections
failureModes.cause: Gasket deterioration, loss of bolt preload, damaged flange or register faces, pipe strain.
failureModes.signs: Drips or spray at the casing joint, flanges or plugs; crystal or corrosion deposits.

failureModes.cause: Abrasive solids, high local velocities, corrosion or cavitation.
failureModes.signs: Gradual loss of head and efficiency, rising power per unit flow, roughened passages at overhaul.

failureModes.mode: Clearance growth at the wear ring
failureModes.cause: Rubbing, abrasive wear, corrosion, shaft deflection when operating far from BEP.
failureModes.signs: Reduced head and flow at the same speed, lower efficiency, sometimes higher vibration.

failureModes.cause: Excessive nozzle loads, freezing, water hammer, thermal shock or casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Leakage through the wall, recurring coupling misalignment, failed hydrostatic test.

inspection: Walk-down checks for external leakage, corrosion and loose fasteners at the casing joint and connections.
Trend suction pressure, discharge pressure, flow and motor power and compare with the original test or commissioning data.
At overhaul, inspect volute passages, tongue, wear ring and cover for erosion, corrosion and cavitation damage.
Measure the wear-ring running clearance and compare it with the OEM limit.
Confirm piping is independently supported so that nozzle loads stay within the OEM allowable values.
maintenance: Use back-pull-out removal: decouple (with a spacer coupling the motor can stay in place), unbolt the cover and withdraw the rotating unit without disturbing the piping.
Fit a new casing gasket at every reassembly and tighten casing fasteners in the OEM sequence and torque.
Renew wear rings when the clearance exceeds the OEM limit.
Drain and, if required, flush the casing before maintenance or before a shutdown in freezing conditions.

keyConcepts.title: Flow path through the hydraulic end
keyConcepts.body: Liquid follows a fixed path: suction flange and suction nozzle, impeller eye, vane channels, volute, throat, discharge nozzle and discharge flange. In the suction nozzle the liquid is accelerated slightly towards the eye. The lowest static pressure in the pump occurs just inside the eye, at the vane leading edges, which is why suction conditions are expressed as net positive suction head (NPSH) referred to a datum at the impeller inlet. In the vane channels the impeller does work on the liquid, raising both its static pressure and its absolute velocity. The volute gathers the flow around the impeller circumference and, with the diffusing discharge nozzle, slows it down so that kinetic energy is recovered as static pressure. A small part of the flow leaks from the high-pressure side back to the eye through the wear-ring clearance and recirculates; this leakage receives energy from the impeller but is never delivered, so it reduces volumetric efficiency. The useful result is the pump total head H, the increase in total energy per unit weight of liquid between the suction and discharge flanges.

keyConcepts.title: Back-pull-out construction
keyConcepts.body: In a back-pull-out design the casing stays bolted to the suction and discharge piping, while the rotating unit (casing cover, impeller, shaft, shaft seal and bearing frame) is withdrawn towards the drive end after unbolting the casing joint. KSB explains that the design meets refinery requirements for rapid dismantling and reassembly, is therefore often used for process pumps and has also been adopted for other applications, and that it lets internal parts be inspected or replaced without removing the casing from the piping. With a spacer coupling, removing the spacer creates enough axial room so that the motor can remain on the baseplate with its electrical connections undisturbed. Benefits include shorter maintenance time, less risk of disturbing pipe alignment and the option of keeping a spare rotating unit. The trade-off is that the casing joint, cover register and bearing-frame fit must be accurately machined so that the reassembled unit is concentric with the casing.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

impeller-assembly.summary: The impeller assembly is the rotating hydraulic element (impeller with its key, washer and locking nut) that transfers shaft power to the liquid.
impeller-assembly.function: It converts the mechanical power delivered by the shaft into an increase of pressure and kinetic energy of the liquid. The key transmits torque from the shaft to the impeller, while the washer and nut locate and clamp the impeller axially on the overhung shaft end. Together with the wear rings, the impeller also defines the internal leakage path back to suction.
impeller-assembly.operatingPrinciple: The impeller rotates at shaft speed and its vanes deflect the liquid, increasing its angular momentum between the eye and the outlet. The rise in angular momentum requires a torque on the shaft, and the corresponding power appears as an increase in the specific energy of the liquid. Centrifugal effects and the deceleration of the relative flow in the vane channels raise static pressure, while the absolute velocity also increases. Pressure differences on the two shrouds produce an axial force, and non-uniform pressure around the outlet produces a radial force, both carried by the shaft and bearings.
impeller-assembly.construction: In this configuration the impeller is a closed, single-suction radial impeller cast in one piece with front shroud, back shroud, vanes, eye and hub, fitted with a renewable impeller wear ring at the eye (variant: open impeller for comparison). It is mounted on the overhung shaft end, driven by a parallel key and clamped against a shoulder or sleeve by a washer and locking nut. The impeller is balanced after machining, in one or two correction planes depending on its proportions and the balance quality specified (ISO 21940-11 gives procedures and tolerances for rotors with rigid behaviour). Axial-thrust balancing features such as balance holes or back vanes are manufacturer variations and are not assumed here.

materials.why: Low cost, easy to cast in complex vane passages and easy to machine; common for clean water.
materials.limitations: Brittle, limited strength and poor resistance to cavitation erosion, corrosion and abrasive wear.
materials.typicalService: Clean cold water, building services and similar non-aggressive liquids.

materials.why: Good castability and corrosion resistance in many waters, better cavitation resistance than grey iron and good tolerance of rubbing contact.
materials.limitations: Attacked by ammonia and by some sulphide-polluted or high-velocity waters; limited abrasion resistance; galvanic effects when combined with other metals.
materials.typicalService: Potable water, cooling water and, after assessment, some seawater applications.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in many process liquids and better cavitation-erosion resistance than cast iron.
materials.limitations: Risk of pitting, crevice corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking in warm chloride-containing liquids; galling risk at rubbing surfaces.
materials.typicalService: Process liquids, hygienic and chemical service within verified limits.

materials.why: Higher strength and generally better chloride and erosion-corrosion resistance than standard austenitic grades; the KSB cavitation-erosion comparison ranks duplex steel among the most resistant common pump materials.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; casting quality and heat treatment must be controlled; upper temperature limits apply.
materials.typicalService: Seawater, brackish water and abrasive or chloride-containing process liquids, subject to verification.

failureModes.cause: Insufficient NPSH margin, operation far from BEP, suction recirculation at low flow.
failureModes.signs: Crackling noise, vibration, pitted or sponge-like damage near vane inlet edges.

failureModes.cause: Solids in the liquid, high velocities, incompatible material.
failureModes.signs: Thinned vanes and shrouds, rounded edges, gradual loss of head.

failureModes.cause: Uneven wear or erosion, blockage of a channel, deposits, loose fit on the shaft.
failureModes.signs: Vibration at 1x running speed, bearing distress, seal leakage.

failureModes.mode: Loosening or fretting on the shaft
failureModes.cause: Reverse rotation, insufficient nut tightening or failed locking, worn key or bore.
failureModes.signs: Knocking, vibration, impeller rubbing the casing, fretting marks at overhaul.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations (for example a small gap to the volute tongue), resonance, casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at vane-to-shroud junctions or vane tips found by visual or dye-penetrant inspection.

inspection: Trend vibration (overall and spectrum) and bearing temperatures to detect unbalance or hydraulic problems early.
At overhaul, inspect vanes, shrouds and eye for cavitation pitting, erosion, corrosion and cracks; use dye-penetrant testing at suspect areas.
Measure wear-ring diameters and running clearance against OEM limits.
Check the hub bore, keyway and key for fretting, wear and correct fit.
maintenance: Re-balance the impeller after any repair, trimming or significant material loss, to the balance quality required by the OEM.
Replace locking elements (lock washer or similar) and tighten the impeller nut to the OEM torque.
Check the motor direction of rotation with the coupling disconnected before first start, because reverse rotation can loosen a threaded impeller fastening.
Record any change of impeller diameter in the pump documentation, because it changes the performance curve.

keyConcepts.title: Energy transfer and the Euler pump equation
keyConcepts.body: The impeller transfers mechanical energy to the liquid by changing its angular momentum. Applying the momentum equation to a control volume around the impeller gives the theoretical (Euler) head: H_th = (u2*c_u2 - u1*c_u1)/g, where u is the blade peripheral speed (u = pi*D*n/60, with D in m and n in rpm), c_u is the circumferential component of the absolute velocity of the liquid, g is gravitational acceleration, and the indices 1 and 2 denote the impeller inlet and outlet. Pumps without inlet guide vanes are usually designed for little or no pre-swirl at the design point (c_u1 close to zero), so H_th is approximately u2*c_u2/g: head rises with impeller diameter and speed. The velocity triangles at inlet and outlet (absolute velocity c, which KSB writes as v, relative velocity w and peripheral speed u) link these quantities to the blade angles. With a finite number of vanes the outlet flow does not follow the blade angle exactly (slip), so c_u2 and H_th are lower than for perfect guidance; slip is not a loss but must be allowed for in design. The actual head H is lower again because of hydraulic losses (friction, incidence, mixing), expressed by the hydraulic efficiency eta_h = H/H_th.

keyConcepts.title: Centrifugal action, velocity increase and pressure distribution
keyConcepts.body: The Euler head can be split into three terms: H_th = [(u2^2 - u1^2) + (w1^2 - w2^2) + (c2^2 - c1^2)]/(2g). The first term is the centrifugal effect: liquid moving outward in a rotating channel experiences a pressure rise that grows with the square of radius. The second term is the static pressure gained as the relative velocity w is reduced in the widening vane channels. The third term is the increase in absolute velocity, which leaves the impeller as kinetic energy that the volute and discharge nozzle must partly convert to pressure. Within the impeller, static pressure is therefore lowest just inside the eye and near the vane leading edges, where cavitation starts if the available NPSH is insufficient, and highest at the impeller outlet. Across each vane the pressure side carries higher pressure than the suction side; this blade loading is what transmits the torque.

keyConcepts.title: Single-suction entry, axial thrust and balancing measures
keyConcepts.body: In a single-suction impeller the liquid enters axially through the eye on one side only and turns through roughly a right angle into the radial vane channels; a double-suction impeller takes liquid from both sides and is nominally balanced by symmetry (KSB lists it as a means of axial thrust elimination). Between the impeller outlet and the wear-ring diameter, the pressures acting on the outside of the two shrouds roughly balance. Inside the wear-ring diameter, however, the front of the impeller is at suction pressure (the eye), while the back shroud still sees the higher pressure of the rear side chamber down to the hub. The resulting axial force on a closed single-suction impeller is usually directed towards the suction side and rises with head and impeller size; KSB notes it is higher during start-up than in steady operation. KSB describes two measures at the impeller: balance holes through the back shroud, combined with a second sealing gap on the back of the impeller, which reduce the rear-chamber pressure towards inlet pressure; and back vanes on the rear shroud, which make the liquid behind the impeller rotate faster and so lower the pressure acting on it (KSB: efficiency may drop by up to three points). KSB adds that such hydraulic balancing is fully effective only at the best efficiency flow, so residual forces at low flow and overload must be carried by the thrust bearing. Whether and how they are used is a manufacturer design choice.

keyConcepts.title: Closed versus open impeller
keyConcepts.body: A closed impeller has vanes enclosed between a front and a back shroud; leakage from discharge to suction is controlled by a radial running clearance at the eye (wear rings). An open impeller has no front shroud (KSB classes such impellers as open; many other sources call the form with a back shroud semi-open); its vanes run against the stationary casing wall with a small axial clearance, and leakage passes over the vane tips. For a closed impeller, efficiency depends mainly on the wear-ring clearance and is relatively insensitive to axial rotor position. For an open impeller, efficiency is sensitive to the axial tip clearance, which increases with wear; some designs allow the clearance to be restored by axial adjustment of the rotor. Open impellers are easier to inspect and clean and are often preferred for solids, fibrous material or liquids that tend to clog shrouded channels, while closed impellers are generally used for clean liquids where sustained efficiency is important. The 3D model shows the open impeller only as a conceptual comparison.

closed-impeller.summary: The closed impeller is a one-piece cast rotor in which the vanes are enclosed between a front shroud and a back shroud, with the inlet (eye) on the suction side and the hub on the drive side.
closed-impeller.function: It adds energy to the liquid by turning it in enclosed vane channels from axial entry to radial exit. The front shroud keeps liquid inside the channels, so that leakage back to suction is limited to the clearance at the impeller wear ring. The hub transmits torque and locates the impeller on the shaft.
closed-impeller.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters the eye axially, turns into the vane channels and is accelerated outward by the rotating vanes. Because the channels are closed on both sides, the flow is guided along its whole path and leakage over the vane edges does not occur. High-pressure liquid surrounding the outer surfaces of the shrouds tends to flow back to the eye; this flow is throttled by the narrow radial gap between the impeller wear ring and the casing wear ring.
closed-impeller.construction: The front shroud, back shroud, vanes, eye and hub are cast as one part, normally by sand or investment casting with cores forming the vane channels. The eye neck is machined to carry a renewable impeller wear ring (or to act as the wear surface itself in some designs). The hub bore and keyway are machined to fit the shaft, the outer diameter is turned to the specified (possibly trimmed) diameter, and the finished impeller is balanced.

failureModes.mode: Cavitation damage at the vane inlets
failureModes.cause: Low NPSH margin or suction recirculation at part load.
failureModes.signs: Pitting on vane surfaces near the eye; noise and vibration in service.

failureModes.mode: Erosion and corrosion of channels and shrouds
failureModes.cause: Solids, high velocities, aggressive liquid.
failureModes.signs: Thinned shrouds, rough channels, falling performance.

failureModes.cause: Fibrous material, debris or deposits.
failureModes.signs: Sudden drop in flow and head, vibration from unbalance.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations, resonance, casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Cracks found at overhaul, possibly fragments in the casing.

inspection: Inspect channels (using a mirror and light or a borescope) for blockage, erosion and cracks.
Check the eye neck or wear ring and the hub bore dimensionally against OEM data.
Dye-penetrant test vane-shroud junctions where cracking is suspected.
maintenance: Clean deposits from channels and re-check balance if material has been added or removed.
Renew the impeller wear ring (or the impeller) when the clearance limit is exceeded.
Replace the impeller when wall loss, cracking or cavitation damage exceed what the OEM allows to be repaired.

shaft-assembly.summary: The shaft assembly is the rotating backbone of the pump (pump shaft with its sleeve, keys and locknut) that carries the overhung impeller and transmits torque from the coupling.
shaft-assembly.function: It transmits driving torque from the coupling to the impeller and carries the impeller weight, hydraulic radial force and axial thrust to the bearings. It positions the impeller axially and radially within the casing, and its stiffness controls deflection at the wear rings and seal faces. The shaft sleeve protects the shaft in the sealing area.
shaft-assembly.operatingPrinciple: Torque enters at the coupling end through a key and is carried by torsional shear stress along the shaft to the impeller key. Radial loads at the overhung impeller bend the shaft about the inboard bearing; each surface element of the rotating shaft passes through tension and compression once per revolution, so bending stress is a fatigue load. Axial thrust is transferred through the shaft to the thrust bearing, which is clamped by the shaft locknut. The shaft-plus-impeller rotor has natural frequencies of bending vibration that must be kept away from the running speed.
shaft-assembly.construction: The shaft is a stepped, machined bar with an impeller section (journal, keyseat and thread) at the overhung end, a sleeve and seal area, bearing seats, a threaded section for the bearing locknut and a keyed coupling section at the drive end. Diameter steps form shoulders that locate the bearings and impeller. A replaceable shaft sleeve covers the shaft through the seal chamber or stuffing box and is sealed to the shaft. Fillets, surface finish and concentricity of all seats are specified by the manufacturer.

materials.family: Carbon or low-alloy steel (with a protective sleeve in the wetted area)
materials.why: High strength and fatigue resistance at low cost; the sleeve keeps the pumped liquid away from the shaft in the seal area.
materials.limitations: Corrodes if the liquid reaches it; requires effective sealing of the sleeve and impeller fit.
materials.typicalService: Water and non-corrosive liquids, and designs where the shaft is not wetted.

materials.why: Combines good strength and hardness with moderate corrosion resistance.
materials.limitations: Lower corrosion resistance than austenitic grades; sensitive to pitting in chloride-containing liquids.
materials.typicalService: Water, mildly corrosive liquids and general process duty.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance where the shaft is wetted by aggressive liquids; duplex adds higher strength.
materials.limitations: Austenitic grades have lower strength, so larger diameters may be needed; galling risk at threaded and rubbing fits.
materials.typicalService: Chemical, hygienic and seawater service after verification.

failureModes.cause: Rotating bending plus torsion, stress concentration at keyways, shoulders or threads, corrosion fatigue, excessive radial load from off-BEP operation or misalignment.
failureModes.signs: Beach marks on the fracture face; preceding rise in vibration.

failureModes.cause: High radial thrust at low or high flow, mishandling, improper straightening.
failureModes.signs: High run-out, wear-ring rubbing, short seal life, vibration at running speed.

failureModes.cause: Loose bearing or coupling fits, micromovement under the impeller hub, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Polished or corroded bands at seats, loose components at disassembly.

failureModes.cause: Leakage between sleeve and shaft due to a failed sleeve seal.
failureModes.signs: Pitting or grooving found under the sleeve at overhaul.

inspection: Measure shaft run-out (total indicated reading) at the seal area and coupling end against OEM limits.
Check bearing seats and coupling seat diameters for wear and fretting.
Inspect keyways, shoulders and thread roots for cracks (magnetic-particle or dye-penetrant testing as appropriate).
Trend vibration and bearing temperatures in service.
maintenance: Replace a shaft that exceeds the OEM run-out limit or shows cracks; straighten only according to OEM-approved procedures.
Renew the shaft sleeve and its sealing element whenever the seal or packing is serviced and the sleeve is worn.
Reassemble with clean, burr-free fits and tighten the bearing locknut and impeller nut as specified by the OEM.
Check and correct coupling alignment after any work on the rotating unit.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission and torsional stress
keyConcepts.body: The shaft carries the driving torque T = P/omega = 60*P/(2*pi*n), where P is shaft power in W, omega the angular velocity in rad/s and n the speed in rpm. For a solid round shaft of diameter d the maximum torsional shear stress at the surface is tau_max = 16*T/(pi*d^3). For a given power, torque is inversely proportional to speed, so a pump designed for a lower speed needs a larger shaft section than one of the same power at a higher speed. (For one pump run at different speeds, the affinity laws give power roughly proportional to n^3 at hydraulically similar operating points, so torque then varies roughly with n^2.) The smallest diameter (usually the coupling end) and the keyseats are critical, since a keyway raises local stress through stress concentration. Starting torque, torque fluctuations and torsional vibration of the pump-coupling-motor train add to the steady value. Design values, safety factors and allowable stresses are manufacturer data based on the shaft material.

keyConcepts.title: Bending stress and deflection of an overhung rotor
keyConcepts.body: In an overhung pump the impeller sits outside the bearings, so its weight and the hydraulic radial force F act at an overhang L from the inboard bearing. The bending moment at the inboard bearing is approximately M = F*L, giving a bending stress sigma = 32*M/(pi*d^3) at the shaft surface. The hydraulic radial force keeps a roughly fixed direction while the shaft turns, so each surface point passes from tension to compression once per revolution: a fully reversed fatigue load, combined with the torsional stress. For a uniform shaft on two rigid simple supports with bearing span S, beam theory gives a deflection at the impeller of delta = F*L^2*(L + S)/(3*E*I), with E the elastic modulus and I = pi*d^4/64. Deflection therefore rises steeply with overhang and falls with the fourth power of diameter: a short overhang and a large diameter make the rotor stiffer. Radial force is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows at low and high flows, especially with a single volute, so off-BEP operation increases deflection at the wear rings and seal faces. Allowable deflection is set by the pump specification or the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Critical speed
keyConcepts.body: Every rotor has natural frequencies of lateral (bending) vibration. KSB defines the critical speed as the rotational speed at which the dynamic forces from rotation make a component such as the shaft or rotor vibrate at its natural frequency, so that resonance can produce large vibration amplitudes and damage; it notes the effect is reduced if such speeds are passed through quickly. For a shaft carrying a mass at its end, the first natural frequency is roughly proportional to sqrt(k/m), where k is the bending stiffness at the impeller and m the rotating mass; a stiffer, shorter shaft raises it. Many single-stage overhung pumps are designed with a stiff shaft so that the first bending critical speed lies above the maximum operating speed; the liquid in the wear-ring gaps and the bearing supports also influence the real (wet) critical speed. When a pump is converted to variable-speed operation, the manufacturer should confirm that no critical speed or structural resonance falls in the new speed range.

keyConcepts.title: Concentricity, alignment and the role of the shaft sleeve
keyConcepts.body: Seal faces and wear rings work with very small gaps, so the shaft must run true: bearing seats, sleeve seat and impeller seat must be concentric, shoulders square, and run-out within the manufacturer limits. Coupling misalignment between pump and motor imposes cyclic forces and moments on the shaft and bearings and is a common cause of vibration, bearing damage and seal leakage; alignment is checked with dial indicators or laser tools after installation and after any work on the rotating unit. In the seal area the shaft is covered by a replaceable sleeve. KSB explains that the sleeve protects the shaft from mechanical wear caused by seals and from chemical attack by aggressive liquids, that liquid entering between sleeve and shaft must not be able to escape to atmosphere (so the sleeve is sealed to the shaft), that it needs room for thermal expansion and that it should be secured against rotation and axial movement. Renewing a worn sleeve is usually much cheaper than replacing the shaft.

shaft-sealing.summary: The shaft sealing group closes the annular gap where the rotating shaft passes through the stationary casing cover, using either a mechanical seal or gland packing.
shaft-sealing.function: It limits leakage of pumped liquid to the atmosphere and, under suction lift, prevents air from being drawn into the pump. It must do this while allowing the shaft to rotate with low friction and acceptable wear. The choice of sealing method affects emissions, maintenance effort and the auxiliary flush or cooling arrangements required.
shaft-sealing.operatingPrinciple: KSB notes that shaft seals are by nature susceptible to leakage, so a claim of zero leakage is misleading. Contact-type seals restrict the leakage path by pressing a sealing element against a moving surface, with a thin liquid film between them for lubrication and cooling. KSB classifies shaft seals by the orientation of the sealing gap: in a mechanical seal the gap lies between two lapped faces at right angles to the shaft, so leakage flows radially across the face width; in gland packing the gap runs parallel to the shaft, so leakage flows axially along the sleeve through the compressed packing rings. Both generate frictional heat that must be removed by the liquid in the seal chamber or stuffing box and by any flush.
shaft-sealing.construction: The casing cover contains either a seal chamber (for the mechanical seal) or a stuffing box (for packing), with a throat at the impeller side and a face for the gland plate or gland follower at the atmospheric side. A replaceable shaft sleeve runs through the sealing area. Connections are provided for flushing or for supplying sealing liquid to a lantern ring. ISO 3069 specifies cavity dimensions for mechanical seals and for soft packing in end-suction centrifugal pumps.

materials.family: Mechanical seal materials (hard and soft face materials, elastomers, stainless metal parts)
materials.why: Allow very low leakage and long life when the seal is suited to the liquid and kept cool and clean.
materials.limitations: Sensitive to dry running, abrasives, vapour formation at the faces and shaft deflection.
materials.typicalService: Most clean and many mildly contaminated liquids; hazardous liquids may require dual seals and systems beyond this single-seal configuration.

materials.family: Compression packing (braided PTFE, graphite, carbon or aramid yarns)
materials.why: Simple, adjustable and tolerant of some shaft movement and solids when correctly flushed.
materials.limitations: Needs visible controlled leakage, periodic adjustment and causes sleeve wear; not suited where leakage to the environment is unacceptable.
materials.typicalService: Water, slurries and non-hazardous liquids where small controlled leakage is acceptable.

failureModes.cause: Worn or damaged seal faces or packing, damaged sleeve, incorrect installation.
failureModes.signs: Continuous drip or stream from the gland; liquid accumulating on the baseplate.

failureModes.cause: Lack of flush or cooling, dry running, packing over-tightened.
failureModes.signs: Hot gland, smoke or steam, discoloured parts, squealing noise.

failureModes.mode: Air ingress when the seal chamber is below atmospheric pressure
failureModes.cause: Worn packing or missing sealing liquid at the lantern ring; a damaged mechanical seal or one not suited to vacuum operation.
failureModes.signs: Loss of prime, noisy operation, falling flow.

inspection: Observe leakage, gland temperature and noise during rounds and compare with the normal condition.
Check the flush or sealing-liquid supply (pressure, flow, cleanliness).
At overhaul, inspect sleeve, seal chamber or stuffing box bore and throat for wear and corrosion.
maintenance: Follow the seal or packing manufacturer instructions for installation, run-in and adjustment.
Keep flush and auxiliary piping open and correctly connected.
Do not run the pump dry; vent the seal chamber or stuffing box before start-up.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
In this model the shaft seal is either a single mechanical seal OR gland packing; only one arrangement is installed at a time.

API 682 (and ISO 21049) cover sealing systems for centrifugal and rotary pumps in the petroleum, natural gas and chemical industries, mainly for hazardous, flammable and/or toxic services, for shaft diameters from 20 mm to 110 mm (API scope statement). They are cited here for concepts such as seal classification and piping plans, not as a requirement for this generic pump.

mechanical-seal.summary: The mechanical seal is a single, component-type end-face seal in which a spring-loaded rotating face runs against a stationary seat to seal the shaft where it leaves the casing cover.
mechanical-seal.function: It reduces leakage along the shaft to a very small amount, which KSB notes escapes to atmosphere as vapour or droplets, while allowing rotation. It replaces the long axial leakage path along packing with a short radial leakage path across an extremely narrow gap between two precisely lapped faces perpendicular to the shaft. It needs a stable liquid film between the faces and a cool, clean seal chamber environment, often provided by a flush.
mechanical-seal.operatingPrinciple: One face rotates with the shaft and the other is fixed in the gland plate; their contact surfaces are perpendicular to the shaft and lapped very flat. Springs push the faces together, and the seal chamber pressure acting on the seal adds a hydraulic closing force. A thin film of liquid, formed by the process liquid or an external liquid, separates the faces partially or fully, lubricating and cooling them. O-rings seal the faces to the shaft sleeve and to the gland, and allow the spring-loaded face to follow small axial movements and wear. Friction in the film generates heat that is carried away by the liquid in the seal chamber.
mechanical-seal.construction: This variant is a single, inside-mounted component seal: the retainer (drive collar) is fixed to the shaft sleeve by set screws, carries the springs and drives the rotating face, which is sealed to the sleeve by its secondary O-ring; the stationary seat with its O-ring sits in the gland plate, which is bolted to the face of the seal chamber with a gasket. A flush connection in the gland plate introduces liquid near the faces. Many plants use pre-assembled cartridge seals instead, which come on their own sleeve and are pre-set; this is a manufacturer and user variation.

materials.family: Face pair: carbon graphite against silicon carbide (hard/soft)
materials.why: Carbon graphite is self-lubricating and conformable; paired with a hard ceramic it gives low friction and low leakage in clean liquids.
materials.limitations: Carbon is damaged by abrasive particles and can blister or chip; chemical compatibility of impregnants must be checked.
materials.typicalService: Clean water, light hydrocarbons and many clean process liquids.

materials.family: Face pair: hard against hard (silicon carbide or tungsten carbide pairs)
materials.why: Resists abrasion where solids may reach the faces; the John Crane tutorial summarised by Turbomachinery Magazine notes that two hard faces are usually necessary in crude oil service.
materials.limitations: Higher friction and poorer tolerance of dry running or marginal lubrication than hard/soft pairs; grades are selected by the seal maker.
materials.typicalService: Liquids with some solids or higher viscosity, as specified by the seal maker.

materials.family: Elastomer secondary seals (for example NBR, EPDM, FKM, FFKM) with springs of stainless spring steel or corrosion-resistant alloy
materials.why: Seal the faces to the sleeve and gland and provide the closing force.
materials.limitations: Elastomer compatibility with the liquid and temperature is often the limiting factor of the whole seal.
materials.typicalService: Selected to match the pumped liquid.

failureModes.mode: Dry running and thermal damage of faces
failureModes.cause: Pump started unprimed, seal chamber not vented, vapour formation at the faces, flush failure.
failureModes.signs: Squealing, smoke, sudden leakage; heat-check cracks, blistering or glazing on faces.

failureModes.cause: Solids entering the face gap; unsuitable face pair.
failureModes.signs: Gradually increasing leakage; grooved or scored faces.

failureModes.cause: Chemical attack, excessive temperature, damage during installation, hang-up of the dynamic O-ring.
failureModes.signs: Leakage that starts after installation or after a process change; swollen, hardened or cut O-rings.

failureModes.mode: Face opening or chipping from mechanical causes
failureModes.cause: Excessive shaft deflection or run-out, misalignment, vibration, cavitation.
failureModes.signs: Intermittent leakage that varies with operating point; chipped face edges.

failureModes.cause: Springs clogged by solids or crystals, corrosion, incorrect setting length.
failureModes.signs: Leakage at low pressure or standstill.

inspection: Check leakage, gland plate temperature and noise during routine rounds.
Verify flush flow (for example by line temperature or a flow indicator where fitted) and that the orifice is not blocked.
On disassembly, inspect faces for wear track, cracks, chips and heat checking, and O-rings for swelling, hardening and cuts.
Check shaft run-out and seal chamber face squareness against OEM and seal-maker limits before installing a new seal.
maintenance: Replace the seal as a matched set (faces, O-rings and springs) or send it to the seal maker for refurbishment.
Set the working length exactly as specified on the seal drawing for component seals; cartridge seals are set by their setting clips.
Keep faces clean during assembly and lubricate O-rings only with a lubricant compatible with the elastomer and the liquid.
Fill and vent the pump and seal chamber completely before start-up; do not run the seal dry.

keyConcepts.title: How a mechanical seal prevents leakage, and why two faces
keyConcepts.body: Without a seal, liquid under pressure in the casing would escape along the gap between the rotating shaft and the stationary cover. A mechanical seal closes this gap with two sealing rings that meet in a plane perpendicular to the shaft: one turns with the shaft, the other is held stationary in the gland. EagleBurgmann lists the basic parts: a rotating face, a secondary seal between that face and the shaft, a stationary seat, a secondary seal between the seat and the housing, and a spring that loads the faces together. Two separate faces are needed because one part must rotate and one must stay still; sealing then happens across their contact plane, where the relative motion is pure sliding. The faces are lapped very flat so the remaining leakage gap is extremely narrow (KSB notes that a gap width below 1 micrometre is normally assumed when leakage is calculated); leakage is much smaller than with packing but, as KSB notes, never exactly zero. Everywhere else in the seal, sealing is static or nearly static and is done by O-rings.

keyConcepts.title: Face interaction: the lubricating film
keyConcepts.body: The two faces do not simply rub dry. EagleBurgmann explains that correct operation depends first and foremost on a lubricating film between the sliding faces, supplied by the process liquid or an external liquid, which both lubricates and cools them. Its thickness and distribution depend on the liquid, the sealing pressure, temperature, sliding velocity and the face material pair. Depending on these, the faces run in full-film, mixed or boundary friction. EagleBurgmann describes full-film running as wear-free but with very high leakage, and boundary friction, with a very thin and frequently interrupted film, as giving moderate wear with minimal leakage; it states that boundary friction should be the aim for seals with sliding velocities up to 20 m/s and pressures up to 50 bar. If the film is lost, for example by dry running or by liquid flashing to vapour between hot faces, friction and temperature rise sharply and the faces can crack, blister or wear rapidly. This is why venting the seal chamber and keeping the faces cool are as important as the seal hardware itself.

keyConcepts.title: Spring loading and secondary sealing elements
keyConcepts.body: Springs provide the closing force that keeps the faces in contact when the pump is not pressurised; EagleBurgmann notes that without spring backing an unpressurised seal would open. Options include a single coil spring, several small springs or metal bellows, normally made from stainless spring steel or more corrosion-resistant alloys. In operation the seal chamber pressure acting on the seal adds a hydraulic closing force, opposed by the pressure of the film in the face gap. KSB characterises this with a load factor k, the ratio of the hydraulically loaded area to the face area: in an unbalanced seal the face carries the full sealed pressure, while in a balanced seal a step on the shaft or sleeve makes only part of it act axially. A smaller k lowers face load and heat but raises leakage, and too small a k can open the faces; KSB notes only balanced seals are used at high pressures and sliding velocities. The secondary seals (here O-rings) seal the rotating face to the sleeve and the seat to the gland. The O-ring on the spring-loaded face must slide slightly on the sleeve so that the face can follow wear, thermal growth and small axial shaft movements; if it sticks (hang-up), the faces can open.

keyConcepts.title: Heat generation at the faces
keyConcepts.body: Sliding friction between the faces converts power into heat at the face contact. A simple estimate is P_f = f*F_c*v_m, where f is the effective coefficient of friction of the face pair, F_c the total closing force (spring plus net hydraulic force) and v_m the sliding velocity at the mean face diameter d_m (v_m = pi*d_m*n/60). EagleBurgmann describes the total power consumption of a seal as the sum of friction losses, turbulence losses from the rotating parts churning the liquid, and the power of any pumping device. All of this heat must be carried away by the liquid around the seal and by conduction into the seal parts. If the temperature at the faces approaches the boiling point of the liquid at seal chamber pressure, the film can flash to vapour, leading to unstable running, face damage and leakage. Higher speed, higher pressure, larger diameter and poor face lubrication all increase heat generation.

keyConcepts.title: Why flushing or cooling may be required: seal piping plans
keyConcepts.body: Without a flush, the seal chamber of an end-suction pump can be a relatively stagnant space behind the impeller, where heat, vapour and solids accumulate around the seal; KSB notes that the temperature in the sealing gap is generally higher than the liquid temperature in the seal housing. A flush continuously replaces this liquid. API 682 classifies seal configurations and, in a normative annex, defines standard seal piping plans; John Crane states that the 4th edition defines 32 plans and describes Plan 11 as the most used. In Plan 11 a line connects the pump discharge to the seal chamber; an orifice in the line reduces the flow rate (John Crane adds that it protects the seal from full discharge pressure). The flush enters close to the faces, where it removes friction heat, helps lubricate the faces and keeps the area clean. Plan 11 relies on the pumped liquid being a suitable flush; according to John Crane, other plans may be needed when the liquid is too hot, contains abrasive particles, or for dual seals with buffer or barrier systems. The required plan is defined by the seal maker and the pump specification, not by the seal hardware alone.

API 682 (and ISO 21049) cover sealing systems for centrifugal and rotary pumps in the petroleum, natural gas and chemical industries, mainly for hazardous, flammable and/or toxic services, for shaft diameters from 20 mm to 110 mm (API scope statement). They are cited here for concepts such as seal classification and piping plans, not as a requirement for this generic pump.
A Plan 11 flush is assumed for teaching; the actual plan depends on the liquid and is specified by the seal maker and purchaser.

gland-packing.summary: Gland packing (soft packing) seals the shaft with several rings of braided compression packing held in a stuffing box and compressed by an adjustable gland follower, with a lantern ring for flushing.
gland-packing.function: It throttles the leakage along the shaft sleeve to a small, controlled amount that lubricates and cools the packing. Under suction lift, with a sealing liquid supplied through the lantern ring, it also prevents air from entering the pump. It is the alternative variant to the mechanical seal in this model; only one of the two is installed.
gland-packing.operatingPrinciple: Tightening the gland follower compresses the packing rings axially, and the packing expands radially against the shaft sleeve and the stuffing box bore. Leakage must pass along these contact surfaces and through the packing, losing pressure across the series of rings. A controlled leakage forms a liquid film between packing and sleeve that removes friction heat; stopping the leakage completely can make the packing burn, harden and damage the sleeve (FSA/ESA installation guidance). As the packing loses volume during service, periodic re-tightening of the gland restores the sealing force.
gland-packing.construction: In this variant the stuffing box in the casing cover contains a set of packing rings with a lantern ring (seal cage) positioned under a flush connection. The gland follower is drawn in by two gland studs and nuts. The packing runs on a replaceable shaft sleeve. A throat at the bottom of the box limits extrusion of packing towards the impeller. The FSA/ESA manual gives guideline stuffing box depths in multiples of the packing cross-section W (about 7W with a lantern ring and 5W without) and recommends consulting the packing maker for the actual arrangement.

materials.family: PTFE and expanded PTFE (ePTFE) yarn packings
materials.why: Chemically resistant and low-friction; suitable for many chemicals and clean liquids.
materials.limitations: Lower thermal conductivity and a tendency to cold flow and extrude at higher temperature or pressure.
materials.typicalService: Chemical and clean process liquids at moderate temperature and speed.

materials.family: Carbon or graphite yarn and flexible graphite packings
materials.why: High thermal conductivity, low friction and inertness to most chemicals.
materials.limitations: Flexible graphite is fragile and susceptible to wear in abrasive service; some grades need corrosion inhibitors.
materials.typicalService: Hot water, steam condensate and many chemical services.

materials.family: Aramid yarn packings (often combined with PTFE or graphite)
materials.why: High strength and resistance to abrasion and extrusion.
materials.limitations: Can wear shaft sleeves; pH range limited according to fibre type.
materials.typicalService: Abrasive liquids and slurries where a flush is provided.

failureModes.cause: Worn or consolidated packing that can no longer be adjusted; grooved sleeve.
failureModes.signs: Leakage that does not respond to gland adjustment; gland bottomed out.

failureModes.cause: Gland over-tightened, leakage stopped completely, flush missing.
failureModes.signs: Hot or smoking gland, hardened and glazed packing, discoloured sleeve.

failureModes.cause: Friction, abrasive particles embedded in packing, loss of lubricant.
failureModes.signs: Groove worn into the sleeve under the packing.

failureModes.cause: No or low sealing-liquid pressure at the lantern ring.
failureModes.signs: Loss of prime, noisy pump, rapid packing and sleeve wear in slurry service.

inspection: Check leakage rate, gland temperature and that the follower is square and not bottomed out.
Check flush or sealing-liquid pressure and flow at the lantern ring connection.
At repacking, inspect the sleeve for grooves and run-out and the stuffing box bore for wear.
maintenance: Adjust the gland gradually and evenly in small steps, allowing time for the packing to settle between adjustments.
Repack when adjustment no longer controls leakage; do not add extra rings on top of old packing (FSA/ESA guidance).
Remove all old packing, cut new rings to size (preferably on a mandrel of shaft diameter), install one ring at a time with joints staggered, and reposition the lantern ring under the flush port.
Allow generous leakage during run-in, then reduce gradually to the level recommended by the packing maker.

keyConcepts.title: How compression packing seals
keyConcepts.body: Compression packing consists of separate rings of relatively soft, braided material placed in the annular space (stuffing box) between the shaft sleeve and the casing cover. When the gland follower is tightened, the axial load makes the rings expand radially against the sleeve and the bore. Leakage has to pass along the sleeve surface and through the packing structure, and the pressure drops progressively across the ring set. The radial contact pressure is not uniform: the FSA/ESA manual shows that most of the sealing force is developed by the rings nearest the gland (it states about 70 % from the first two rings). The packing relies on a fluid film between it and the moving sleeve; the film comes from leakage of pumped liquid, a flush, or lubricants built into the packing. Unlike a mechanical seal, packing is adjustable: KSB notes that, unlike other shaft seals, it can be readjusted, and the FSA/ESA manual describes compensating the gradual loss of packing volume by further gland take-up.

keyConcepts.title: Why controlled leakage is required
keyConcepts.body: Friction between packing and the rotating sleeve generates heat continuously. The leaking liquid carries this heat away and lubricates the contact; if the gland is tightened until leakage stops, the packing overheats, its lubricants are lost, it hardens and it wears the sleeve rapidly. The FSA/ESA installation guidance therefore says not to stop leakage entirely, to allow the packing to leak freely when a newly packed pump is started, and then to take up the gland gradually to a tolerable level; it suggests about 8-10 drops per minute per inch (25.4 mm) of shaft diameter as a preferred level, while noting that some packings can run nearly leak-free and that the packing maker should be consulted. One packing manufacturer (Chesterton, for its product 1760) specifies a slow run-in starting with considerably higher leakage and warns never to let the box heat up. Because leakage is visible and continuous, packing is generally used where a small leakage of the liquid is acceptable.

keyConcepts.title: Lantern ring and flush
keyConcepts.body: A lantern ring (seal cage) is a perforated or grooved spacer placed between packing rings and aligned with a connection in the stuffing box. Clean liquid supplied through it spreads around the shaft and flows partly towards the pump and partly out through the outer rings. This keeps abrasive particles out of the packing, cools and lubricates it, and under suction lift prevents air from being drawn in. The FSA/ESA manual advises a flush pressure at least 1 bar above the stuffing box pressure and gives an approximation for the stuffing box pressure of end-suction pumps: SBP = p_s + 0.25*TDH, where p_s is suction pressure and TDH the total dynamic head expressed as pressure; with balance holes in the impeller the stuffing box pressure is close to suction pressure. The lantern ring must stay under the inlet as the packing is compressed, so its position is set during installation.

keyConcepts.title: Sleeve wear and gland adjustment
keyConcepts.body: Packing rubs continuously on the sleeve, so sleeve wear is unavoidable; abrasive particles embedded in the packing and loss of packing lubricant accelerate it. A replaceable sleeve, rather than the shaft itself, therefore runs under the packing. Gland adjustment should be gradual and even on both studs so the follower stays square; uneven tightening cocks the follower, overloads one side and can bring the follower into contact with the sleeve. As the packing consolidates, each adjustment restores the sealing force until the follower approaches the stuffing box face. The FSA/ESA manual states that packing should be replaced when the frequency of adjustment increases or leakage can no longer be controlled by gland take-up, and that extra rings must not be added on top of old packing.

keyConcepts.title: Packing versus mechanical seal in this model
keyConcepts.body: Gland packing and the mechanical seal are alternative solutions for the same task; the model shows one or the other, never both. The mechanical seal seals across two lapped faces perpendicular to the shaft, needs no adjustment and gives very low leakage, but it is sensitive to dry running, solids and shaft deflection. Packing seals along the shaft sleeve, needs visible controlled leakage and periodic adjustment, and wears the sleeve, but it is simple, can be adjusted in service and tolerates some shaft movement. The FSA/ESA manual notes that mechanical seals are usually chosen where near-zero leakage is critical (for example toxic or flammable liquids), while packing is often chosen for its simplicity and reliability in services such as liquids with solids. KSB gives an example for a volute casing pump at 20 m/s sliding speed and 15 bar: about 5-8 l/h leakage with gland packing against roughly 6 cm3/h with a mechanical seal. ISO 3069 specifies cavity dimensions for both in end-suction pumps; some pumps can be converted from one to the other where the OEM supplies the parts.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
In this model the shaft seal is either a single mechanical seal OR gland packing; only one arrangement is installed at a time.
Leakage and flush values quoted from the FSA/ESA manual and Chesterton are general or product-specific guidance; the packing maker and OEM instructions govern a specific installation.

volute-casing.summary: The volute casing is the spiral, pressure-containing housing that surrounds the impeller, collects the liquid it discharges and leads it to the discharge nozzle.
volute-casing.function: It contains the pumped liquid at discharge pressure and provides the suction and discharge connections to the piping. Its spiral channel collects the flow leaving the impeller around the full circumference and decelerates it, so that part of the kinetic energy is converted into static pressure. It also carries the casing feet, the register for the casing cover and the seat for the casing wear ring.
volute-casing.operatingPrinciple: The impeller discharges liquid around its whole periphery with a high absolute velocity that has a large circumferential (swirl) component. The volute cross-section grows from the tongue towards the throat because each section must carry the flow accumulated from all impeller sectors upstream of it; a common design rule sizes the sections so that the swirl follows roughly constant angular momentum (c_u*r approximately constant), so the velocity in the volute is lower than at the impeller outlet. Beyond the throat the discharge nozzle widens further at constant flow and acts as a diffuser. Because mean velocity equals flow divided by area (c = Q/A), a larger area for the flow carried means a lower velocity, and the velocity energy given up appears as a rise in static pressure, less friction and mixing losses. The geometry is matched to the impeller at one flow rate, the best efficiency point (BEP); at other flows the mismatch causes extra losses and an unbalanced radial force on the impeller.
volute-casing.construction: The casing is normally a one-piece casting that incorporates the volute, tongue, suction nozzle, top centreline discharge nozzle and feet. In this radially split, back-pull-out design the drive-side opening is closed by a separate casing cover, centred in a machined register and clamped with studs over a gasket. Other machined surfaces are the flange faces, the bore for the casing wear ring and the foot mounting faces; tapped holes are provided for drain, vent and pressure-tapping connections. Wall thickness must satisfy the pressure rating and hydrostatic test pressure at temperature, plus a corrosion allowance, and must also respect the minimum section that can be reliably cast.

materials.why: Good castability, machinability and vibration damping at low cost; widely used for clean water and similar non-aggressive liquids.
materials.limitations: Brittle, with low tensile strength and poor resistance to thermal and mechanical shock; limited corrosion and erosion resistance. Pressure-temperature limits are set by the OEM and applicable codes.
materials.typicalService: Clean cold or moderately warm water, HVAC and general building services.

materials.why: Considerably higher strength and ductility than grey iron with similar castability, giving better tolerance of pressure, pipe loads and shock.
materials.limitations: Corrosion and erosion resistance similar to other cast irons; not suitable for acidic, chloride-rich or abrasive service without assessment.
materials.typicalService: Water and general industrial liquids where higher pressure capability or robustness is needed.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in many chemical, food and process liquids; good ductility and toughness.
materials.limitations: Susceptible to pitting, crevice corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking in warm chloride-containing liquids; relatively soft, so limited erosion resistance; higher cost.
materials.typicalService: Mildly corrosive process liquids, hygienic and chemical service within verified limits.

materials.why: Higher strength and generally better resistance to chloride pitting, stress corrosion cracking and erosion-corrosion than standard austenitic grades; KSB names duplex steels as casing materials for highly corrosive service such as seawater desalination.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; casting, heat treatment and any weld repair must be well controlled; upper temperature limits apply.
materials.typicalService: Seawater, brackish water and chloride-containing process liquids, subject to verification.

failureModes.cause: Excessive pipe forces and moments, freezing of liquid left in the casing, water hammer, thermal shock or casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Weeping or leakage through the wall, visible cracks, failed hydrostatic test.

failureModes.mode: Erosion and corrosion of the volute passages
failureModes.cause: Abrasive solids, high local velocities near tongue and throat, unsuitable material for the liquid.
failureModes.signs: Gradual loss of head and efficiency; roughened, thinned or pitted walls at overhaul.

failureModes.cause: Piping not supported independently or forced into alignment with the nozzles.
failureModes.signs: Coupling misalignment that recurs after realignment, wear-ring rubbing, rising vibration, seal leakage.

failureModes.cause: Prolonged operation at low flow or overload with a single volute.
failureModes.signs: Higher vibration and shaft deflection, wear-ring and seal damage, bearing distress.

inspection: Check for external leakage, cracks and corrosion at flanges, joints and connections during routine rounds.
Trend suction and discharge pressure, flow and power to detect performance loss that may indicate internal erosion or wear-ring wear.

At overhaul, inspect volute passages, tongue and throat for erosion, corrosion and cavitation pitting; measure remaining wall thickness (for example by ultrasonic gauging) where wall loss is suspected.
Check the cover register, gasket face and wear-ring bore for damage and correct fit according to OEM data.
When flanges are connected or disconnected, check that the pipework does not spring out of position, which would indicate nozzle loads.
maintenance: Drain the casing when out of service in freezing conditions, or where the liquid may solidify or become corrosive at standstill.
Renew the casing wear ring when the running clearance exceeds the OEM limit; repair or replace the casing if wall loss exceeds the allowance determined by the OEM.
Clean gasket and register faces, fit a new gasket and tighten casing fasteners in the OEM sequence and torque.
After weld repairs or other major repairs, apply the hydrostatic test and procedures required by the OEM and the applicable specification.
Operate within the OEM allowable operating range around BEP to limit radial thrust, recirculation and erosion.

keyConcepts.title: How the casing surrounds the impeller and collects the flow
keyConcepts.body: The volute casing encloses the impeller completely, so the pumped liquid is contained and guided from inlet to outlet. On the suction side the casing forms the inlet nozzle leading to the impeller eye; around the impeller outlet it forms a spiral channel that starts at the tongue (cutwater) and ends at the throat, where the discharge nozzle begins. Liquid leaves the impeller at every point of its circumference, so the flow carried by the volute grows with angle: at the tongue the channel carries almost nothing, and at the throat it carries the full pump flow. The cross-sectional area therefore increases steadily around the spiral. KSB describes the volute as collecting the liquid discharged by the impeller and directing it to the discharge nozzle. Narrow side gaps between the impeller shrouds and the casing walls are filled with liquid whose mean angular velocity, according to KSB, reaches about half the impeller speed; the pressure distribution in these gaps contributes to axial thrust.

keyConcepts.title: Converting velocity energy into pressure energy
keyConcepts.body: A substantial part of the energy added by the impeller leaves it as kinetic energy, because the liquid has a high absolute velocity at the impeller outlet. The system needs pressure rather than velocity, so the casing recovers part of the kinetic energy in two steps. In the spiral, the swirling flow moves to a larger radius, where its circumferential velocity is lower (approximately constant angular momentum c_u*r), and the area at each section grows in step with the flow it collects. In the discharge nozzle the area keeps growing while the flow Q stays the same, so by continuity (c = Q/A) the mean velocity falls further. Along a streamline, ignoring losses, Bernoulli gives p/(rho*g) + c^2/(2*g) = constant at constant height, so the lost velocity head appears as pressure head. The recovery is not perfect: friction, mixing and flow separation in an over-rapid expansion turn part of the kinetic energy into heat. KSB summarises the purpose of the volute as converting the kinetic energy of the flow into static pressure.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing geometry matters: performance and radial thrust
keyConcepts.body: Volute areas, especially the throat area, are matched to the impeller so that at the design flow the volute accepts the flow from the impeller with little loss; this largely fixes the flow rate at which the pump reaches its best efficiency. At BEP the pressure around the impeller outlet is nearly uniform. At lower or higher flows the volute is too large or too small for the flow, the pressure around the circumference becomes uneven, and a net radial force acts on the impeller. KSB gives the steady radial force as F_R = K*rho*g*H*D2*B2, where D2 is the impeller outside diameter, B2 the impeller outlet width and K a coefficient that depends strongly on specific speed and on Q/Q_opt; for a centred impeller the force is smallest near BEP and rises rapidly at low flow and overload. The Hydraulic Institute notes that single volutes typically show the highest radial thrust at zero flow, and that high radial thrust increases shaft deflection, shaft stress, bearing wear, seal problems and vibration. Double volutes (two partial volutes offset by 180 degrees) reduce the force; in circular (annular) casings, KSB notes, it is lowest at low flow and rises towards overload.

keyConcepts.title: Why wall thickness and material depend on pressure, temperature and service
keyConcepts.body: The casing is the main pressure boundary of the pump, so its walls must contain the maximum allowable working pressure at the maximum temperature, plus the hydrostatic test pressure applied during manufacture, with an appropriate margin. Material strength falls as temperature rises, so the same casing has a lower pressure capability when hot. To the stress-based thickness the designer adds a corrosion or erosion allowance for the expected service life and respects the minimum wall that the casting process can produce reliably. External loads from the connected piping (nozzle forces and moments) also stress the casing. KSB notes that higher pressures require thicker walls and that codes often specify materials and sometimes wall thicknesses. The pumped liquid decides the material family: corrosion (pH, chlorides, dissolved oxygen, temperature), erosion by solids and cavitation resistance all matter. For example, ISO 2858 covers end-suction pumps with a 16 bar rating, while API 610, within its petroleum and petrochemical scope, sets its own pressure-casing requirements. Actual ratings and allowances are OEM data.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.
A single volute is assumed; some manufacturers use double volutes to reduce radial thrust.

volute-tongue.summary: The volute tongue (cutwater) is the sharp-edged lip of the casing where the volute spiral begins and the discharge throat separates from the liquid circulating around the impeller.
volute-tongue.function: It divides the flow leaving the impeller into the part that passes into the discharge throat and the part that continues around the volute. Its position and shape largely set the throat area and therefore strongly influence the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency. Its radial distance from the impeller tip limits recirculation of liquid from the throat back into the volute.
volute-tongue.operatingPrinciple: At the design flow the liquid approaches the tongue roughly parallel to its surfaces and splits smoothly with low loss. At part load or overload the flow angle changes, the stagnation point moves to one side of the tongue, and local separation, recirculation and higher losses occur. Each time an impeller vane passes the tongue, the non-uniform flow leaving the vane produces a pressure pulse, so the casing experiences pulsations at the vane-pass frequency and its harmonics. These pulsations increase as the gap to the impeller is reduced, as speed increases and as operation moves away from BEP.
volute-tongue.construction: The tongue is an integral, cast feature of the volute casing, not a separate part. Its angular location, thickness, leading-edge profile and radial gap to the impeller outlet diameter are hydraulic design parameters chosen by the manufacturer to match the impeller. Trimming the impeller to a smaller diameter increases this gap. Because the tongue sits in the highest-velocity region of the casing, it is often where erosion is first seen.

materials.family: Same material as the volute casing (integral casting)
materials.why: The tongue is cast in one piece with the volute casing, so it has the same material and pressure rating as the casing.
materials.limitations: Local velocities, solids or cavitation can make this area wear faster than the rest of the casing; any upgrade (overlay, coating, different casing material) needs OEM agreement.

failureModes.cause: Abrasive solids and high local velocities.
failureModes.signs: Blunted, thinned or roughened tongue at overhaul; gradual performance change.

failureModes.cause: Too small a gap between impeller and tongue, high speed, operation away from BEP.
failureModes.signs: Tonal noise and vibration peaks at vane-pass frequency; in severe cases fatigue cracks at impeller vane tips or shrouds.

failureModes.mode: Local cavitation or recirculation damage on one side of the tongue
failureModes.cause: Operation far from BEP moves the stagnation point and creates local low-pressure and recirculation zones.
failureModes.signs: Pitting concentrated on one face of the tongue.

inspection: Include vane-pass frequency (number of impeller vanes times running speed) in vibration spectrum analysis.
At overhaul, inspect the tongue for erosion, pitting and cracks.
If the impeller diameter is changed, check the resulting gap to the tongue against OEM guidance.
maintenance: Operate within the OEM allowable operating range to limit pulsations and incidence losses at the tongue.
Restore an eroded tongue only by OEM-approved repair methods, or replace the casing.
Consult the OEM before changing impeller diameter or vane count, because both alter the tongue gap and pulsation behaviour.

keyConcepts.title: Cutwater role and the throat
keyConcepts.body: The tongue, also called the cutwater, splitter or flow divider, is where the end of the volute meets its beginning. Liquid arriving from the last impeller sectors either passes the tongue into the throat and discharge nozzle, or is carried round again into the start of the volute. The throat is the cross-section at the end of the spiral, just before the discharge diffuser; together with the impeller outlet it governs where on the flow axis the best efficiency point lies. At BEP the flow approaches the tongue at roughly the right angle. Below BEP the volute and throat are too large for the flow, and part of the liquid recirculates past the tongue back into the start of the volute; above BEP the throat becomes a restriction. In both cases the approach angle no longer matches the tongue, the stagnation point moves off its nose onto one face or the other, and local separation and losses increase. Pumps & Systems notes that the placement, length, thickness, leading-edge profile and flow angle of the cutwater all affect casing efficiency and overall pump performance, and that casing and impeller must be matched.

keyConcepts.title: Clearance to the impeller and vane-pass pressure pulsations
keyConcepts.body: The radial gap between the impeller outer diameter and the tongue is a key design parameter (often called gap B in pump literature). The flow leaving each vane channel is not uniform: there is a wake behind each vane. When a vane tip passes the tongue, the local pressure at the tongue changes abruptly, so the casing sees pressure pulses at the vane-pass frequency f_VP = z*n/60 (in Hz, with z the number of impeller vanes and n the speed in rpm) and its harmonics. Pumps & Systems reports that with too small a gap the pulses are audible, add to inefficiency, cause recirculation near the vane tips and send pressure waves upstream into the impeller, and that in high-energy pumps they can break off vane tips and shrouds; their magnitude rises as the gap is reduced, with speed and as operation moves away from BEP. KSB notes that unsteady radial forces at this frequency occur to some extent in all pump types. A larger gap reduces the pulsation, but trimming the impeller for this costs some efficiency. Gap values are manufacturer design data and are not given here.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Tongue geometry and the impeller-to-tongue gap are manufacturer design data; no values are implied by the 3D model.

suction-nozzle.summary: The suction nozzle is the flanged inlet branch of the volute casing that leads liquid axially from the suction pipe into the impeller eye.
suction-nozzle.function: It connects the pump to the suction pipe and delivers liquid to the impeller eye with as uniform a velocity profile and as little loss as practical. This matters because the pressure at the impeller inlet sets the margin against cavitation (NPSH available versus NPSH required).
suction-nozzle.operatingPrinciple: In an end-suction pump the nozzle is coaxial with the shaft, so the flow enters the eye without turning. The nozzle usually converges slightly towards the eye, accelerating the flow and helping to make the velocity profile more uniform. Any loss or disturbance here reduces the pressure available at the impeller inlet. Fittings such as elbows, valves or reducers too close upstream can create swirl and uneven inflow that degrade suction performance and increase noise and vibration.
suction-nozzle.construction: The suction nozzle is cast integrally with the volute casing and finished with a machined flange face and bolt holes to the specified flange standard. It usually carries a tapped hole for a suction pressure tapping. On end-suction pumps the suction nozzle is usually larger than the discharge nozzle. For pumps dimensioned to ISO 2858, the pump size designation is built from the nominal suction and discharge diameters and the nominal impeller diameter.

materials.family: Same material as the volute casing (integral casting)
materials.why: The suction nozzle is cast in one piece with the volute casing, so it has the same material and pressure rating as the casing.
materials.limitations: Local velocities, solids or cavitation can make this area wear faster than the rest of the casing; any upgrade (overlay, coating, different casing material) needs OEM agreement.

failureModes.mode: Flange joint leakage or air ingress
failureModes.cause: Damaged gasket or flange face, loose bolts, pipe strain; under suction lift the leak draws air inward.
failureModes.signs: External leakage, or loss of prime, noisy running and reduced flow when air is drawn in.

failureModes.cause: Unsupported or misaligned suction piping, thermal expansion of piping, water hammer.
failureModes.signs: Cracks near the flange or nozzle root, recurring misalignment.

failureModes.cause: Solids, high velocity, aggressive liquid.
failureModes.signs: Roughened or thinned nozzle bore at overhaul.

inspection: Check the suction flange for leaks and, on suction-lift installations, for air ingress.
Verify that suction piping is supported independently and aligned to the flange without forcing.
Monitor suction pressure to confirm adequate NPSH available and to detect strainer blockage.
maintenance: Fit new flange gaskets when the joint is opened and tighten bolts evenly in a cross pattern.
Keep upstream strainers clean and avoid flow-disturbing fittings close to the pump inlet, following the OEM installation instructions.
Inspect and clean the nozzle bore at overhaul.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.
Flange standard, rating and nozzle size depend on the pump size and purchaser specification.

discharge-nozzle.summary: The discharge nozzle is the flanged outlet branch at the top of the casing that leads the pumped liquid from the volute throat to the discharge pipe.
discharge-nozzle.function: It connects the pump to the discharge pipe and acts as a diffuser that continues the conversion of velocity into pressure started in the volute. With a top centreline arrangement it also helps air and gas leave the casing towards the discharge.
discharge-nozzle.operatingPrinciple: Downstream of the throat the flow area increases gradually up to the flange, so the mean velocity falls and the static pressure rises. The expansion has to be gradual: an excessive divergence angle causes flow separation, which wastes energy instead of recovering pressure. The discharge pressure measured here, corrected for velocity head and elevation, is used together with the suction pressure to determine the pump total head.
discharge-nozzle.construction: The nozzle is cast integrally with the volute casing on the vertical centreline above the shaft (top centreline discharge), with a machined flange face and a tapped hole for the discharge pressure tapping. Because it is attached to the pressure boundary at the highest-pressure point, the nozzle and its root must resist both internal pressure and the forces and moments imposed by the discharge piping.
