materials.family: Same material as the volute casing (integral casting)
materials.why: The discharge nozzle is cast in one piece with the volute casing, so it has the same material and pressure rating as the casing.
materials.limitations: Local velocities, solids or cavitation can make this area wear faster than the rest of the casing; any upgrade (overlay, coating, different casing material) needs OEM agreement.

failureModes.cause: Gasket failure, uneven bolt tightening, pipe strain, thermal cycling.
failureModes.signs: Drips or spray at the flange.

failureModes.mode: Cracking or distortion from pipe loads
failureModes.cause: Heavy or poorly supported discharge piping, thermal expansion, water hammer from valve closure or check-valve slam.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at the nozzle root, recurring misalignment, rising vibration.

failureModes.cause: High velocity combined with abrasive solids.
failureModes.signs: Local metal loss downstream of the throat at overhaul.

inspection: Check flange joints for leakage and the piping for adequate support and free thermal movement.
Monitor discharge pressure and compare with the expected value for the operating flow.
Inspect the nozzle bore for erosion during overhaul.
maintenance: Use new gaskets and even, cross-pattern bolt tightening at reassembly.
Correct pipe supports if the flange moves when bolts are released.
Avoid prolonged operation against a closed discharge valve.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.
Top centreline discharge as configured in this model; other end-suction designs use tangential or side discharge.

casing-feet.summary: The casing feet are cast supports under the volute casing that carry the casing on the baseplate and fix the height of the shaft centreline.
casing-feet.function: They carry the weight of the casing and liquid and transfer the reactions to pipe forces, hydraulic forces and torque into the baseplate. Together with the bearing-frame support they fix the position of the pump shaft for alignment to the motor. They allow the casing to stay in place when the rotating unit is pulled out.
casing-feet.operatingPrinciple: The feet are bolted to machined pads on the baseplate, and their flatness and coplanarity determine whether the casing sits without distortion. If one foot does not bear evenly (soft foot), tightening its bolt distorts the casing and bearing frame, changing alignment and internal clearances. When the casing temperature differs strongly from the baseplate, thermal growth of the casing between the feet and the shaft centreline shifts the shaft height; for hot service many designs therefore use centreline-mounted supports instead of feet under the casing.
casing-feet.construction: Here the feet are cast integrally with the volute casing below the shaft axis and machined flat on their underside, with bolt holes for hold-down bolts. Shims between feet and baseplate pads are used during alignment. Some pumps are dowelled to the baseplate after final alignment so the position can be re-established after maintenance.

materials.family: Same material as the volute casing (integral casting)
materials.why: The feet is cast in one piece with the volute casing, so it has the same material and pressure rating as the casing.
materials.limitations: Local velocities, solids or cavitation can make this area wear faster than the rest of the casing; any upgrade (overlay, coating, different casing material) needs OEM agreement.

failureModes.cause: Uneven pads, dirt or corrosion under the foot, incorrect shims.
failureModes.signs: Alignment changes when hold-down bolts are tightened; higher vibration.

failureModes.cause: Excessive pipe loads, overtightened bolts on uneven pads, impact.
failureModes.signs: Visible cracks at the foot root, loosening of the casing.

failureModes.cause: Vibration, missing locking, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Movement at the joint, fretting marks, increasing vibration.

inspection: Check soft foot with a dial indicator or feeler gauges by loosening one bolt at a time.
Check hold-down bolts for tightness and corrosion during periodic inspections.
Inspect feet for cracks after any severe pipe-load or impact event.
maintenance: Clean pads and feet and use clean, flat, corrosion-resistant shims.
Correct soft foot before final alignment, then tighten hold-down bolts to the specified torque.
Recheck alignment after maintenance, and at operating temperature if the OEM recommends it.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.
Feet under the casing are assumed; centreline-mounted casings are a manufacturer variation typical of hot process service.

casing-nameplate.summary: The casing identification plate is a permanently attached plate that records the pump identity and its rated design data.
casing-nameplate.function: It identifies the pump unambiguously for operation, spare parts and maintenance. It records the information needed to operate the pump within its design limits and to order matching spare parts. It links the physical pump to its documentation and test records.
casing-nameplate.operatingPrinciple: The plate carries data that do not change during normal service, such as manufacturer, type and size designation, serial number and the rated duty, so that personnel can check that the pump is used within its intended limits. The exact data required depend on the manufacturer, the applicable regulations and the purchaser specification; commonly listed items are rated flow and head, speed, impeller diameter, and maximum allowable pressure and temperature. For pumps dimensioned to ISO 2858 the size designation is built from the nominal suction and discharge diameters and the nominal impeller diameter.
casing-nameplate.construction: Usually a stamped or engraved corrosion-resistant metal plate fixed to the casing (or bearing frame) with drive screws or rivets in a visible position. It is not a pressure-retaining part.

materials.why: Corrosion resistant and durable, keeps stamped data legible for the life of the pump.
materials.limitations: Fixing method must avoid creating crevices or weakening the casing wall.

materials.why: Easy to engrave or stamp, low cost.
materials.limitations: Lower corrosion resistance in aggressive environments.

failureModes.cause: Corrosion, painting over, mechanical damage, loss of fixing screws.
failureModes.signs: Pump cannot be identified for spare parts or re-rating.

failureModes.cause: Impeller trimmed, speed changed or pump re-rated without updating records.
failureModes.signs: Measured performance does not match the plate data.

inspection: Check that the plate is present, legible and matches the plant records.
Confirm plate data after any re-rating or impeller change.
maintenance: Keep the plate clean and mask it during painting.
Record any modification (impeller diameter, speed, materials) in the plant documentation and, where required, obtain an updated plate from the OEM.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Required nameplate content depends on the manufacturer, applicable regulations and purchaser specification; the items listed are common examples, not a complete or mandatory list.

casing-drain.summary: The casing drain connection is a plugged or valved opening at the lowest point of the casing used to empty the pump.
casing-drain.function: It allows the casing to be emptied before maintenance, before a cold shutdown where freezing is possible, or before decontamination. For hazardous liquids it allows controlled draining to a closed system instead of spilling when the casing is opened.
casing-drain.operatingPrinciple: Liquid drains by gravity from the lowest point of the volute when the pump is isolated and the vent is opened to admit air. In service the drain is closed and is part of the pressure boundary, so the plug or valve must withstand the full casing pressure.
casing-drain.construction: A tapped or flanged boss at the bottom of the volute, closed by a threaded plug with a sealing washer or thread sealant, or by a valve and piping to a drain system. Thread type and size are manufacturer data.

materials.family: Carbon steel or cast iron plug (with cast iron casings)
materials.why: Compatible with the casing material and low cost.
materials.limitations: Can corrode and seize in the thread; not suitable for corrosive liquids.

materials.why: Corrosion resistant and reusable.
materials.limitations: Galling risk in stainless threads; galvanic effects in cast iron casings must be considered.

failureModes.cause: Damaged thread or sealing washer, insufficient tightening, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Drips under the casing.

failureModes.cause: Corrosion in the thread, overtightening.
failureModes.signs: Plug cannot be removed; damaged thread.

failureModes.cause: Solids settling at the low point.
failureModes.signs: Casing does not empty when the drain is opened.

inspection: Check for leakage at the drain during rounds.
Before opening the pump, confirm through the drain that the casing is empty and depressurised.
maintenance: Use a new sealing washer or an appropriate thread sealant compatible with the liquid when refitting the plug.
Route drains of hazardous liquids to a closed drain system according to plant procedures.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.

casing-vent.summary: The casing vent connection is a plugged or valved opening at a high point of the casing that releases trapped air or gas.
casing-vent.function: It lets air or gas escape while the pump and suction line are filled before start-up (priming), so the impeller is fully flooded. It also allows gas that collects during operation or after standstill to be released.
casing-vent.operatingPrinciple: The pressure rise produced by an impeller at a given speed is proportional to the density of the fluid in it, so a centrifugal pump that is not self-priming cannot develop useful pressure while its casing is full of air; gas at the seal faces can also cause dry running. KSB notes that centrifugal pumps in suction head (positive inlet pressure) operation are equipped with a vent valve or manually operated air vent at the apex of the casing, so that the pump can be primed before start-up. In common practice the vent is opened during filling until liquid free of air bubbles emerges. A top centreline discharge also helps gas leave the volute towards the discharge pipe.
casing-vent.construction: A tapped boss at a high point of the casing, closed by a plug or a small vent valve and sometimes piped to a safe location. For hot or hazardous liquids the vent must discharge to a collection system and not towards personnel.

materials.family: Carbon steel plug or valve body (with cast iron casings)
materials.why: Compatible with cast iron casings and low cost.
materials.limitations: Corrosion and seizure in threads.

materials.why: Corrosion resistant and reusable.
materials.limitations: Galling risk in threads; galvanic effects with cast iron.

failureModes.cause: Vent not opened during filling, blocked vent.
failureModes.signs: Pump fails to deliver after start, noisy running, seal overheating.

failureModes.cause: Damaged thread or seal, vent valve not fully closed.
failureModes.signs: Drips or spray at the top of the casing.

failureModes.cause: Venting hot, toxic or flammable liquid without a closed system.
failureModes.signs: Release of liquid or vapour to the work area.

inspection: Confirm the casing is vented before every start-up after draining or maintenance.
Check the vent for leakage during rounds.
maintenance: Keep the vent clear and the plug or valve sealing in good condition.
Pipe vents of hazardous or hot liquids to a safe location according to plant procedures.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.

suction-pressure-tapping.summary: The suction pressure tapping is a small tapped connection on the suction nozzle for a pressure gauge or transmitter.
suction-pressure-tapping.function: It allows measurement of the static pressure at the pump inlet. The reading is used to check NPSH available, to calculate pump total head together with the discharge pressure, and to detect suction-side problems such as a blocked strainer or a falling suction level.
suction-pressure-tapping.operatingPrinciple: A small hole drilled normal to the nozzle wall senses the static pressure of the flowing liquid. The total head of the pump is H = (p_d - p_s)/(rho*g) + (z_d - z_s) + (c_d^2 - c_s^2)/(2*g), where p is static pressure, z the gauge elevation and c the mean velocity at the measuring point, with index s for suction and d for discharge. For acceptance testing, ISO 9906 defines the measurement arrangement in the test circuit; readings from casing tappings on site are useful for monitoring and trending but are not equivalent to an acceptance test.
suction-pressure-tapping.construction: A threaded boss on the suction nozzle, closed by a plug when not used, or fitted with an isolation valve and a gauge or transmitter. A pulsation damper (snubber) may be added to steady the reading.

materials.family: Stainless steel plug, valve and instrument fittings
materials.why: Corrosion resistant and compatible with instrument fittings.
materials.limitations: Galvanic effects with cast iron casings; galling in threads.

materials.family: Carbon steel plug (with cast iron casings)
materials.why: Low cost and compatible with cast iron.
materials.limitations: Corrosion of thread and plug in wet conditions.

failureModes.cause: Solids, scale or deposits in the small bore.
failureModes.signs: Gauge does not respond to changes in operation.

failureModes.cause: Damaged thread or fitting; under suction lift air is drawn in.
failureModes.signs: Drips, or bubbles and unsteady pump operation under vacuum.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations, pressure surges, freezing.
failureModes.signs: Erratic or stuck readings.

inspection: Compare readings with expected suction conditions and with previous trends.
Check fittings for leakage and the gauge for damage.
maintenance: Fit an isolation valve so the instrument can be changed without draining the pump.
Clear blocked tappings with the pump isolated and depressurised; calibrate instruments periodically.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Tapping size and position are manufacturer data.

discharge-pressure-tapping.summary: The discharge pressure tapping is a small tapped connection on the discharge nozzle for a pressure gauge or transmitter.
discharge-pressure-tapping.function: It allows measurement of the static pressure at the pump outlet. Together with the suction pressure, it gives the pump total head and therefore the operating point on the pump curve. Changes over time can reveal wear, blockage or system changes.
discharge-pressure-tapping.operatingPrinciple: The tapping senses the static pressure at the wall of the discharge nozzle. Total head follows from H = (p_d - p_s)/(rho*g) + (z_d - z_s) + (c_d^2 - c_s^2)/(2*g). With a known flow, a lower head than expected at the same speed can indicate internal wear (for example increased wear-ring clearance) or a damaged impeller, once instrument errors, gas in the liquid and cavitation have been ruled out. Because the tapping sits close to the volute and diffuser, the reading can fluctuate at vane-pass frequency; damping is often used for a steady indication.
discharge-pressure-tapping.construction: A threaded boss on the discharge nozzle closed by a plug or fitted with an isolation valve and an instrument. A snubber or needle valve may be used to damp pulsations.

materials.family: Stainless steel plug, valve and instrument fittings
materials.why: Corrosion resistant and suitable for the full discharge pressure.
materials.limitations: Galvanic effects with cast iron casings; galling in threads.

materials.family: Carbon steel plug (with cast iron casings)
materials.why: Low cost and compatible with cast iron.
materials.limitations: Corrosion in wet conditions.

failureModes.cause: Solids, scale or deposits.
failureModes.signs: Reading does not change with operating point.

failureModes.cause: Damaged thread, fitting or gauge.
failureModes.signs: Drips or spray at the connection.

failureModes.cause: Pressure surges (water hammer), pulsations, freezing.
failureModes.signs: Erratic reading or damaged gauge.

inspection: Trend discharge pressure against flow and compare with the pump curve.
Check fittings and gauges for leakage and damage.
maintenance: Use an isolation valve and pulsation damper for long instrument life.
Calibrate instruments periodically and clear blocked tappings with the pump isolated.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Tapping size and position are manufacturer data.

casing-wear-ring.summary: The casing wear ring is a renewable stationary ring fitted in the casing opposite the impeller eye, forming a close running clearance with the impeller wear ring.
casing-wear-ring.function: It throttles the leakage of high-pressure liquid from the volute back to the impeller eye, maintaining volumetric efficiency. It is a sacrificial, replaceable part, so wear at the clearance does not require repair of the casing itself. The liquid in the narrow gap also provides some radial support to the rotor.
casing-wear-ring.operatingPrinciple: The pressure in front of the front shroud near the eye neck is well above suction pressure, while the eye is at suction pressure. This pressure difference drives a leakage flow through the annular gap between the casing ring and the impeller ring. The narrow gap creates a high flow resistance, so only a small leakage passes. As the clearance grows through wear, leakage rises and head, flow and efficiency fall. KSB describes such clearance gaps as controlled gap seals whose width and shape are chosen to limit leakage while avoiding contact under thermal expansion, shaft deflection and vibration.
casing-wear-ring.construction: The ring is pressed or shrunk into a machined bore in the casing at the suction side and secured against rotation, for example by an interference fit plus screws, dowels or tack welding, depending on the manufacturer. Its bore is machined to give the specified diametral clearance with the impeller ring. Plain, stepped or grooved (labyrinth) profiles are used. In this model the casing wear ring is fitted only with the closed impeller; in the open-impeller comparison the vanes run against the casing wall (or a wear plate) instead.

materials.why: Good tolerance of occasional contact and low galling tendency against steel or iron impeller rings.
materials.limitations: Limited abrasion resistance and corrosion limits in some waters and chemicals.

materials.why: Low cost and reasonable wear behaviour in clean water.
materials.limitations: Corrosion; risk of seizure if contact occurs.
materials.typicalService: Clean water with cast iron casings.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance plus higher wear resistance; a hardness difference to the mating ring reduces galling risk.
materials.limitations: Stainless-to-stainless pairs can gall and seize on contact; within its scope, API 610 gives minimum running clearances for metal wear rings (as summarised by Pumps & Systems).

materials.why: Used by some manufacturers and users to allow reduced clearances with lower seizure risk.
materials.limitations: Temperature, chemical and pressure limits of the polymer; must be approved by the OEM.
materials.typicalService: Selected process services after OEM review.

failureModes.cause: Abrasive particles, corrosion, normal running-in.
failureModes.signs: Falling head and efficiency at the same speed and flow; increased power per unit flow.

failureModes.cause: Shaft deflection at low or high flow, misalignment, thermal distortion, dry running, incompatible material pair.
failureModes.signs: Noise, sudden load increase, smeared or torn ring surfaces, possible pump seizure.

failureModes.mode: Ring loosening or rotation in its bore
failureModes.cause: Loss of interference fit through corrosion or thermal cycling, failed locking.
failureModes.signs: Fretting marks in the bore, ring displaced, increased leakage.

inspection: Trend head, flow and power to detect leakage growth between overhauls.
At overhaul, measure ring bore diameter and impeller ring diameter at several positions and compare the clearance with the OEM new and maximum values.
Check the ring for rub marks, galling, cracks and secure fit in the casing.
maintenance: Replace casing and impeller rings together when the clearance exceeds the OEM limit, machining new rings to the OEM-specified clearance.
Secure the new ring against rotation using the OEM method.
Investigate the cause of any rubbing (deflection, alignment, operating point) before restarting.

keyConcepts.title: Running clearance, internal recirculation leakage and volumetric efficiency
keyConcepts.body: The wear-ring gap is the main internal leakage path of a closed impeller. The pressure difference across it, a large part of the static pressure rise of the impeller, drives a leakage flow that can be estimated like an orifice: Q_L = mu*A_gap*sqrt(2*dp/rho), with A_gap = pi*D_gap*s, where s is the radial clearance, D_gap the gap diameter and mu a flow coefficient that depends on gap length, roughness and Reynolds number. KSB notes that this clearance flow returns to the suction side and that the corresponding loss falls roughly in proportion to the gap width. Because the impeller must pump Q + Q_L to deliver Q, the volumetric efficiency is eta_v = Q/(Q + Q_L). The returning leakage also disturbs the inflow at the eye. KSB and Pumps & Systems point out that clearance effects are most significant for low specific-speed pumps, where the pressure difference is high and leakage is large relative to the delivered flow. Note that wear-ring clearances are usually quoted as diametral values; the radial running clearance s is half of that.

keyConcepts.title: Choosing the clearance: why it cannot simply be minimised
keyConcepts.body: A smaller clearance reduces leakage but increases the risk of contact. KSB lists the factors that limit how small the gap can be: shaft deflection, vibration, the type of liquid, contamination and abrasive particle size, temperature, and different thermal expansion of rotating and stationary parts during start-up. Contact between two metal rings, especially similar stainless steels, can cause galling and seizure, which is why manufacturers specify material pairs, hardness differences or non-galling materials. Pumps & Systems notes that the API 610 chart for petroleum-industry pumps gives minimum, not maximum, clearances, because tighter clearances would risk contact. The pressure drop across the gap also produces a centring restoring force on the rotor (the Lomakin effect, which KSB describes as essential for smooth running), adding stiffness and damping; KSB notes that grooved, honeycomb or cellular gap surfaces reduce leakage but weaken this centring force. The clearance value is therefore a balanced manufacturer design choice.

keyConcepts.title: Wear and replacement
keyConcepts.body: Clearance grows over time through abrasion by solids, erosion-corrosion, rubbing during off-design operation and corrosion. As it grows, leakage rises, the head-flow curve drops, efficiency falls and, because the rings lose part of their centring effect, vibration can increase. The Hydraulic Institute guidance on efficiency prediction includes an estimate (based on HI 20.3) of the efficiency decrease caused by increased wearing-ring clearance, illustrating that the effect is significant and predictable. In practice, operators trend head, flow and power and measure the clearance at overhaul; when it exceeds the OEM maximum, both rings are replaced and machined to the OEM new clearance. Renewing the rings is usually one of the most cost-effective ways to recover the performance lost to internal leakage in a worn closed-impeller pump, although it does not repair other damage such as impeller erosion.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.
API 610 covers pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry services; it is not automatically applicable to general water or building-services pumps.

casing-fasteners.summary: The casing studs and nuts clamp the casing cover to the volute casing and keep the casing joint pressure-tight.
casing-fasteners.function: They provide the clamping force that compresses the casing gasket and holds the cover against the internal pressure. They also maintain the register fit that keeps the cover and rotating unit concentric with the casing.
casing-fasteners.operatingPrinciple: Tightening the nuts stretches the studs elastically, producing a preload. Internal pressure acting on the cover produces a separating force of roughly p*A_eff, where A_eff is the area enclosed by the effective gasket line. The preload must exceed this force plus the residual load needed to keep the gasket sealed, at the maximum allowable pressure and temperature and during the hydrostatic test. Even tightening in a cross pattern seats the gasket uniformly and avoids tilting the cover.
casing-fasteners.construction: Studs are screwed into tapped holes in the casing and fitted with nuts (and washers if specified) bearing on the cover flange. Thread size, number of studs, material class and tightening torque are manufacturer data.

materials.family: Carbon or alloy steel studs and nuts
materials.why: High strength and preload capability at low cost.
materials.limitations: Corrode in wet or chemical environments; coatings or corrosion-resistant materials may be required.
materials.typicalService: Indoor or dry environments, water service.

materials.family: Austenitic stainless steel studs and nuts
materials.why: Corrosion resistance for washdown, outdoor or chemical environments.
materials.limitations: Lower strength than alloy steel bolting; galling of threads unless lubricated; preload must be recalculated.

failureModes.cause: Gasket creep and relaxation, thermal cycling, vibration, incorrect tightening.
failureModes.signs: Weeping at the casing joint; nuts found loose.

failureModes.cause: Leakage of liquid onto bolting, external environment.
failureModes.signs: Rust, reduced section, seized nuts.

failureModes.cause: Overtightening, no or wrong lubricant, stainless-on-stainless threads.
failureModes.signs: Nuts seize, studs stretched or broken during assembly.

inspection: Check for corrosion, leakage and loose nuts during inspections.
At disassembly, inspect threads for damage and studs for necking or stretch.
maintenance: Replace damaged or corroded studs and nuts with parts of the OEM-specified material and property class.
Lubricate threads as specified and tighten in a cross pattern in stages to the OEM torque.
Retighten after initial heat-up only if the OEM procedure requires it.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

casing-gasket.summary: The casing gasket seals the joint between the volute casing and the casing cover.
casing-gasket.function: It fills the microscopic surface irregularities between the casing and cover faces, preventing leakage of pumped liquid from the pressurised joint. In some designs its compressed thickness also affects the axial position of the cover relative to the casing.
casing-gasket.operatingPrinciple: Bolt preload compresses the gasket so that it flows into the surface roughness of the flange faces and blocks the leakage path. In service, internal pressure tends to separate the faces and unload the gasket, so sufficient residual gasket stress must remain. KSB notes that pump casing components are sealed against internal pressure by gaskets, O-rings or, in ultra-high-pressure designs, direct metal-to-metal contact. A confined gasket (held in a recess) resists blow-out better than an unconfined one.
casing-gasket.construction: In this generic design a flat ring gasket sits between the casing and cover at the register, located by the spigot. Some manufacturers use an O-ring in a groove instead of a flat gasket. Gasket type, material and thickness are specified by the OEM, because thickness can influence internal axial clearances.

materials.why: General-purpose gasket material for water and many liquids at moderate temperature and pressure.
materials.limitations: Creep relaxation; temperature and chemical limits depend on binder and fibre.

materials.family: Flexible graphite (often with a metal insert)
materials.why: Wide chemical and temperature resistance, good conformability.
materials.limitations: Fragile when handled; oxidises at high temperature in air; can promote galvanic corrosion of some flange materials.
materials.typicalService: Hot water, chemical and higher-temperature services.

materials.why: Very broad chemical resistance.
materials.limitations: Cold flow and creep under load unless filled or restructured.

materials.family: Elastomer O-ring (NBR, EPDM, FKM and similar)
materials.why: Reliable sealing with low bolt load in a machined groove.
materials.limitations: Chemical and temperature compatibility of the elastomer must be checked.
materials.typicalService: Designs with grooved joints in compatible liquids.

failureModes.cause: Insufficient or uneven bolt load, gasket relaxation, damaged faces.
failureModes.signs: Weeping or spray at the casing joint.

failureModes.cause: Pressure surge, unconfined gasket, loss of preload.
failureModes.signs: Sudden large leak at the joint.

failureModes.cause: Material incompatible with the liquid or temperature.
failureModes.signs: Hardened, swollen or disintegrated gasket at disassembly.

inspection: Check the casing joint for leakage during rounds.
At disassembly, check gasket faces for scratches, corrosion and old gasket residue.
maintenance: Always fit a new gasket of the OEM-specified type and thickness at reassembly; do not reuse a compressed gasket.
Clean faces without scoring them and tighten bolts evenly in stages.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

casing-cover.summary: The casing cover (backplate) closes the drive side of the volute casing and forms the seal chamber or stuffing box around the shaft.
casing-cover.function: It completes the pressure boundary on the drive side and forms the rear wall of the impeller chamber. It houses the shaft seal (seal chamber or stuffing box). It provides concentric registers that align the casing, the cover and the bearing frame, so that the impeller is centred in the casing.
casing-cover.operatingPrinciple: The cover is loaded by the pressure in the rear side chamber behind the back shroud, which is close to the impeller outlet pressure at large radius and decreases towards the shaft unless balancing features alter it. The pressure in the seal chamber depends on this side-chamber pressure and on any balance holes or back vanes. Because it carries both the seal and the register fits, the cover controls how square and concentric the seal is with the shaft.
casing-cover.construction: A cast, machined disc-shaped part with a register to the volute casing, a register to the bearing frame (adapter), the seal chamber or stuffing box bore with its throat, the gland face and connections for flush or sealing liquid. In back-pull-out pumps it is removed together with the rotating unit. Some designs include a rear wear ring or a cooling or heating jacket; these are manufacturer variations.

materials.family: Same material family as the volute casing (cast iron, ductile iron, stainless or duplex steel)
materials.why: The cover is part of the pressure boundary and is wetted by the same liquid.
materials.limitations: Mixing materials between casing and cover can create galvanic couples and different thermal expansion.

failureModes.mode: Erosion or corrosion behind the impeller and in the seal area
failureModes.cause: Solids circulating in the side chamber, aggressive liquid.
failureModes.signs: Grooves or metal loss on the cover face and in the seal chamber.

failureModes.cause: Careless assembly, corrosion, impact.
failureModes.signs: Seal or wear-ring problems after reassembly, increased run-out of the seal chamber face.

failureModes.cause: Damaged gasket face.
failureModes.signs: Weeping at the casing joint.

inspection: Inspect the cover face, seal chamber bore and throat for erosion and corrosion.
Check register fits and, with the rotating unit assembled, the face run-out and bore concentricity of the seal chamber relative to the shaft against OEM limits.
maintenance: Clean registers and gasket faces before reassembly and fit a new gasket.
Repair or replace a cover whose registers or seal chamber surfaces are damaged.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. Selection is driven by fluid temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation risk, and must be confirmed with the pump manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.
Balance holes and back vanes are manufacturer variations and are not assumed in this generic configuration.

impeller-front-shroud.summary: The front shroud is the suction-side disc of the closed impeller that covers the vanes and contains the impeller eye.
impeller-front-shroud.function: It closes the vane channels on the suction side so that liquid is guided along the whole channel without leaking over the vane edges. It carries the eye neck on which the impeller wear ring is mounted and stiffens the vanes.
impeller-front-shroud.operatingPrinciple: Inside, the shroud forms one wall of the vane channels. Outside, it faces a narrow side gap to the casing filled with liquid that rotates at roughly half the impeller speed; the pressure in this gap decreases from the impeller outlet towards the eye neck. This pressure field contributes to the axial thrust, and the rotating liquid causes disc friction losses.
impeller-front-shroud.construction: Cast integrally with the vanes, back shroud and hub. Its outer surface is usually left as cast or lightly finished, while the eye neck is machined for the wear ring. Its thickness and the fillets at the vane junctions affect strength and fatigue resistance.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The front shroud is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.cause: Solids and high-velocity liquid in the side gap, aggressive liquid.
failureModes.signs: Thinned or roughened shroud at overhaul.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations, resonance, casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at vane-shroud fillets.

failureModes.cause: Excessive axial movement, wrong assembly, thrust bearing failure.
failureModes.signs: Scoring on the shroud outer face and casing wall.

inspection: Visually inspect for erosion and rub marks at overhaul.
Dye-penetrant test vane junctions where cracks are suspected.
maintenance: Replace the impeller if wall loss or cracks exceed OEM repair limits.
Investigate thrust bearing condition and axial setting after any rubbing.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

impeller-back-shroud.summary: The back shroud is the drive-side disc of the impeller that supports the vanes and joins them to the hub.
impeller-back-shroud.function: It closes the vane channels on the drive side, supports the vanes and transmits torque from the hub to the vanes. Its outer face forms one wall of the rear side chamber behind the impeller, where the pressure acting on it largely determines axial thrust and seal chamber pressure.
impeller-back-shroud.operatingPrinciple: Liquid in the rear side chamber rotates at roughly half the impeller speed, and its pressure decreases towards the shaft. Inside the wear-ring diameter this pressure acts on the back shroud while the corresponding area at the front (the eye) is at suction pressure, so a net axial force results. KSB describes balance holes and back vanes on the rear shroud as measures some manufacturers use to reduce this pressure and the thrust.
impeller-back-shroud.construction: Cast integrally with the hub, vanes and front shroud. Some designs add balance holes near the hub together with a rear wear ring, or radial back vanes on the outer face; these are manufacturer variations not assumed here.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The back shroud is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.cause: Solids circulating in the rear side chamber.
failureModes.signs: Grooved back face and casing cover.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations, resonance, casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at the hub junction or vane fillets.

failureModes.cause: Aggressive liquid in a low-flow region.
failureModes.signs: Pitting on the back face.

inspection: Inspect the back face and the matching casing cover face for erosion and rubbing.
Where balance holes are present, check that they are not blocked.
maintenance: Replace the impeller when erosion or cracking exceed OEM limits.
Clean deposits from balancing features where fitted.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Balance holes and back vanes are manufacturer variations and are not assumed in this generic configuration.

impeller-vanes.summary: The impeller vanes are the curved blades between the shrouds that turn and accelerate the liquid, transferring energy from the shaft to the flow.
impeller-vanes.function: They deflect the liquid and increase its angular momentum, which is how shaft power becomes pump head. Their shape, number and angles determine the head, flow, efficiency, NPSH behaviour and stability of the head-flow curve. KSB describes impeller vanes as the parts that convert mechanical energy into pump power output.
impeller-vanes.operatingPrinciple: Relative to the rotating impeller the liquid flows through the channels between vanes. The pressure side of each vane pushes the liquid in the direction of rotation, so pressure on that side is higher than on the suction side; the integral of this pressure difference over the vanes produces the torque. At the inlet the vane leading edge must meet the relative flow at a suitable angle, and at the outlet the vane angle and the slip of the flow determine the circumferential velocity c_u2 and therefore the head.
impeller-vanes.construction: The vanes are cast integrally with the shrouds and hub, normally as backward-curved, three-dimensionally shaped blades in a radial impeller. Leading edges are usually rounded or profiled and trailing edges thinned. Surface finish of the channels affects friction losses. Impeller trimming reduces the vane outer diameter and is a common way to adapt a pump to a lower duty.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The vanes is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.mode: Cavitation erosion near the leading edges
failureModes.cause: Insufficient NPSH margin, operation far from BEP, suction recirculation.
failureModes.signs: Pitting near the vane inlets; noise and vibration in service.

failureModes.cause: Solids, especially at high velocity near the trailing edges.
failureModes.signs: Thinned or shortened vanes, rounded edges, falling head.

failureModes.cause: Pressure pulsations at the tongue, resonance, casting defects.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at vane tips or vane-shroud junctions.

failureModes.cause: Fibres, debris, deposits or scale.
failureModes.signs: Loss of flow and head, unbalance vibration.

inspection: Inspect leading and trailing edges for cavitation pitting, erosion and cracks.
Measure vane outer diameter and compare with the plate data if the trimming history is uncertain.
Check channels for blockage and deposits.
maintenance: Rebalance after any repair or trimming.
Replace the impeller when vane damage cannot be repaired within OEM limits.
Address the cause of cavitation (NPSH margin, operating point) rather than only repairing the damage.

keyConcepts.title: Blade angles, vane number and backward-curved vanes
keyConcepts.body: KSB defines the vane angle as the angle between the vane chord and the circumferential direction; in the velocity triangle the flow angle beta is measured between the relative velocity w and the negative circumferential direction. At the inlet the blade angle beta_1 is chosen to match the relative flow at the design flow so that the liquid enters with little incidence; at other flows incidence increases losses and can trigger cavitation or recirculation. At the outlet, most radial pump impellers use backward-curved vanes (outlet angle beta_2 well below 90 degrees). Backward curvature gives a smaller circumferential velocity c_u2 than radial or forward-curved vanes, so the theoretical head falls as flow increases. This favours a stable, falling head-flow curve (although other effects, such as part-load recirculation, can still cause instability), a lower absolute exit velocity and less kinetic energy to be recovered in the volute, which favours efficiency. The number of vanes is a compromise: more vanes guide the flow better and reduce slip, raising head, but add friction and blockage at the inlet; impellers for solids use very few vanes to keep wide passages, as KSB notes.

keyConcepts.title: How vane geometry affects head, flow and efficiency
keyConcepts.body: From the Euler equation, head depends on the outlet peripheral speed u2 = pi*D2*n/60 and on c_u2, which is set by the outlet angle, the slip and the outlet flow area. Increasing the outlet diameter D2 or the speed raises head; reducing D2 by trimming lowers head and flow and moves the curve down, which is why trimming is used to match a pump to a lower duty. The outlet width b2 and the throat of the volute set the flow at which impeller and casing match best. Inlet geometry (eye diameter, leading-edge angle and thickness) determines NPSH required and the onset of part-load recirculation. Channel shape and surface finish govern friction losses, and the vane loading distribution affects flow separation. These parameters are linked through specific speed: low specific-speed impellers are narrow with a large outlet-to-eye diameter ratio, high specific-speed impellers are wider. Real performance is established by test, for example under ISO 9906, and published by the manufacturer.

assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Vane number, angles and outlet width of the modelled impeller are illustrative, not design data.

impeller-eye.summary: The impeller eye is the central inlet opening of the impeller through which liquid enters from the suction nozzle.
impeller-eye.function: It admits the full pump flow plus the wear-ring leakage into the vane channels. Its diameter and the vane inlet geometry largely determine the NPSH required by the pump. KSB defines the suction eye as the inlet cross-section of an impeller.
impeller-eye.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters the eye axially and turns into the vane channels. The static pressure here is the lowest in the pump, and it drops further locally at the vane leading edges as the liquid accelerates around them. If the local pressure falls to the vapour pressure, vapour bubbles form and collapse further downstream, causing cavitation. A larger eye lowers inlet velocity and can improve suction performance at design flow, but makes the impeller more prone to suction recirculation at part load.
impeller-eye.construction: The eye is bounded by the front shroud neck (outer) and the hub (inner). On a closed impeller the outside of the neck carries the impeller wear ring. The impeller nut and washer sit at the centre of the eye and are usually shaped to disturb the inflow as little as possible.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The eye is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.cause: Low NPSH available relative to NPSH required, high flow, high liquid temperature.
failureModes.signs: Crackling noise; pitting on vane inlets and inner shroud surfaces.

failureModes.cause: Operation far below BEP.
failureModes.signs: Noise and vibration at low flow; cavitation damage on unexpected surfaces at the inlet.

failureModes.cause: Debris or fibres collecting at the eye and vane leading edges.
failureModes.signs: Loss of flow and head.

inspection: Check suction pressure and temperature to confirm NPSH margin.
At overhaul, inspect the eye and vane inlets for cavitation damage and debris.
maintenance: Keep suction strainers clean and maintain the suction conditions specified by the OEM.
Avoid prolonged operation below the OEM minimum continuous flow.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

impeller-hub.summary: The impeller hub is the central boss of the impeller that is bored and keyed to fit the shaft and clamped by the impeller nut.
impeller-hub.function: It transmits torque from the shaft key to the shrouds and vanes and locates the impeller radially and axially on the shaft. Its faces bear against the shaft shoulder or sleeve on one side and the impeller washer on the other.
impeller-hub.operatingPrinciple: Torque passes from the shaft through the key into the keyway in the hub bore, while the bore fit centres the impeller on the shaft. The impeller nut clamps the hub axially, so that the hub faces seal against liquid entering along the shaft and the impeller cannot move axially. A loose fit allows fretting and can cause unbalance.
impeller-hub.construction: Cast integrally with the back shroud and machined with a precision bore, keyway and square end faces. The type of fit (clearance, transition or light interference) is manufacturer data. The hub length gives the impeller a stable seat on the overhung shaft.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The hub is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.mode: Fretting or wear of the bore
failureModes.cause: Loose fit, insufficient clamping, vibration.
failureModes.signs: Polished or corroded bore, impeller rocks on the shaft.

failureModes.cause: Corrosion between hub and shaft, deposits.
failureModes.signs: Impeller cannot be removed without heavy force.

failureModes.cause: Overload, stress concentration, improper removal methods (hammering or local heating).
failureModes.signs: Cracks at keyway corners.

inspection: Check bore diameter, keyway and end-face squareness against OEM data.
Inspect for cracks at keyway corners.
maintenance: Use the OEM-recommended removal device rather than impact; apply anti-seize compound only if the OEM permits it.
Clean the bore and shaft before reassembly and tighten the impeller nut to the OEM value.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

impeller-keyway.summary: The impeller keyway is the axial slot machined in the hub bore that receives the impeller key.
impeller-keyway.function: It allows torque to be transmitted from the shaft to the impeller through a key, independently of friction in the bore fit. It also fixes the angular position of the impeller relative to the shaft.
impeller-keyway.operatingPrinciple: The key bears on the side walls of the keyway; torque produces a bearing (contact) pressure on these walls and shear in the key. The keyway corners are stress concentrations in the hub. For balancing, ISO 21940-32 describes a convention for how keys are accounted for when shafts and fitted components are balanced separately.
impeller-keyway.construction: Machined in the hub bore with dimensions and tolerances matching the key; corners usually have small radii to reduce stress concentration. Dimensions follow the manufacturer drawing and the key standard it references.

materials.family: Same material as the impeller (integral casting)
materials.why: The keyway is cast in one piece with the impeller, so its material is chosen for the impeller as a whole.
materials.limitations: Locally higher velocities, cavitation or solids impact can make this region wear first.

failureModes.cause: Loose key fit, torque fluctuations, start-stop cycles.
failureModes.signs: Rounded or stepped keyway walls, play between key and keyway.

failureModes.cause: Stress concentration, overload, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Cracks running from the keyway corners.

failureModes.cause: Liquid reaching the bore because the hub joint is not sealed.
failureModes.signs: Rust or pitting, seized key.

inspection: Check key-to-keyway fit and keyway walls for deformation at disassembly.
Inspect corners for cracks.
maintenance: Replace a worn key; replace the impeller if the keyway is damaged beyond OEM limits.
Keep the key convention used for balancing unchanged when parts are replaced.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

impeller-wear-ring.summary: The impeller wear ring is a renewable rotating ring fitted on the impeller eye neck that runs inside the casing wear ring with a small radial clearance.
impeller-wear-ring.function: Together with the casing wear ring it forms the controlled gap that limits leakage from the high-pressure side back to the impeller eye. It is replaceable, so the impeller itself does not have to be scrapped when the running surface wears.
impeller-wear-ring.operatingPrinciple: The ring rotates with the impeller inside the stationary casing ring. Leakage flows axially through the narrow annulus between them, driven by the difference between the pressure in the front side gap and the eye pressure. The liquid in the gap is sheared by the rotating ring, and the pressure drop across the gap produces a centring force on the rotor (Lomakin effect). Wear on either ring enlarges the gap and increases leakage.
impeller-wear-ring.construction: The ring is shrunk or pressed onto a machined neck of the front shroud and secured, for example by screws, pins or tack welds, depending on manufacturer practice. Some designs omit a separate ring and use the machined impeller neck as the running surface; in that case wear may be corrected by machining the neck and fitting an undersized casing ring, if the OEM allows it.

materials.why: Good tolerance of occasional contact; used with bronze or cast iron impellers in water service.
materials.limitations: Limited abrasion resistance; corrosion limits in some waters.

materials.why: Hardness and wear resistance with moderate corrosion resistance; a hardness difference to the casing ring reduces galling risk.
materials.limitations: Pitting in chloride-containing liquids; galling if paired with a similar material of similar hardness.
materials.typicalService: Process liquids and hot water within verified limits.

materials.family: Austenitic or duplex stainless steel (possibly hard-faced)
materials.why: Corrosion resistance in aggressive liquids.
materials.limitations: High galling tendency against stainless counterparts unless hard-faced or paired with a non-galling material.

failureModes.cause: Abrasive particles, erosion-corrosion, rubbing.
failureModes.signs: Falling head and efficiency; measured clearance above limit.

failureModes.cause: Contact due to shaft deflection, misalignment, thermal distortion or dry running; incompatible material pair.
failureModes.signs: Smeared metal, torn surfaces, sudden stop or high motor current.

failureModes.cause: Loss of shrink fit due to temperature or corrosion; failed locking.
failureModes.signs: Ring displaced axially, fretting marks, increased leakage.

inspection: Measure the ring outer diameter at several positions and compare the clearance with OEM values.
Check for rub marks, cracks and secure fit on the impeller neck.
maintenance: Replace both rings when clearance exceeds the OEM maximum; machine new rings concentric with the impeller bore.
Rebalance the impeller after fitting a new ring if required by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Rotating side of the clearance seal: leakage and volumetric efficiency
keyConcepts.body: The impeller ring is the rotating half of the wear-ring seal. The leakage through the annulus between it and the casing ring is driven by the pressure difference between the front side gap and the eye; it can be estimated as Q_L = mu*A_gap*sqrt(2*dp/rho), with A_gap = pi*D_gap*s for a radial clearance s. This leakage passes through the impeller again, so the impeller handles Q + Q_L while only Q is delivered; the volumetric efficiency is eta_v = Q/(Q + Q_L). KSB notes that the leakage loss falls roughly linearly with gap width and is most important for low specific-speed pumps, where leakage is large relative to the delivered flow. Rotation of the ring also adds shear and swirl to the gap flow, which influences the effective flow coefficient and the centring (Lomakin) force of the gap.

keyConcepts.title: Wear mechanisms, monitoring and renewal
keyConcepts.body: Wear of the impeller ring comes from abrasive particles carried by the leakage flow, erosion-corrosion at the high gap velocity, and contact with the casing ring when the rotor deflects at low or high flow, when alignment is poor or when the pump runs dry. Contact between similar stainless steels can gall and seize; that is why manufacturers specify hardness differences, hard facing or non-galling material pairs. The effect of wear is gradual: as the clearance increases, head and efficiency fall and power per unit flow rises; the Hydraulic Institute efficiency-prediction guidance includes an estimate (based on HI 20.3) of the efficiency decrease caused by increased wearing-ring clearance. Because the rings also provide some rotor support, heavily worn rings can contribute to higher vibration. Renewal restores the clearance: both rings are replaced and finish-machined to the OEM new clearance, concentric with the impeller bore, and the impeller is rebalanced if required.

open-impeller.summary: The open impeller is a comparison variant in which the vanes are attached to a back shroud only (a form many sources call semi-open) and run against the stationary casing wall with a small axial clearance.
open-impeller.function: It performs the same energy transfer as the closed impeller, but without a front shroud. It is shown in the model to compare constructions; in service, open impellers are often chosen for liquids containing solids or fibres and where easy inspection and cleaning are valued.
open-impeller.operatingPrinciple: Liquid is guided on one side by the back shroud and on the other by the stationary casing wall. Leakage from the pressure side to the suction side of each vane passes over the vane tips through the axial clearance, bypassing part of the energy transfer, so head and efficiency fall as this clearance grows through wear; some designs allow it to be restored by axial adjustment of the rotor. Without a front shroud the suction-side pressure force is much lower than on a closed impeller, so KSB notes that the net axial force on an open radial impeller is higher; cut-outs in the back shroud between vanes reduce it.
open-impeller.construction: A single casting with vanes, hub and back shroud (sometimes partly cut back between vanes), without a front shroud or eye wear ring. The axial clearance between vane tips and the casing or a renewable wear plate is set at assembly according to the OEM instructions. Back vanes for thrust reduction are common on open impellers but are a manufacturer variation.

materials.why: Low cost, easy to cast in complex vane passages and easy to machine; common for clean water.
materials.limitations: Brittle, limited strength and poor resistance to cavitation erosion, corrosion and abrasive wear.
materials.typicalService: Clean cold water, building services and similar non-aggressive liquids.

materials.why: Good castability and corrosion resistance in many waters, better cavitation resistance than grey iron and good tolerance of rubbing contact.
materials.limitations: Attacked by ammonia and by some sulphide-polluted or high-velocity waters; limited abrasion resistance; galvanic effects when combined with other metals.
materials.typicalService: Potable water, cooling water and, after assessment, some seawater applications.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in many process liquids and better cavitation-erosion resistance than cast iron.
materials.limitations: Risk of pitting, crevice corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking in warm chloride-containing liquids; galling risk at rubbing surfaces.
materials.typicalService: Process liquids, hygienic and chemical service within verified limits.

materials.why: Higher strength and generally better chloride and erosion-corrosion resistance than standard austenitic grades; the KSB cavitation-erosion comparison ranks duplex steel among the most resistant common pump materials.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; casting quality and heat treatment must be controlled; upper temperature limits apply.
materials.typicalService: Seawater, brackish water and abrasive or chloride-containing process liquids, subject to verification.

failureModes.mode: Growth of the axial tip clearance
failureModes.cause: Abrasive wear of vane tips and casing face.
failureModes.signs: Gradual loss of head and efficiency.

failureModes.cause: Clearance set too small, thermal growth, thrust bearing wear.
failureModes.signs: Noise, scoring of vane tips and casing face, increased power.

failureModes.cause: Solids, low NPSH margin, off-design operation.
failureModes.signs: Thinned or pitted vanes.

inspection: Measure the axial clearance using the OEM method and compare it with OEM values.
Inspect vane tips and the opposing casing face for wear and rub marks.
maintenance: Reset the axial clearance according to the OEM procedure when performance falls.
Replace the impeller or wear plate when wear exceeds OEM limits.

Shown for conceptual comparison only; in this model the open impeller replaces the closed impeller and its wear rings.

impeller-key.summary: The impeller key is a parallel key that transmits torque from the shaft to the impeller hub.
impeller-key.function: It provides a positive torque-transmitting connection between shaft and impeller so that driving torque does not rely only on friction in the bore fit. It also fixes the angular position of the impeller on the shaft.
impeller-key.operatingPrinciple: The torque T acting at the shaft produces a tangential force on the key of about F = 2*T/d (d = shaft diameter at the key). This force causes shear stress across the key and bearing (contact) stress on the key sides and keyway walls. The key length and section are chosen so these stresses remain acceptable with margin. When the rotor is balanced, the presence of the key is handled according to a defined convention, such as that described in ISO 21940-32.
impeller-key.construction: A rectangular or square bar with square or rounded ends, fitted in matching keyseats in the shaft and hub. Dimensions follow the manufacturer drawing and the key standard it references. Because it sits in the liquid-wetted area under the impeller, its material must suit the liquid.

materials.why: Standard key material with good strength and machinability.
materials.limitations: Corrodes if wetted by water or aggressive liquids.
materials.typicalService: Non-wetted or protected locations, non-corrosive liquids.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance where the key is wetted by the pumped liquid.
materials.limitations: Lower strength in some austenitic grades; galling risk against stainless keyways.

failureModes.cause: Torque overload, seizure of the impeller or rotor.
failureModes.signs: Impeller turns on the shaft; sheared key at disassembly.

failureModes.cause: Loose fit, torque fluctuations.
failureModes.signs: Play in the key, worn key sides.

failureModes.cause: Wetting by liquid entering along the shaft.
failureModes.signs: Rust or pitting, seized key.

inspection: Check the key and keyseats for wear, fretting, corrosion and fit at every disassembly.
maintenance: Replace keys whenever worn or corroded, using the OEM-specified material and dimensions.
Keep the same key convention when rebalancing the rotor.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

impeller-washer.summary: The impeller washer sits between the impeller nut and the hub face and spreads the clamping load of the nut onto the hub.
impeller-washer.function: It distributes the nut load over the hub face, protects the hub from damage when the nut is tightened and, depending on the design, helps seal the joint so that liquid cannot reach the shaft threads and key. In some designs it is combined with a locking element.
impeller-washer.operatingPrinciple: The tightened nut presses the washer against the hub, which in turn is clamped against the shaft shoulder or sleeve. The washer provides a flat, hard bearing surface for the nut so that the preload is maintained. Where a gasket or O-ring is used at this joint, the clamping load also keeps the liquid out of the bore.
impeller-washer.construction: A machined ring or disc, sometimes with a recess for an O-ring or a tab to lock the nut. Arrangement details vary between manufacturers.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in the wetted area at the impeller eye.
materials.limitations: Galling against stainless nuts unless lubricated as specified.

materials.family: Same material family as the shaft or impeller
materials.why: Avoids galvanic couples in the wetted joint.
materials.limitations: Must still resist the pumped liquid.

failureModes.cause: Wetted by the incoming liquid at the eye.
failureModes.signs: Pitting or thinning at disassembly.

failureModes.cause: Washer deformation, missing or failed locking element.
failureModes.signs: Loose impeller, fretting marks.

failureModes.cause: Damaged sealing element at the washer joint.
failureModes.signs: Corrosion of the shaft thread and key.

inspection: Check flatness, corrosion and the condition of any sealing element at disassembly.
maintenance: Replace damaged washers and sealing elements; fit locking elements new if they are single-use.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
The washer arrangement and any sealing element are manufacturer specific.

impeller-nut.summary: The impeller locking nut screws onto the threaded end of the shaft and clamps the impeller axially against its seat.
impeller-nut.function: It holds the impeller in its axial position and maintains the clamping that keeps the hub tight on the shaft. Its locking arrangement prevents it from loosening in service.
impeller-nut.operatingPrinciple: The nut preload clamps the hub between the nut (with washer) and the shaft shoulder or sleeve. Manufacturers commonly choose the thread hand so that drag and start-up torque tend to tighten the nut in the normal direction of rotation; running the pump in reverse can therefore loosen it, which is why the direction of rotation is checked before the coupling is connected. A locking element such as a lock washer, thread-locking compound or a cap nut design prevents loosening from vibration.
impeller-nut.construction: A machined nut, often shaped as a streamlined cap to reduce disturbance of the inflow at the eye. Thread hand, locking method and tightening torque are manufacturer data.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in the wetted eye region.
materials.limitations: Galling against stainless shaft threads unless the specified lubricant is used.

materials.family: Same material family as the impeller
materials.why: Matches the corrosion behaviour of the impeller and limits galvanic effects.
materials.limitations: Strength and galling behaviour must suit the required preload.

failureModes.cause: Reverse rotation, insufficient tightening, failed locking element.
failureModes.signs: Knocking, impeller rubbing, vibration; impeller moves on the shaft.

failureModes.cause: Stainless-on-stainless threads without lubricant, overtightening.
failureModes.signs: Nut seizes or threads tear at removal.

failureModes.mode: Corrosion or erosion of the nut
failureModes.cause: Aggressive liquid, cavitation at the eye.
failureModes.signs: Pitted or thinned cap.

inspection: Confirm the correct direction of rotation of the motor with the coupling disconnected before first start.
At disassembly, check threads, locking element and nut condition.
maintenance: Tighten to the OEM torque with the specified lubricant; renew single-use locking elements.
Replace nuts with damaged threads; do not reuse a nut that has galled.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.
Thread hand and locking method vary by manufacturer.

pump-shaft.summary: The pump shaft is the stepped steel shaft that carries the overhung impeller, runs in the bearings and receives torque from the coupling.
pump-shaft.function: It transmits torque from the coupling to the impeller and carries the radial and axial loads of the rotor to the bearings. Its stiffness keeps deflection at the wear rings and seal faces within acceptable limits.
pump-shaft.operatingPrinciple: Torque produces torsional shear stress; radial loads at the impeller produce bending stress that reverses every revolution (rotating bending), so fatigue strength is usually a governing design criterion, together with stiffness (deflection). Axial thrust is transmitted through the shaft and locknut to the thrust bearing. The rotor bending natural frequency must be kept clear of the operating speed range.
pump-shaft.construction: A machined, stepped bar with an impeller section, sleeve seat, bearing seats, locknut thread and coupling section. Diameter steps form shoulders with fillet radii to limit stress concentration; bearing seats are finished to tight tolerances. Straightness and concentricity of the seats are checked after manufacture.

materials.why: High strength and fatigue resistance at low cost; used with a shaft sleeve so that the shaft is not wetted.
materials.limitations: Corrodes if liquid reaches it.
materials.typicalService: Water and non-corrosive liquids with sleeve protection.

materials.why: Strength combined with moderate corrosion resistance.
materials.limitations: Pitting in chloride-containing liquids; properties depend on heat treatment.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance where the shaft is wetted; duplex offers higher strength.
materials.limitations: Austenitic grades have lower strength; galling of threads.
materials.typicalService: Chemical and seawater service after verification.

failureModes.cause: Rotating bending plus torsion, stress raisers, corrosion fatigue, misalignment.
failureModes.signs: Rising vibration before failure; beach marks on the fracture surface.

failureModes.cause: Handling damage, high radial loads, thermal bow.
failureModes.signs: High run-out, vibration at 1x running speed, wear-ring rubbing.

failureModes.cause: Loose fits, bearing ring creep, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Undersize seats, polished bands.

inspection: Measure run-out at specified locations (in V-blocks, between centres or in the frame) against OEM limits.
Measure bearing and coupling seat diameters.
Crack-test keyways, shoulders and threads at major overhauls.
maintenance: Replace shafts that exceed OEM run-out or dimensional limits, or show cracks.
Protect seats during handling and store shafts supported so that they cannot bend.
