shaft-impeller-section.summary: The impeller mounting section is the overhung end of the shaft that carries the impeller, its key and the threaded end for the impeller nut.
shaft-impeller-section.function: It centres the impeller, transmits torque through the keyseat and provides the thread for the impeller nut. It sits furthest from the bearings, so its run-out directly affects wear-ring and seal clearances.
shaft-impeller-section.operatingPrinciple: Torque is transferred through the key, and the impeller is clamped axially between the nut and a shoulder or sleeve end. Radial loads at the impeller create the largest bending moment at the inboard bearing, while this section itself is mainly loaded by torque and clamping force. Corrosion or fretting at the fit can make impeller removal difficult.
shaft-impeller-section.construction: A precision-finished journal with keyseat, a shoulder or sleeve abutment and a threaded end; dimensions and fit are OEM data. Thread undercuts and keyseat ends are stress concentration sites.

materials.family: Same material as the pump shaft (machined feature)
materials.why: The impeller mounting section is machined on the shaft, so its strength, hardness and corrosion resistance are those of the shaft material.
materials.limitations: Stress concentrations at diameter changes, keyseats and threads reduce fatigue strength locally; surface damage here is a common crack initiation site.

failureModes.cause: Galling, overtightening, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Nut does not run freely; torn threads.

failureModes.mode: Fretting or corrosion under the hub
failureModes.cause: Loose fit, liquid ingress.
failureModes.signs: Pitting or polished bands on the journal.

failureModes.mode: Cracking at the keyseat end or thread root
failureModes.cause: Fatigue from torque and bending fluctuations.
failureModes.signs: Cracks detected by dye-penetrant or magnetic-particle testing.

inspection: Measure journal diameter and run-out at the impeller seat.
Inspect threads and keyseat for damage and cracks.
maintenance: Clean and protect threads; use the specified lubricant at assembly.
Replace the shaft if the journal or threads are out of tolerance.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

shaft-coupling-section.summary: The coupling mounting section is the drive end of the pump shaft that carries the pump coupling hub and its key.
shaft-coupling-section.function: It receives the driving torque from the coupling hub through a key and fit. Its concentricity with the bearing seats is essential for good coupling alignment.
shaft-coupling-section.operatingPrinciple: The coupling hub is held on the shaft by a fit (clearance, transition or interference, as specified by the pump and coupling manufacturers) and the key, often with a set screw or end retainer. Torque produces torsional shear stress, which is highest where the diameter is smallest, often at this section. Misalignment between pump and motor produces cyclic bending here.
shaft-coupling-section.construction: A keyed cylindrical (or in some designs tapered) journal at the drive end, sometimes with a centre hole for hub pulling tools. Fit and keyseat dimensions are manufacturer data.

materials.family: Same material as the pump shaft (machined feature)
materials.why: The coupling mounting section is machined on the shaft, so its strength, hardness and corrosion resistance are those of the shaft material.
materials.limitations: Stress concentrations at diameter changes, keyseats and threads reduce fatigue strength locally; surface damage here is a common crack initiation site.

failureModes.cause: Loose hub fit, torque fluctuations, misalignment.
failureModes.signs: Worn keyseat, polished bands, hub slipping.

failureModes.mode: Damage during hub fitting or removal
failureModes.cause: Hammering, uneven heating, unsuitable pullers.
failureModes.signs: Burrs, bent shaft end, increased run-out.

failureModes.cause: Torsion plus bending from misalignment, keyseat stress concentration.
failureModes.signs: Cracks at the keyseat end.

inspection: Measure run-out and diameter of the coupling seat.
Inspect the keyseat for wear and cracks.
maintenance: Fit and remove hubs only with the methods given by the coupling and pump manufacturers.
Check alignment after fitting the coupling.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

shaft-shoulder.summary: The shaft shoulder is a step in shaft diameter that provides an axial locating face for a bearing, sleeve or the impeller.
shaft-shoulder.function: It locates components axially and transmits axial loads from them into the shaft. Its squareness to the shaft axis ensures that the parts it locates run true.
shaft-shoulder.operatingPrinciple: Axial clamping forces from the impeller nut or bearing locknut press components against the shoulder face. The change of diameter concentrates stress, so a fillet radius is used; the radius must be smaller than the corner chamfer of the part it locates so that the part bears fully on the face.
shaft-shoulder.construction: A machined step with a square face and a specified fillet radius or undercut. Dimensions and radius are manufacturer data.

materials.family: Same material as the pump shaft (machined feature)
materials.why: The shoulder is machined on the shaft, so its strength, hardness and corrosion resistance are those of the shaft material.
materials.limitations: Stress concentrations at diameter changes, keyseats and threads reduce fatigue strength locally; surface damage here is a common crack initiation site.

failureModes.cause: Sharp fillet, machining marks, high rotating bending stress.
failureModes.signs: Circumferential crack at the step.

failureModes.cause: Fretting under a loose component, careless assembly.
failureModes.signs: Uneven bearing contact, components not square.

failureModes.cause: Moisture or liquid trapped at the shoulder.
failureModes.signs: Pitting that can initiate fatigue cracks.

inspection: Check face squareness and fillet condition at overhaul.
Crack-test the fillet region when required by the OEM or after a failure.
maintenance: Remove burrs carefully without changing the fillet; replace the shaft if a crack is found.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

shaft-sleeve.summary: The shaft sleeve is a replaceable tube fitted over the shaft where it passes through the seal chamber or stuffing box.
shaft-sleeve.function: It protects the shaft against wear by the packing or seal parts and against corrosion by the pumped liquid. It carries the rotating parts of the mechanical seal or forms the running surface for the packing. Because it is replaceable, wear in the sealing area does not require a new shaft.
shaft-sleeve.operatingPrinciple: KSB describes the shaft protecting sleeve as protecting the shaft from mechanical damage caused by shaft seals and from chemical attack by aggressive liquids. Liquid that enters between sleeve and shaft must not escape to atmosphere, so the sleeve is sealed to the shaft, usually by an O-ring or gasket at the impeller end. The sleeve needs axial room to expand thermally and is secured against rotation and axial movement, ideally at the impeller end.
shaft-sleeve.construction: A precision-bored and finished tube, slid over the shaft, driven by a key, pin or the impeller hub, and clamped axially between the impeller hub and a shaft shoulder or retained by other means. Its outer surface finish and hardness are specified for the sealing method; sleeves for packing are often hardened or coated. Fit and dimensions are manufacturer data.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance and a good surface for seal O-rings and set screws.
materials.limitations: Relatively soft, so wears under packing; galling risk.

materials.why: Higher wear resistance under packing.
materials.limitations: Pitting risk in chloride-containing liquids.

materials.family: Stainless steel with a hard surface treatment in the packing zone (for example chrome plating, nitriding or plasma-sprayed coating)
materials.why: Very high wear resistance in the packing contact zone; KSB recommends a surface hardness above 800-1000 HV and notes that a hard, wear-resistant sleeve surface generally lengthens packing life.
materials.limitations: KSB notes that such coatings are very thin, so the sleeve cannot be remachined at service; coatings can also crack or spall under impact or thermal shock.

failureModes.cause: Packing friction, abrasive particles, over-tightened gland.
failureModes.signs: Leakage that cannot be controlled by gland adjustment; visible groove.

failureModes.mode: Fretting or damage under seal components
failureModes.cause: Set screw marks, O-ring fretting, seal slippage.
failureModes.signs: Damage marks where the seal retainer and O-ring sit.

failureModes.cause: Failed sleeve O-ring or gasket.
failureModes.signs: Leakage that persists with a good seal; corrosion of the shaft under the sleeve.

failureModes.cause: Unsuitable material for the liquid.
failureModes.signs: Pitting on the sleeve surface.

inspection: Inspect the sleeve surface for grooves, scoring and pitting each time the seal or packing is serviced.
Check sleeve run-out with the shaft mounted.
Inspect the sleeve-to-shaft sealing element.
maintenance: Replace the sleeve when grooved or pitted; replace its sealing element every time it is removed.
Check that the sleeve is properly secured against rotation and that thermal expansion room is maintained.

shaft-key.summary: The shaft key at the coupling end is a parallel key that transmits torque between the pump shaft and the pump coupling hub.
shaft-key.function: It provides a positive torque connection between the coupling hub and the shaft, supplementing the hub fit, and fixes the angular position of the hub.
shaft-key.operatingPrinciple: Torque produces a tangential force on the key of about F = 2*T/d, causing shear in the key and bearing stress on the key sides. The keyseat in the shaft is a stress concentration, which matters because the coupling section often has the smallest shaft diameter. For balancing of coupling hubs and shafts, conventions such as that in ISO 21940-32 define how the key is accounted for.
shaft-key.construction: A rectangular or square bar fitted into matching keyseats in shaft and hub, with dimensions from the manufacturer drawing and its referenced key standard.

materials.why: Standard, strong and economical; this location is normally dry.
materials.limitations: Corrosion in humid or washdown environments.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in wet or washdown environments.
materials.limitations: Lower strength of some grades; galling.

failureModes.cause: Torque overload or seizure.
failureModes.signs: Hub slipping, deformed key.

failureModes.cause: Loose fit, misalignment, torque fluctuation.
failureModes.signs: Rust-coloured fretting debris, play in the keyway.

failureModes.cause: Humid or washdown environment.
failureModes.signs: Rust, seized key, difficult hub removal.

inspection: Check key fit and condition whenever the coupling hub is removed.
maintenance: Replace worn keys; use the specified key and keep the balancing convention consistent.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.

shaft-locknut.summary: The shaft locknut and lock washer clamp the outboard (thrust) bearing inner ring against its shaft shoulder.
shaft-locknut.function: They fix the thrust bearing axially on the shaft so that the axial thrust of the impeller is transferred from the shaft to the bearing. The lock washer prevents the nut from loosening.
shaft-locknut.operatingPrinciple: The slotted nut is tightened on a threaded section of the shaft, clamping the bearing inner ring against the shoulder. A tab lock washer engages a slot in the shaft with its inner tab, and one outer tab is bent into a slot of the nut. SKF states, for its lock nuts that require a keyway, that an undamaged nut can be reused but a new lock washer should be used each time the nut is reinstalled.
shaft-locknut.construction: A slotted locknut with a fine thread and a stamped tab lock washer, sized to the shaft thread and bearing. Some designs use other locking methods, such as nuts with locking screws.

materials.family: Carbon steel nut and steel sheet lock washer
materials.why: Standard bearing accessory materials with adequate strength inside the lubricated bearing housing.
materials.limitations: Not intended for wetted, corrosive locations.

failureModes.cause: Reused or improperly bent lock washer, insufficient tightening.
failureModes.signs: Axial play of the rotor, bearing noise and overheating.

failureModes.cause: Reuse of a previously bent tab, fatigue.
failureModes.signs: Tab fragments in the oil, loose nut.

failureModes.cause: Overtightening, burrs, misuse of tools.
failureModes.signs: Nut tight before seating, damaged threads.

inspection: Check rotor axial float and bearing condition during inspections.
At disassembly, inspect threads, nut and washer.
maintenance: Use a new lock washer each time the nut is reinstalled (SKF guidance for keyway-type lock nuts).
Tighten the nut with a suitable spanner to the OEM requirement and bend a tab fully into a nut slot.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.
Clearances, tightening torques, fits and run-out limits are manufacturer data; always use the values in the OEM instruction manual for the specific pump size and material.
Bearing details belong to the bearing-assembly content; this record covers the locking device only.

seal-chamber.summary: The seal chamber is the bore in the casing cover that surrounds the shaft sleeve and houses the mechanical seal.
seal-chamber.function: It provides the space and the mounting face for the mechanical seal and contains the liquid that lubricates and cools the seal faces. Its geometry influences heat removal, venting and the accumulation of solids around the seal.
seal-chamber.operatingPrinciple: The seal chamber is connected to the impeller rear side chamber through a throat around the shaft. Its pressure therefore depends on the pressure behind the impeller and on any balance holes or back vanes; EagleBurgmann notes that with back vanes the sealing pressure lies between suction and discharge pressure. A flush (here Plan 11) circulates liquid through the chamber to remove heat and keep solids and vapour away from the faces. Gas in the chamber is dangerous for the seal: KSB notes that, because of its low density, gas tends to move to small diameters, usually the sealing gap, causing dry running and heat-stress cracks, so the chamber is vented before start-up.
seal-chamber.construction: A machined bore in the casing cover with a throat at the impeller end and a flat, square face at the outboard end for the gland plate. ISO 3069 specifies cavity dimensions for mechanical seals and soft packing in end-suction pumps. Some manufacturers offer enlarged or tapered-bore chambers intended to improve circulation and solids handling; this is a manufacturer variation.

stuffing-box.summary: The stuffing box is the bore in the casing cover that holds the packing rings and lantern ring around the shaft sleeve.
stuffing-box.function: It provides the cylindrical space and the end face against which the packing is compressed by the gland follower. It includes the connection to the lantern ring for flush or sealing liquid.
stuffing-box.operatingPrinciple: The gland follower compresses the packing against the bottom of the box (the throat), so the packing expands radially against the sleeve and the bore. The FSA/ESA manual describes the stuffing box as a cylindrical recess around the shaft designed to prevent leakage of process liquid or the ingress of air or other contaminants. Its pressure depends on suction pressure, the pressure behind the impeller and any balance holes.
stuffing-box.construction: A machined bore in the casing cover with a throat at the impeller end, a tapped flush connection aligned with the lantern ring position and a face with studs for the gland follower. The FSA/ESA manual gives guideline depths of about 7 packing cross-sections (7W) with a lantern ring and 5W without, while recommending that the packing maker confirm the arrangement. ISO 3069 specifies cavity dimensions for soft packing in end-suction pumps.

gland-plate.summary: The seal gland plate is the bolted cover at the outboard end of the seal chamber that holds the stationary seal face and contains the flush connection.
gland-plate.function: It locates and seals the stationary seat of the mechanical seal, closes the seal chamber and provides the flush port. It keeps the stationary face square and concentric with the shaft.
gland-plate.operatingPrinciple: The gland plate is clamped to the seal chamber face over a gasket or O-ring. The stationary seat sits in a bore of the plate on its secondary O-ring and is prevented from rotating by an anti-rotation pin or similar feature. Any tilt or eccentricity of the gland plate is transmitted directly to the seat and causes uneven face loading.
gland-plate.construction: A machined plate with a pilot (register) to the seal chamber, a seat bore, a gasket or O-ring groove, bolt holes and a tapped flush connection. Additional quench, vent or drain ports are used in some designs.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance and dimensional stability; common for seal glands.

seal-flush-connection.summary: The seal flush connection is the port and piping that bring flush liquid into the seal chamber close to the mechanical seal faces.
seal-flush-connection.function: It supplies a continuous flow of liquid to remove frictional heat from the seal faces, help maintain the lubricating film and keep solids and vapour away from the seal. In this generic configuration it is a Plan 11 arrangement fed from the pump discharge.
seal-flush-connection.operatingPrinciple: In Plan 11, liquid is taken from the pump discharge, flows through an orifice that reduces the flow rate (John Crane adds that it protects the seal from full discharge pressure), and enters the seal chamber near the faces. John Crane describes Plan 11 as using process fluid to flush and cool a single mechanical seal, as suited to clean, non-polymerising fluids and as the most used piping plan. Other plans may be needed when the liquid is too hot or contains abrasive particles.
seal-flush-connection.construction: A tapped port in the gland plate (or seal chamber) connected by small-bore tubing or pipe to a discharge-side connection, with a restriction orifice in the line. Sizes, orifice diameter and routing are specified by the seal maker and the pump specification.

materials.family: Austenitic stainless steel tubing and fittings
materials.why: Corrosion resistance and reliable compression fittings.
materials.limitations: Chloride stress corrosion cracking limits in hot chloride service.

materials.why: For liquids that attack standard stainless steel.
materials.limitations: Higher cost.

failureModes.signs: Seal overheating, increased leakage, cold flush line.

failureModes.cause: Vibration, poor assembly, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Drips at the tubing joints.

failureModes.cause: Pumped liquid too hot, abrasive or close to its vapour pressure.
failureModes.signs: Short seal life despite a working flush.

Check fittings for leaks and vibration damage.
maintenance: Clean or replace a blocked orifice and line; support tubing to avoid vibration fatigue.
Do not change orifice size or piping plan without the agreement of the seal maker.

mech-seal-stationary-face.summary: The stationary seal face (seat) is the non-rotating sealing ring of the mechanical seal, mounted in the gland plate.
mech-seal-stationary-face.function: It provides the stationary half of the sealing interface against which the rotating face slides. Its lapped face, together with the rotating face, forms the narrow gap that controls leakage.
mech-seal-stationary-face.operatingPrinciple: The seat is held in the gland plate on a secondary O-ring and prevented from rotating, usually by a pin. Its sealing face must be very flat and square to the shaft so that the rotating face runs on it with a stable lubricating film. EagleBurgmann notes that sliding faces are lapped or ground surfaces that wear in service and deform under force, pressure and temperature.
mech-seal-stationary-face.construction: A ring of face material with a lapped sealing face; its back face and outside diameter fit the gland plate bore. In the common hard/soft pairing, one face is a hard ceramic or carbide and the other a carbon graphite; which ring carries which material is the seal maker choice.

materials.why: Very hard, wear-resistant ceramic; the John Crane tutorial summarised by Turbomachinery Magazine credits it with high temperature strength and thermal shock resistance.
materials.limitations: Brittle and sensitive to impact and edge chipping; chemical resistance differs between grades, so the grade is chosen by the seal maker.
materials.typicalService: Hard face in hard/soft pairs or both faces in hard/hard pairs.

materials.why: Very tough with good wear resistance; common binders are nickel and cobalt.
materials.limitations: More susceptible to heat checking than advanced ceramics; the binder can be attacked by some liquids.
materials.typicalService: Hard face for liquids with some solids or shock loads.

materials.why: Soft, self-lubricating and conformable, tolerant of short emergency running; usually paired with a hard face.
materials.limitations: Damaged by abrasives; the impregnant limits chemical compatibility.
materials.typicalService: Soft face in hard/soft pairs in clean liquids.

mech-seal-orings.summary: The secondary seals (O-rings) seal the rotating face to the shaft sleeve and the stationary seat to the gland plate.
mech-seal-orings.function: They close the leakage paths behind the two seal faces, leaving the face gap as the only intended leakage path. The O-ring on the spring-loaded face also allows that face to move axially to follow wear and shaft movements.
mech-seal-orings.operatingPrinciple: EagleBurgmann defines secondary seals as the seals that close off the rotating component on the shaft or sleeve and the stationary component in the housing. The O-rings are squeezed in their grooves and pressed further by the pressure of the liquid. The dynamic O-ring under the spring-loaded face must slide slightly on its counter-surface; if it swells, hardens or is trapped by deposits, the face cannot follow and the seal can open (hang-up). KSB stresses that a shaft seal is only as good as its O-rings and gives, as a selection guide, elastomers that swell less than 10 % in the operating liquid and do not react chemically with it.
mech-seal-orings.construction: Elastomer O-rings in machined grooves or bores of the rotating face holder and the gland plate. Some seals use PTFE wedges, bellows or other forms instead of O-rings.

materials.why: Economical elastomer with good resistance to water and mineral oils at moderate temperatures.
materials.limitations: Limited resistance to ozone, many solvents and higher temperatures.
materials.typicalService: Water and oil-containing liquids at moderate temperature.

materials.limitations: Some compounds are unsuitable for hot water, steam, amines or certain ketones; poorer low-temperature flexibility.

mech-seal-rotating-face.summary: The rotating seal face is the sealing ring of the mechanical seal that turns with the shaft and is pressed against the stationary seat.
mech-seal-rotating-face.function: It provides the rotating half of the sealing interface. In this design it is the spring-loaded face, so it moves axially to compensate for wear, thermal growth and small shaft movements.
mech-seal-rotating-face.operatingPrinciple: The face is driven by the retainer and pressed against the seat by the springs and by the hydraulic force of the seal chamber pressure. A thin liquid film forms between the faces. EagleBurgmann notes that the spring-backed ring can be either the rotating or the stationary one; here the springs rotate with the shaft. The face width and the balance diameter determine the face pressure and therefore heat generation and wear.
mech-seal-rotating-face.construction: A ring with a lapped sealing face, driven by lugs or pins of the retainer and sealed to the sleeve by a dynamic O-ring. In a hard/soft pair it is often the carbon graphite ring, but the material arrangement is a seal-maker choice.

materials.why: Self-lubricating, conformable and tolerant of brief emergency running.
materials.limitations: Damaged by abrasive particles; impregnants limit chemical compatibility; can blister in some services.

materials.why: Very hard and wear-resistant; used in hard/hard pairs for liquids with solids.
materials.limitations: Brittle; needs robust drive features to avoid damage.
materials.typicalService: Abrasive or viscous liquids as selected by the seal maker.

materials.why: Very tough with good wear resistance.
materials.limitations: Heat checking; binder corrosion in some liquids.

failureModes.signs: Reduced nose height (carbon), increasing leakage.

failureModes.cause: Dry running, vapour at the faces.

mech-seal-springs.summary: The seal springs provide the axial closing force that keeps the seal faces in contact, especially when the seal is not pressurised.
mech-seal-springs.function: They load the rotating face against the seat at standstill and start-up and compensate for face wear and axial shaft movement. EagleBurgmann notes that without spring backing an unpressurised mechanical seal would open.
mech-seal-springs.operatingPrinciple: The springs are compressed to a defined working length at installation, which sets the spring force. In operation the hydraulic force from the seal chamber pressure adds to the spring force. As the faces wear, the springs extend slightly and the force changes; the seal is designed so that the force remains adequate over its wear life.
mech-seal-springs.construction: This component seal uses springs mounted in the rotating retainer. Designs include a single large coil spring, multiple small springs or metal bellows; the choice is made by the seal maker. EagleBurgmann notes that springs are made almost exclusively from stainless spring steel or highly corrosion-resistant alloys, and that they can be protected or placed outside the liquid for contaminated or aggressive media. KSB notes that designs for higher sliding velocities use a stationary spring assembly, because rotating springs risk breaking under centrifugal force.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance with adequate spring properties.
materials.limitations: Chloride stress corrosion cracking in hot chloride-containing liquids.

materials.why: Higher resistance to chloride and chemical attack.
materials.limitations: Higher cost.

failureModes.cause: Solids, crystallisation or polymerisation of liquid around the springs.
failureModes.signs: Loss of closing force, leakage at low pressure or standstill.

failureModes.cause: Unsuitable spring material for the liquid.
failureModes.signs: Broken springs, corrosion products.

failureModes.cause: Incorrect setting length at installation.
failureModes.signs: Leakage (too little force) or rapid face wear and heat (too much force).

inspection: Inspect springs for corrosion, breakage and deposits when the seal is removed.
maintenance: Set the seal working length exactly to the seal drawing at installation.
Replace springs at seal refurbishment.

mech-seal-retainer.summary: The seal retainer (drive collar) is fixed to the shaft sleeve and transmits rotation to the rotating face while holding the springs.
mech-seal-retainer.function: It drives the rotating face so it turns with the shaft, holds and guides the springs, and fixes the axial position of the rotating part of the seal, which sets the spring compression.
mech-seal-retainer.operatingPrinciple: Set screws clamp the retainer to the sleeve at a measured axial position. Friction torque at the faces is transferred through drive pins or lugs from the face to the retainer and into the sleeve. If the retainer slips axially, the spring force changes and the faces can open or become overloaded.
mech-seal-retainer.construction: A machined ring with set-screw holes, spring pockets and drive features. In cartridge seals the equivalent part is mounted on a seal sleeve and pre-set by the seal maker.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance and good machinability.
materials.limitations: Chloride limits; set screws indent the sleeve.

materials.family: Duplex stainless steel or nickel alloys
materials.why: For more corrosive liquids.
materials.limitations: Higher cost.

failureModes.signs: Leakage due to changed spring compression.

failureModes.cause: Aggressive or solids-laden liquid.

maintenance: Mark and set the retainer position exactly as shown on the seal drawing; tighten set screws to the seal-maker requirement.

gland-follower.summary: The gland follower is the adjustable ring that is drawn into the stuffing box by the gland studs to compress the packing.
gland-follower.function: It applies and adjusts the axial load on the packing rings, which controls the sealing pressure and the leakage rate. It also retains the packing in the stuffing box.
gland-follower.operatingPrinciple: Tightening the gland nuts pushes the follower into the stuffing box, compressing the packing axially so that it expands radially against the sleeve and bore. The FSA/ESA manual shows that most of the radial sealing pressure develops in the rings nearest the follower. The follower must move squarely; if it tilts, the packing is loaded unevenly and the follower may touch the sleeve.
gland-follower.construction: A flanged ring with a nose that enters the stuffing box bore and two bolt holes for the gland studs; solid and split designs exist. Its bore has clearance to the sleeve. The FSA/ESA manual suggests limiting gland take-up to about two packing cross-sections (2W), after which repacking is due, and keeping at least 1W of nose entry to reduce the risk of cocking.

materials.why: Economical for water services with cast iron pumps.
materials.limitations: Corrosion from leakage; grey iron can crack if tightened unevenly.

materials.why: Corrosion resistant and less likely to damage the sleeve if contact occurs.
materials.limitations: Lower strength; limits in some chemicals.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance in chemical service.
materials.limitations: Galling if it contacts a stainless sleeve.

failureModes.signs: Leakage on one side, hot spot, follower rubbing the sleeve.

failureModes.cause: Packing consolidated over time.
failureModes.signs: No further adjustment possible, uncontrollable leakage.

failureModes.cause: Leakage onto the part, overtightening.
failureModes.signs: Rust, cracks at the bolt lugs.

Check the follower bore for contact marks.
maintenance: Tighten the nuts evenly in small steps; repack when the follower approaches the end of its travel.

packing-rings.summary: The packing rings are individual rings of braided compression packing installed in the stuffing box to seal along the shaft sleeve.
packing-rings.function: They form the sealing element of the packed gland, throttling leakage along the sleeve to a small, controlled amount that lubricates and cools the contact.
packing-rings.operatingPrinciple: Axial compression by the follower makes the rings expand radially against sleeve and bore. Leakage passes along the sleeve and through the packing, losing pressure progressively across the rings; according to the FSA/ESA manual most of the sealing force is developed in the rings nearest the gland. The packing structure retains lubricant, and the liquid film carries away friction heat. As the packing loses volume, gland adjustment restores the load.
packing-rings.construction: Rings are cut from braided packing or supplied die-formed. The FSA/ESA pump installation guidance recommends cutting rings on a mandrel of shaft diameter (butt, or square, joints are typical in rotating pumps), installing one ring at a time, seating each ring firmly, staggering joints at least 90 degrees apart, and never winding a continuous coil of packing into the box.

materials.family: PTFE and expanded PTFE yarn packings
materials.why: Chemically resistant with low friction.
materials.limitations: Cold flow and extrusion at higher temperatures and pressures; lower heat dissipation.
materials.typicalService: Chemical and clean liquids at moderate temperature.

materials.family: Carbon, graphite and flexible graphite packings (including ePTFE/graphite composites)
materials.why: Good heat dissipation and broad chemical inertness; low friction.
materials.limitations: Flexible graphite is fragile and wears in abrasive service.

lantern-ring.summary: The lantern ring (seal cage) is a perforated spacer between packing rings that distributes flush or sealing liquid around the shaft sleeve.
lantern-ring.function: It creates an annular space under the flush connection so that clean liquid can be introduced into the middle of the packing set. This cools and lubricates the packing, keeps abrasive particles out and, under suction lift, prevents air from entering the pump.
lantern-ring.operatingPrinciple: Liquid supplied at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure enters through the lantern ring and flows both towards the pump and out through the outer rings, so the packing is wetted by clean liquid instead of the pumped liquid. The FSA/ESA manual advises that the lantern ring must be installed so that it remains under the inlet as gland pressure is applied, and that the flush pressure should be at least 1 bar above the stuffing box pressure.
lantern-ring.construction: A split or solid ring with radial holes and grooves on its inner and outer diameters. The FSA/ESA manual gives a guideline lantern-ring length of about two packing cross-sections (2W) and notes that its position within the ring set (for example 2W on the pressure side and 3W on the gland side, or the reverse) should be agreed with the packing maker. KSB describes, for suction-lift operation with clean liquid, a lantern ring after the first packing ring fed from the discharge, and for contaminated liquids an external clean supply with the lantern ring as the innermost ring.

gland-studs.summary: The gland studs and nuts attach the gland follower to the stuffing box face and are used to adjust packing compression.
gland-studs.function: They transmit the adjustment force to the gland follower and hold it in position. Adjusting them evenly keeps the follower square.
gland-studs.operatingPrinciple: Turning the nuts moves the follower axially, increasing or reducing packing compression. Because adjustment is frequent and the area is wetted by leakage, thread condition and corrosion resistance are important. The FSA/ESA manual recommends taking up the gland bolts evenly and gradually.
gland-studs.construction: Two (sometimes more) studs screwed into the casing cover, with nuts and washers bearing on the follower. Some designs use swing bolts to make repacking easier.

materials.why: Resists corrosion from leakage, so nuts remain adjustable.
materials.limitations: Thread galling unless lubricated.

packing-flush-connection.summary: The packing flush connection is the port in the stuffing box that supplies flush or sealing liquid to the lantern ring.
packing-flush-connection.function: It delivers clean liquid to the lantern ring to cool and lubricate the packing, exclude abrasive solids and prevent air ingress under suction lift.
packing-flush-connection.operatingPrinciple: The supply may come from the pump discharge (filtered if necessary) or from an external clean source. The FSA/ESA manual advises a flush pressure at least 1 bar above stuffing box pressure and gives the approximation SBP = p_s + 0.25*TDH for end-suction pumps, with the stuffing box pressure close to suction pressure when the impeller has balance holes. KSB quotes a different rule of thumb for barrier liquid (about 10 % or at least 2 bar above the highest pressure to be sealed), so the packing maker and OEM values govern. Too little pressure lets pumped liquid or air enter the packing; the FSA/ESA manual warns that excessive flush pressure increases packing friction and wear and may dilute the product.
packing-flush-connection.construction: A tapped hole in the casing cover aligned with the lantern ring position, connected by tubing or pipe with an isolation valve and, often, a flow-control valve or flow indicator.

materials.why: Corrosion resistance and reliable joints.

bearing-assembly.summary: The bearing assembly is the oil-lubricated bearing frame that supports the overhung pump shaft radially and axially, locates the impeller in the casing and carries the hydraulic and mechanical loads into the pump support.
bearing-assembly.function: It supports the rotating shaft on two rolling bearings so that the impeller runs concentric with its wear rings and the seal faces run true. The inboard (radial) bearing near the impeller carries most of the radial load, while the outboard (thrust, locating) bearing near the coupling carries the residual axial thrust and fixes the axial position of the rotor. The housing also holds the oil bath, keeps contaminants out and conducts friction heat away from the bearings.
bearing-assembly.operatingPrinciple: Rolling elements roll between hardened raceways, so loads pass through small, elastically deformed contact areas with low friction. Hydraulic forces on the impeller (steady and fluctuating radial thrust and axial thrust) act at the overhung end of the shaft and are reacted by the two bearings, so shaft and housing behave like a beam on two supports. The bearings dip into an oil bath, and the rotating parts carry oil into the rolling contacts, where a thin pressure-generated oil film separates the surfaces when viscosity, speed and cleanliness are adequate. Heat generated by bearing friction flows into the housing and is dissipated to the surrounding air.
bearing-assembly.construction: The assembly consists of a bearing frame (adapter) bolted to the casing, a bearing housing forming the oil sump, an inboard radial bearing and an outboard thrust bearing. The thrust bearing inner ring is clamped against a shaft shoulder by a locknut and lock washer, and its outer ring is held axially in the housing by a retaining ring and end cover; the radial bearing is free to move axially in its housing bore (arrangement A) or permits axial movement inside the bearing (arrangement B). End covers with housing seals close both ends, and the housing carries an oil fill/vent plug, a sight glass and a drain plug. In back-pull-out construction the whole assembly is withdrawn together with the impeller, shaft seal and casing cover while the casing stays connected to the piping.

materials.why: Castable into complex shapes with oil sumps, bosses and fins, easy to machine and good at damping vibration; widely used for general-duty bearing frames and covers. Grey iron castings are specified, for example, to ASTM A48/A48M, which classifies them by tensile strength.
materials.limitations: Brittle, with low impact and thermal-shock resistance; it can crack if struck, if bolted onto an uneven surface or if overloaded through the structure.
materials.typicalService: General industrial and water services in normal ambient conditions.

materials.why: Higher strength and much greater ductility and impact resistance than grey iron while remaining castable; chosen where housings must tolerate shock, handling loads or vibration.
materials.limitations: More expensive than grey iron and with lower inherent vibration damping.
materials.typicalService: Process pumps with higher reliability requirements or exposure to mechanical shock.

materials.family: Through-hardened high-carbon chromium bearing steel (rings and rolling elements)
materials.why: Very high hardness and rolling-contact fatigue strength; standard dynamic load ratings (ISO 281) assume hardened bearing steel. Bearing-quality steel is specified, for example, to ASTM A295/A295M.
materials.limitations: Corrodes readily in the presence of water; hardness and dimensional stability are lost if the bearing is overheated, for example by flame heating during mounting.
materials.typicalService: Standard rolling bearings in oil-bath lubricated pump bearing frames.

failureModes.cause: Wrong oil level, wrong or degraded oil, excessive load or preload, misalignment, rubbing housing seals or heat from the pumped liquid.

inspection: Check the oil level in the sight glass and the oil appearance (clarity, colour, water) on every round; the reference level applies with the pump stopped, because the running level fluctuates slightly.
Trend bearing-housing temperatures against a baseline taken in good condition and against OEM limits.
Measure vibration on both bearing housings in horizontal, vertical and axial directions, using velocity for unbalance and misalignment and enveloped acceleration for bearing defects.
Take oil samples for analysis (water content, particles, viscosity, oxidation) at a frequency set from experience.
Look for oil leakage and contamination paths at housing seals, end covers, breather and drain.
maintenance: Change the oil at the OEM interval or as indicated by oil analysis, using the specified oil type and viscosity grade.
Keep the vent/breather clean and the fill point closed; clean the area before opening the housing.
Replace bearings with controlled mounting methods (heating or pressing on the interference-fit ring only, cleanliness, correct orientation) and renew lock washers and housing seals.
Re-check coupling alignment after any work on the bearing frame or after reinstalling the back-pull-out unit.

keyConcepts.title: Why the pump needs bearings: radial and axial load
keyConcepts.body: A rotating shaft must be held concentric with the stationary parts and fixed in its axial position while it turns. In this pump a closed impeller runs with small radial clearances at the wear rings (an open impeller with a small axial clearance to the casing), and the mechanical seal faces need a stable shaft, so excessive shaft movement shortens their life. Bearings provide this support with low friction. A radial load acts perpendicular to the shaft axis (rotor weight, hydraulic radial thrust, unbalance, coupling reaction forces). An axial (thrust) load acts along the axis (hydraulic axial thrust and any axial force from a coupling set at the wrong shaft-end distance). Bearing types suit different load directions: deep groove ball bearings carry mainly radial load but also some axial load, NU-type cylindrical roller bearings carry radial load only, and angular contact ball bearings combine radial load with substantial axial load in the direction set by their contact angle. The basic rating life of a rolling bearing under a constant equivalent load P is L10 = (C/P)^p million revolutions, where C is the basic dynamic load rating and p = 3 for ball bearings or 10/3 for roller bearings; at speed n in r/min, L10h = (10^6/(60*n))*L10 hours.

keyConcepts.title: How impeller loads reach the bearings
keyConcepts.body: The impeller sits on the overhung end of the shaft, outside the two bearings, and two hydraulic forces act on it. Radial thrust arises because the pressure around a single-volute impeller is not uniform; KSB gives the steady value as R = K*rho*g*H*D2*B2, where K is an empirical coefficient that is smallest near the best efficiency point and rises steeply at part load and overload, H is the head, D2 the impeller outside diameter and B2 the impeller outlet width. Axial thrust results mainly from the different pressures acting on the front and back shrouds of a single-suction impeller, plus momentum and shaft-seal pressure forces; KSB notes that it is higher during start-up than in steady operation and that doubling the suction-side gap-seal (wear-ring) clearance raises its axial thrust coefficient by about 8 percent. The radial force passes from the impeller hub into the shaft through the bore fit and key, and the axial force through the shaft shoulder or the impeller nut and washer, depending on its direction. Treating the shaft as a beam on two supports with a radial force F at an overhang a beyond the inboard bearing and a bearing span L, statics gives an inboard reaction F*(L + a)/L and an outboard reaction F*a/L acting in the opposite direction, so the inboard bearing carries more than the impeller force itself. Axial thrust is reacted only by the outboard locating bearing, via the shaft shoulder or locknut, the bearing, its retaining ring and the housing.

keyConcepts.title: Lubrication: oil bath, correct level and contamination
keyConcepts.body: SKF states that the bearings of horizontal process pumps are most frequently oil-bath lubricated. With the pump stopped, the oil level is set at about the centre of the lowest rolling element of the bearing; a sight glass is needed to set and check it, and the level seen while running varies slightly because of splashing. Too low a level starves the rolling contacts; too high a level increases churning friction and temperature and can push oil past the housing seals. Some designs add a constant-level oiler that holds the set level, or an oil ring or slinger that lifts oil to the bearings; the required level then differs, so the OEM marking governs. The oil type and ISO viscosity grade (ISO 3448) are chosen by the OEM for the expected housing temperature: SKF recommends quality mineral oils with a viscosity index of at least 95 and advises against multigrade oils and oils with detergents, and one pump manufacturer specifies rust- and oxidation-inhibited oil and prohibits detergent oils. Contamination is a leading cause of bearing distress: water from condensation, wash-down or seal leakage weakens the oil film and corrodes the raceways, and solid particles dent them. Regular oil analysis helps set the change interval.

keyConcepts.title: Why bearings overheat
keyConcepts.body: Bearing temperature is the balance between heat generated in the bearing (friction moment multiplied by speed) and heat removed through shaft, housing and baseplate, plus heat flowing in from the pumped liquid or from rubbing contact seals (SKF). Common causes of overheating are: an oil level that is too high (churning) or too low (starvation); wrong, degraded or contaminated oil; excessive load from operation far from the best efficiency point, worn wear rings that raise axial thrust, unbalance or misalignment; excessive preload or interference from wrong fits or too little internal clearance; a thrust pair mounted in the wrong orientation; an inboard bearing whose outer ring cannot slide, so that shaft growth preloads both bearings; rubbing housing seals; and a housing that is insulated, covered in dirt or starved of air. Rising temperature can become self-reinforcing: oil viscosity falls as temperature rises, thinning the lubricant film, and a shaft and inner ring that run hotter than the housing reduce the internal clearance or raise the preload of the bearings. Temperature should therefore be trended against a baseline and compared with OEM limits rather than judged by touch.

keyConcepts.title: How rolling bearings fail (ISO 15243 classification)
keyConcepts.body: ISO 15243 classifies rolling bearing damage that occurs in service into six main modes: rolling contact fatigue (subsurface-initiated, or surface-initiated by poor lubrication or contamination), wear (abrasive or adhesive), corrosion (moisture corrosion, and frictional corrosion such as fretting and false brinelling), electrical erosion (current passing through the bearing), plastic deformation (overload, or indentations from debris and handling) and cracking and fracture. Classic subsurface fatigue at the end of the calculated life is the minority case in pumps: SKF notes that field failures are more often caused by contamination, wear, misalignment, corrosion, or lubrication or seal failure. Examining the damaged bearing (load-zone pattern, discolouration, indentations, corrosion marks) together with the drained oil usually points to the root cause, which must be corrected before a replacement bearing is fitted, otherwise the new bearing is likely to fail in the same way. In vibration data, developing rolling-element defects appear first as low-amplitude, high-frequency signals, which enveloped-acceleration measurements are designed to detect before overall vibration rises.

keyConcepts.title: Vibration and misalignment
keyConcepts.body: Bearings are both a path and a victim of vibration. Unbalance gives a dominant once-per-revolution (1x) vibration; SKF notes that angular misalignment between shafts causes axial vibration at running speed and parallel misalignment causes radial vibration at twice or three times running speed, with 1x and 2x often appearing together. Misalignment makes the flexible coupling impose cyclic forces and moments on both shafts, adding load to the thrust and radial bearings. Back-to-back angular contact pairs and cylindrical roller bearings tolerate only a few minutes of arc of misalignment between shaft and housing before internal stresses rise sharply (SKF). Vibration is measured on the bearing housings in horizontal, vertical and axial directions. ISO 10816-7 gives instructions for evaluating bearing-housing vibration of industrial rotodynamic pumps, and ISO 20816-3 covers other industrial machines including flexibly coupled electric motors; such evaluations consider both the vibration magnitude and changes from a baseline, and in practice they are used together with trends and the OEM acceptance values. Causes outside the bearing (low-flow hydraulic forces, cavitation, pipe strain, a weak foundation) must be ruled out before bearings are blamed.

keyConcepts.title: Replacing bearings correctly
keyConcepts.body: Bearing replacement is precision work. Before dismantling, record the bearing designations and the orientation of angular contact bearings, paired sets and retaining rings, and compare the old part numbers with the OEM specification. Work in a clean area and keep new bearings in their packaging until they are fitted. Check the shaft and housing seats for size, roundness, profile and damage against the OEM drawing. Bearings with an interference fit are mounted either mechanically, with the force applied only to the ring that has the interference fit, or by heating: SKF recommends an induction heater with a thermostat, warns never to heat a bearing above 120 °C and states that an open flame is never acceptable. Rings, cages and rolling elements must never receive direct blows, and mounting or dismounting force must never pass through the rolling elements, because this dents the raceways. Paired angular contact bearings are heated and fitted together, and the locknut is tightened again after cooling to remove gaps. Renew lock washers and housing seals, refill with the specified oil, and re-check coupling alignment.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing arrangements A and B in this model
keyConcepts.body: The model offers two common arrangements; real pumps vary by manufacturer, size and specification. In both, the inboard bearing (nearest the impeller) is the radial, non-locating bearing and the outboard bearing (nearest the coupling) is the locating thrust bearing, so shaft thermal growth is accommodated at the inboard end while the impeller axial position is fixed from the outboard end. Arrangement A uses a single-row deep groove ball bearing inboard, free to slide axially in its housing bore, and a double-row angular contact ball bearing outboard that carries axial load in both directions; one ANSI chemical-process pump manufacturer, for example, lists exactly this combination. Arrangement B uses an NU-type cylindrical roller bearing inboard, which carries higher radial load and allows axial displacement inside the bearing, and a pair of single-row angular contact ball bearings mounted back-to-back outboard; SKF describes cylindrical roller bearings as typically used as the non-locating radial bearing in end-suction process pumps and recommends the back-to-back pair for most pump applications. Other designs use deep groove ball bearings in both positions, duplex angular contact sets with a deep groove inboard bearing, tapered roller bearings where combined radial and axial loads are high (SKF cites slurry applications), or plain bearings, such as the product-lubricated bearings of magnetic-drive pumps.

bearing-frame.summary: The bearing frame (adapter) is the cast intermediate structure that joins the bearing housing to the pump casing and keeps the shaft centred in the casing bore.
bearing-frame.function: It connects the bearing housing to the hydraulic end and carries the bearing reaction forces into the casing and the pump support. Machined spigot (rabbet) fits at both ends keep the shaft axis concentric with the casing, seal chamber and wear rings. Openings in the frame give access to the shaft seal and allow seal leakage to be seen and drained.
bearing-frame.operatingPrinciple: The frame acts as a stiff bracket loaded in bending and torsion by the overhung rotor loads that the bearings pass to it. Its stiffness limits the relative deflection between bearing housing and casing, helping to keep the impeller centred under radial thrust. Because it locates the casing cover and bearing housing by machined fits rather than by bolts alone, concentricity is restored each time the back-pull-out unit is reassembled.
bearing-frame.construction: It is usually a single casting with a front flange that bolts to the casing and a rear bore or flange that receives the bearing housing. The front and rear spigot fits are machined for concentricity, and one manufacturer describes a spigot fit between casing and bearing housing (adapter) for this purpose. Windows give access to the gland or seal and are normally closed by splash or shaft guards, and a drain may be provided for seal leakage. Many designs combine frame and bearing housing in one bearing bracket, and the support foot may be on either part.

Carry out the run-out checks the OEM specifies after reassembly.

bearing-housing.summary: The bearing housing holds the inboard and outboard bearings in precision bores and forms the oil sump that lubricates them.
bearing-housing.function: It positions both bearings on a common axis and passes their loads to the bearing frame and the support foot. It contains the oil bath, carries the sight glass, fill/vent and drain connections, and together with the end covers and housing seals keeps lubricant in and contaminants out. Its outer surface dissipates bearing friction heat to the surroundings.
bearing-housing.operatingPrinciple: The two bearing bores are machined in line so that the bearings are not misaligned relative to each other, which matters because angular contact pairs and cylindrical roller bearings tolerate only small misalignment. SKF gives ISO H6 as its standard recommended housing tolerance for pump bearings; it results in a slight clearance between outer ring and housing that eases assembly and, in the non-locating position, lets a ball bearing outer ring slide axially, while SKF advises an interference housing fit for cylindrical roller bearings where impeller unbalance could make the outer ring rotate. The outboard bearing is located axially. The rotating bearings dip into and splash the oil, which drains back into the sump, and heat flows by conduction to the housing walls and by convection to ambient air.
bearing-housing.construction: It is typically one casting with two machined bearing bores, an oil sump below the shaft and bosses for the sight glass, fill/vent plug and drain plug. End covers bolt to each end and carry the housing seals. Manufacturer variations include cooling fins, a water-cooling jacket or coil, a constant-level oiler connection, a purge-air or oil-mist connection, and an adjustable outboard bearing carrier for setting the axial clearance of open impellers.

failureModes.signs: Polished or oxidised bores, outer ring loose in bore, rising 1x vibration.

inboard-bearing-dgbb.summary: In arrangement A the inboard (radial) bearing is a single-row deep groove ball bearing that supports the shaft near the impeller and lets the shaft grow axially.
inboard-bearing-dgbb.function: It supports the shaft radially at the end nearest the impeller, where the radial reaction is largest because of the overhang. It acts as the non-locating bearing, so that thermal expansion of the shaft does not load the bearings axially against each other. Deep groove ball bearings can also carry some axial load, but in this arrangement the axial thrust is assigned to the outboard bearing.
inboard-bearing-dgbb.operatingPrinciple: Balls roll in deep, closely conforming grooves in the inner and outer rings, and the inner ring rotates with the shaft on an interference fit. The outer ring sits in the housing bore with a slight clearance fit, so it can slide axially when the shaft lengthens with temperature while its load zone stays stationary. Load passes through small elastic contact areas separated by a thin oil film, so friction and heat stay low as long as the film is maintained. Like all rolling bearings it needs a minimum load to prevent the balls skidding; for horizontal pumps SKF notes that the weight of the supported components together with external forces generally exceeds the required minimum load.
inboard-bearing-dgbb.construction: The bearing consists of an inner ring, an outer ring, a set of balls and a cage of pressed steel, polyamide or machined brass. For pumps SKF prefers Conrad-type bearings, assembled without a filling slot, because they run at lower temperatures than filling-slot designs in similar conditions. Open bearings are used with oil-bath lubrication, whereas shielded versions are used in some grease-lubricated designs. The designation, internal clearance class and cage type are specified by the pump OEM.

inboard-bearing-crb.summary: In arrangement B the inboard (radial) bearing is an NU-type single-row cylindrical roller bearing that gives high radial capacity near the impeller while letting the shaft grow axially inside the bearing.
inboard-bearing-crb.function: It carries the large radial reaction at the impeller end of the overhung shaft. Because an NU bearing has no flanges on its inner ring, the shaft and inner ring can move axially relative to the rollers and outer ring, so it is the non-locating bearing of the arrangement. It carries no axial load; axial thrust goes to the outboard angular contact pair.
inboard-bearing-crb.operatingPrinciple: Cylindrical rollers make line contact with the raceways, which gives a higher radial load capacity and stiffness than ball contact in a bearing of similar size. The rollers are guided between flanges on the outer ring and run on a plain cylindrical inner-ring raceway, so thermal expansion is taken as axial movement inside the bearing rather than between a ring and its seat. As a result both rings can have firm fits, and SKF notes that an interference housing fit should be used where impeller unbalance could otherwise make the outer ring rotate. Line contact makes the bearing sensitive to misalignment, and like all rolling bearings it needs a minimum radial load to prevent the rollers skidding.
inboard-bearing-crb.construction: The bearing is separable: the outer ring with rollers and cage is mounted separately from the inner ring, which SKF notes simplifies mounting. NU and NUP types are used in pumps, and SKF prefers the NU type in the non-locating position because it accommodates axial displacement inside the bearing. Cages are glass-fibre reinforced polyamide 66, pressed steel or machined brass. SKF gives the maximum allowable misalignment of these bearings as three to four minutes of arc depending on series, which is usually achievable when both housing bores are machined in one setup.

outboard-bearing-ddrac.summary: In arrangement A the outboard (thrust) bearing is a double-row angular contact ball bearing that fixes the shaft axially and carries the impeller axial thrust in either direction together with radial load.
outboard-bearing-ddrac.function: It is the locating bearing: its inner ring is clamped to the shaft and its outer ring is held in the housing, so it sets the axial position of the rotor and the impeller in the casing. It carries the residual hydraulic axial thrust, whose magnitude changes with flow rate and during start-up and whose direction can reverse, for example with high suction pressure (SKF), together with the smaller radial reaction at the outboard end.
outboard-bearing-ddrac.operatingPrinciple: Each ball row has a contact angle, so the line through the ball contacts is inclined to the radial plane and the row can transmit axial as well as radial load. The two rows face opposite directions in a back-to-back configuration, so one row carries thrust towards the impeller and the other carries thrust towards the coupling; the contact angle differs between makers and series (30 degrees in SKF and MRC standard designs, 40 degrees in an SKF two-piece-inner-ring series, 25 degrees in one NSK series). A double-row bearing behaves like two single-row bearings arranged back-to-back in less axial space, giving a stiff support that also resists tilting moments. SKF states that it must always be subjected to a given minimum radial load, particularly at high speed, high acceleration or rapid changes in load direction, otherwise damaging sliding between balls and raceways can occur.
outboard-bearing-ddrac.construction: The bearing has one outer ring and one inner ring (a two-piece inner ring in some series), two rows of balls and a cage. Its axial internal clearance is set by the bearing maker. The inner ring is clamped against a shaft shoulder by a locknut and lock washer, and SKF advises that the outer ring be clamped only loosely or, preferably, given a very small axial clearance in the housing. Designs with filling slots exist; SKF prefers Conrad-type bearings for pumps and warns that filling-slot bearings must be oriented so that the axial load does not pass through the filling-slot side.

keyConcepts.title: Why angular contact bearings carry the axial thrust
keyConcepts.body: In a deep groove ball bearing the balls touch the raceways close to the radial plane, so axial load is carried only through a small inclination of the contact under load. An angular contact bearing has raceways offset so that the contact line is deliberately inclined at a contact angle alpha to the radial plane. A force along that line has a radial component proportional to cos(alpha) and an axial component proportional to sin(alpha), so the bearing carries substantial axial load in one direction; the larger the contact angle, the better suited the bearing is to axial load relative to radial load. The same geometry means that a purely radial load also generates an internal axial force (NSK), which must be reacted by an opposed row or bearing. Pump axial thrust is therefore given to angular contact bearings at the locating position, while the radial bearing at the impeller end is left free axially. In a double-row bearing the two opposed rows take thrust in both directions, which matters because the impeller thrust changes with operating conditions and can reverse, for example at high suction pressure or when balance holes or back vanes no longer work as designed (SKF).

keyConcepts.title: Why the rows are arranged back-to-back
keyConcepts.body: In a back-to-back (O) arrangement the contact lines of the two rows diverge towards the bearing axis, so their effective load centres are spread further apart than the physical width of the bearing. This wider effective spread gives a stiff support that resists tilting moments, which helps hold the overhung rotor and impeller in position. In a double-row bearing the axial internal clearance is built in by the maker, and in a pair of single-row bearings it results from clamping the inner rings together, so in neither case does the outer ring need heavy axial clamping. The price is sensitivity to misalignment: because the arrangement resists tilting, any angular error between shaft and housing becomes extra ball load and cage stress. A face-to-face (X) arrangement, in which the contact lines converge, tolerates misalignment better and is used where misalignment cannot be avoided, while a tandem arrangement adds capacity in one direction only. NSK describes a double-row angular contact bearing as essentially a back-to-back arrangement of two single-row bearings sharing one inner and one outer ring, able to carry radial loads, axial loads in both directions and moments; SKF adds that it is compact and easy to mount.

outboard-bearing-pair.summary: In arrangement B the outboard (thrust) bearing is a matched pair of single-row angular contact ball bearings mounted back-to-back, which locates the shaft and carries axial thrust in both directions.
outboard-bearing-pair.function: The pair is the locating bearing: the inner rings are clamped together on the shaft and the outer rings are held in the housing, so the axial position of the rotor is fixed. One bearing of the pair carries thrust towards the impeller, the other carries thrust towards the coupling, and both share the outboard radial reaction. SKF states that single-row 40 degree angular contact ball bearings are widely used in medium- and heavy-duty centrifugal pumps, and that universally matchable versions can be arranged in pairs to carry load in either axial direction.
outboard-bearing-pair.operatingPrinciple: Each single-row angular contact bearing can carry axial load in one direction only, and a radial load on it produces an internal axial force component, so it must always work against a second bearing. Mounted back-to-back, the two contact lines diverge, giving a wide effective spread and high stiffness against tilting. Universally matchable bearings are manufactured so that, mounted immediately adjacent and clamped through the inner rings, the pair has a defined axial internal clearance or preload class without shims. SKF explains that a suitable preload limits ball skidding and contact-angle variation and increases stiffness, but too much preload raises friction and can lead to loss of heat balance.
outboard-bearing-pair.construction: Two single-row bearings, commonly with a 40 degree contact angle, are mounted back-to-back with their inner rings clamped together by a locknut and lock washer. SKF recommends machined brass cages for heavy-duty service and reports that API 610 calls for pump thrust loads to be carried by two 40 degree single-row angular contact bearings arranged back-to-back; check the current edition of the standard. Matched sets combining a 40 degree and a 15 degree bearing also exist for thrust acting mainly in one direction, and SKF cautions that they should not be used where the direction of axial load is unknown.

keyConcepts.title: Why angular contact bearings carry the axial thrust
keyConcepts.body: An angular contact ball bearing has its raceways offset so that the line of contact between ball and rings is inclined at a contact angle alpha to the radial plane. A load along this line has a radial component proportional to cos(alpha) and an axial component proportional to sin(alpha), so with a steep angle such as the 40 degrees commonly used for pump thrust bearings a large share of its capacity is available for axial load. Each single-row bearing carries axial load in one direction only; NSK notes that, because of the contact angle, a radial load on it also generates an axial force, which is why such bearings are mounted in pairs or sets. In the pump, the hydraulic axial thrust of a closed impeller is usually directed towards the suction side, but its magnitude changes with flow rate and during start-up (KSB), and SKF notes that its direction can reverse, for example with increased suction pressure, so the locating bearing must hold the rotor in both directions. A pair of opposed angular contact bearings at the outboard end does this, while the inboard cylindrical roller bearing allows the shaft to grow freely.

keyConcepts.title: Why back-to-back pairs are used
keyConcepts.body: Three standard arrangements exist for a pair of angular contact bearings. In a back-to-back (O, DB) pair the contact lines diverge towards the axis; the effective load centres lie far apart, giving high stiffness against tilting moments, and the clearance or preload of the pair is set by clamping the inner rings, so the outer rings need no axial clamping. In a face-to-face (X, DF) pair the contact lines converge; the pair is less stiff against tilting but more tolerant of misalignment, and SKF uses it where misalignment is unavoidable, for example with slender shafts. In a tandem (DT) pair both bearings face the same way and share load in one direction only. SKF recommends the back-to-back arrangement for most pump applications because of its ability to support tilting moments and its simple clamping, and it reports that API 610 specifies back-to-back pairs of 40 degree bearings for pump thrust loads. The trade-off is sensitivity to misalignment between shaft and housing, which back-to-back pairs can only accommodate through increased ball loads and cage stresses.

bearing-retainer.summary: The bearing retaining ring holds the outer ring of the outboard thrust bearing axially in the housing so that axial thrust is passed from the bearing into the housing.
bearing-retainer.function: Together with a housing shoulder or the outboard end cover it fixes the outer ring of the locating bearing in both axial directions. It therefore carries the axial thrust acting in one direction and helps set the axial position of the rotor.
bearing-retainer.operatingPrinciple: Axial thrust travels from the impeller through the shaft shoulder or locknut into the inner ring, across the balls to the outer ring and then into the housing through either the housing shoulder or the retainer, depending on the thrust direction. The retainer must be seated correctly and be stiff enough to carry the maximum reverse thrust without shifting, otherwise the rotor gains axial float. SKF advises that the outer rings of double-row and paired back-to-back bearings be clamped only loosely or, preferably, given a very small axial clearance, so the retainer locates the bearing without distorting it.
bearing-retainer.construction: Depending on design it is a spring-steel snap ring seated in a groove of the housing or bearing carrier, or a machined ring bolted to the housing with cap screws. One pump manufacturer uses a snap ring on its smaller frame groups and a bearing retainer secured by cap screws on its largest group and with duplex angular contact bearings, and stresses the correct orientation of each. The retainer is distinct from the shaft locknut and lock washer, which clamp the inner rings to the shaft.

materials.limitations: Permanently deformed if over-compressed during fitting; corrodes if water enters the housing.

materials.why: Gives a rigid, flat clamping face and a reliable bolted fixing for higher thrust loads.
materials.limitations: Screws need controlled tightening and securing against loosening.
materials.typicalService: Thrust bearing retention in medium and large bearing housings.

bearing-end-cover-inboard.summary: The inboard bearing end cover closes the impeller end of the bearing housing and carries the inboard housing seal.
bearing-end-cover-inboard.function: It closes the housing bore on the side facing the shaft seal and impeller, keeping oil in the sump and helping to exclude water, product leakage and dirt. It holds the inboard housing seal concentric with the shaft. In some designs it also forms an axial stop for a bearing ring or a deflector against spray from the seal area.
bearing-end-cover-inboard.operatingPrinciple: The cover is a stationary closure piloted on the housing bore, so the seal it carries runs concentric with the shaft. Oil thrown off by the bearing is returned to the sump, in many designs through drain-back passages in the cover. Because the inboard end faces the shaft seal, it is the side most exposed to liquid leakage, wash-down water and condensation, so cover and seal together form the first barrier against water entering the oil.
bearing-end-cover-inboard.construction: It is a cast or machined ring bolted or pressed into the housing and sealed to it by a gasket or O-ring. Its central bore holds a lip seal, labyrinth seal or bearing isolator. Some housings have no separate inboard cover, and the seal is fitted directly in the housing or frame.

materials.why: Castable into complex shapes with oil sumps, bosses and fins, easy to machine and good at damping vibration; widely used for general-duty bearing frames and covers. Grey iron castings are specified, for example, to ASTM A48/A48M, which classifies them by tensile strength.
materials.limitations: Brittle, with low impact and thermal-shock resistance; it can crack if struck, if bolted onto an uneven surface or if overloaded through the structure.
materials.typicalService: General industrial and water services in normal ambient conditions.

materials.why: High toughness and weldability; used for larger frames, for designs fabricated from plate, or where a purchaser specification calls for steel.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection; welded designs may need stress relieving before final machining to keep the bores and fits accurate.

failureModes.cause: Damaged or reused gasket or O-ring, uneven tightening.
failureModes.signs: Oil weeping at the cover joint, falling oil level.

failureModes.cause: Worn housing seal or blocked drain-back path in a wet environment.
failureModes.signs: Milky oil, corrosion inside the cover.

failureModes.cause: Over-tightening or impact.
failureModes.signs: Seal running eccentric, rubbing or leakage.

inspection: Check for oil leakage and corrosion around the cover on routine rounds.
At overhaul, check the seal bore, pilot fit and drain-back passages.
Check that the seal runs concentric and does not rub.
maintenance: Renew the gasket or O-ring whenever the cover is removed.
Clean drain-back passages and tighten fasteners evenly to the OEM torque.
Install the housing seal square and concentric using the correct tool.

bearing-end-cover-outboard.summary: The outboard bearing end cover closes the coupling end of the bearing housing, carries the outboard housing seal and in many designs helps locate the thrust bearing.
bearing-end-cover-outboard.function: It closes the housing at the coupling end and supports the outboard housing seal around the shaft extension. In many designs its spigot bears against the thrust bearing outer ring, or against the retainer, to fix the outer ring axially. In some pumps with open impellers this part is an adjustable bearing carrier used to set the impeller axial clearance.
bearing-end-cover-outboard.operatingPrinciple: When the cover clamps the outer ring of the thrust bearing, the axial position of the rotor depends on the spigot length and on any shims or gasket thickness, and thrust towards the coupling passes through the cover and its bolts into the housing. Its bore guides the housing seal concentric with the shaft. In adjustable-carrier designs, turning the carrier moves the whole rotor axially by a known amount per step, so the impeller clearance can be reset after wear (one manufacturer example).
bearing-end-cover-outboard.construction: It is a cast or machined flanged part bolted to the housing with a gasket or O-ring and a central bore for the housing seal. Depending on design it includes a clamping spigot, a shim pack or a threaded bearing carrier with lugs for adjustment. Its outer face faces the coupling area and is exposed to airborne dust, weather and any wash-down spray there.

materials.why: Castable into complex shapes with oil sumps, bosses and fins, easy to machine and good at damping vibration; widely used for general-duty bearing frames and covers. Grey iron castings are specified, for example, to ASTM A48/A48M, which classifies them by tensile strength.
materials.limitations: Brittle, with low impact and thermal-shock resistance; it can crack if struck, if bolted onto an uneven surface or if overloaded through the structure.
materials.typicalService: General industrial and water services in normal ambient conditions.

materials.why: High toughness and weldability; used for larger frames, for designs fabricated from plate, or where a purchaser specification calls for steel.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection; welded designs may need stress relieving before final machining to keep the bores and fits accurate.

failureModes.cause: Wrong spigot length, shims or gasket thickness; over- or under-tightening.
failureModes.signs: Excess rotor end play, or a hot thrust bearing from start-up.

failureModes.cause: Damaged gasket, worn seal bore, overfilling.
failureModes.signs: Oil on the coupling guard area and baseplate.

failureModes.cause: Vibration or thrust load reversals.
failureModes.signs: Axial movement of the rotor, fretting on the cover face.

inspection: Check rotor end play against the OEM value after assembly.
Look for oil leakage at the joint and around the shaft.
Check fastener tightness on routine inspections.
maintenance: Renew the gasket or O-ring and set shims exactly as the OEM specifies.
Tighten fasteners evenly to the OEM torque.
For adjustable carriers, follow the OEM procedure for setting impeller clearance and lock the carrier afterwards.
