bearing-oil-seal-inboard.summary: The inboard bearing housing seal seals the shaft where it leaves the bearing housing towards the shaft seal, keeping oil in and water, product and dust out.
bearing-oil-seal-inboard.function: It retains the lubricating oil at the impeller end of the bearing housing. It excludes liquids and solids, which on this side include seal leakage, flush or wash-down water and condensation. Because contamination is one of the main causes of pump bearing failure, the condition of this seal directly affects bearing life.
bearing-oil-seal-inboard.operatingPrinciple: Two principles are common. A radial lip seal presses a spring-loaded elastomer lip onto the shaft; SKF notes that it depends on a lubricant supply and a good shaft finish, that excessive friction causes heat and wear of seal and shaft, and that lip seal life is usually short. A labyrinth seal or bearing isolator is non-contacting: a rotor and stator form a narrow labyrinth path that returns oil to the housing and resists the entry of contaminants, with little friction, no shaft wear and long life. Magnetic face seals are a further option used in some housings.
bearing-oil-seal-inboard.construction: It is either an elastomer lip seal with a metal case and garter spring pressed into the cover bore, or a two-part bearing isolator consisting of a stationary stator fitted in the bore and a rotor driven by the shaft through an O-ring. Garlock notes that isolators can often fit in the same space as a lip seal. One pump manufacturer states that bearing isolators must not be reused once removed.

materials.family: Elastomer lip on a metal case (radial lip seal)
materials.why: Simple and inexpensive, with good sealing while new and well lubricated.
materials.limitations: Contacting design: wears and can groove the shaft, generates heat, and fails quickly if run dry or if dirt embeds under the lip; elastomer compatibility with oil and temperature must be checked.
materials.typicalService: Clean, dry environments and general-duty pumps.

materials.family: Metallic or polymer labyrinth seal / bearing isolator
materials.why: Non-contacting rotor-stator design with long life that does not wear the shaft and protects against contaminants in harsh environments.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; some designs need a sealed (flooded) version where the oil level reaches the seal; follow the maker on shaft run-out and misalignment limits.
materials.typicalService: Process pumps in wet, dusty or wash-down environments.

failureModes.cause: Dry running, dirt embedded under the lip, long service time.
failureModes.signs: Oil leakage, groove on the shaft or sleeve, water in oil.

failureModes.cause: Worn seal, direct spray or wash-down at the shaft, blocked isolator drain.
failureModes.signs: Milky oil, corrosion inside the housing.

failureModes.cause: Excessive lip pressure, misalignment or lack of oil at the lip.
failureModes.signs: Hardened, cracked lip; local heat at the cover.

inspection: Check for oil leakage at the shaft and for water in the oil on routine rounds.
At overhaul, inspect the shaft surface under a lip seal for grooving.
Check that isolator drain or expulsion openings are clear and oriented as the maker specifies.
maintenance: Replace lip seals whenever the bearings are replaced, and do not reuse isolators where the OEM forbids it.
Protect the lip during installation by covering keyways and sharp edges, and lightly lubricate it.
Avoid directing wash-down water at the shaft and housing seals.

bearing-oil-seal-outboard.summary: The outboard bearing housing seal seals the shaft where it leaves the bearing housing towards the coupling, keeping oil in and dust, rain and spray out.
bearing-oil-seal-outboard.function: It retains the oil at the coupling end of the bearing housing around the shaft extension. It excludes dust, rain and splash from the coupling side. With the inboard seal it keeps the oil bath clean, which is a precondition for long bearing life.
bearing-oil-seal-outboard.operatingPrinciple: It works on the same principles as the inboard seal: a contacting lip seal relies on a lubricated lip pressed onto the shaft, while a non-contacting labyrinth or bearing isolator uses a narrow rotor-stator path that returns oil and resists the entry of dirt. On the outboard side the main contaminants are airborne dust and weather rather than seal leakage. Because the coupling hub sits close to this seal, dirt can accumulate in the gap between hub and cover unless it is kept clean.
bearing-oil-seal-outboard.construction: It is a radial lip seal or a bearing isolator fitted in the outboard end cover around the shaft extension. Its size and type usually match the inboard seal. Some housings use a magnetic face seal instead.

materials.family: Elastomer lip on a metal case (radial lip seal)
materials.why: Simple and economical seal for clean environments.
materials.limitations: Wears and can groove the shaft; short life if run dry or exposed to dirt.

materials.family: Metallic or polymer labyrinth seal / bearing isolator
materials.why: Non-contacting, long-life protection against dust and weather without shaft wear.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; installation tolerances specified by the maker must be respected.

failureModes.cause: Worn lip, damaged isolator O-ring, overfilled housing or blocked vent.
failureModes.signs: Oil on the shaft, coupling hub and guard.

failureModes.cause: Worn seal in a dusty environment.
failureModes.signs: Dark oil with fine particles, rising bearing vibration.

failureModes.mode: Shaft grooving under a lip seal
failureModes.cause: Long service, dirt embedded under the lip, poor lubrication of the lip.
failureModes.signs: Visible groove at the seal position on the shaft.

inspection: Check for oil on the shaft and coupling hub during guarded inspections.
Inspect oil for fine dust in dusty locations.
At overhaul, inspect the shaft surface at the seal and the seal bore.
maintenance: Replace with the OEM-specified seal type whenever bearings are replaced.
Clean the area between coupling hub and end cover during coupling work.
Do not overfill the housing; correct the cause of any oil leakage before refilling.

oil-fill-plug.summary: The oil fill/vent plug closes the filling opening at the top of the bearing housing and, in vented designs, lets the housing breathe as it warms and cools.
oil-fill-plug.function: It provides a clean opening for adding oil to the sump and closes it against dirt and water in operation. In vent or breather versions it equalises the housing pressure with the atmosphere, so that thermal expansion of air and oil does not push oil past the housing seals. Some designs use a solid plug instead of a breather.
oil-fill-plug.operatingPrinciple: As the housing warms, the air above the oil expands; a breather lets it escape and lets air back in on cooling. If the breather is blocked, the pressure difference can force oil out through the housing seals or draw air in through them. Every breathing cycle can also draw in humid air, so condensation becomes a source of water in the oil; one manufacturer offers a purge connection for instrument air or nitrogen to limit dirt ingress and dew-point problems.
oil-fill-plug.construction: It is a threaded plug or breather cap screwed into a boss on top of the bearing housing, sometimes with a small filter element. In one manufacturer manual the filling procedure is to clean and remove the vent/breather, pour oil until it is halfway up the sight glass and refit the breather. On one of that manufacturer's power-end versions the breather is replaced by a plug.

materials.family: Zinc-plated or painted carbon steel (plugs and fittings)
materials.why: Inexpensive and strong enough for threaded plugs in cast housings.
materials.limitations: Corrodes in wet or marine atmospheres; threads can seize if not lubricated.

materials.family: Stainless steel or brass (plugs and fittings)
materials.why: Better corrosion resistance where the pump is washed down, installed outdoors or near the sea.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; stainless threads in stainless or steel bosses can gall if assembled dry.

failureModes.cause: Dirty surroundings, dirty containers or wrong oil added.
failureModes.signs: Particles or water in the oil soon after topping up; mixed oil types.

failureModes.cause: Dirt, paint or dried oil in the vent.
failureModes.signs: Oil leaking at housing seals, oil level in sight glass behaving erratically.

failureModes.cause: Not refitted after filling, vibration.
failureModes.signs: Open fill point, dust or water in the oil.

inspection: Check that the plug or breather is present, tight and clean on every round.
Look for oil mist or leakage around the fill point.
Confirm that the oil used for top-up is the type and grade on the lubrication schedule.
maintenance: Clean the area around the plug before opening and use clean, labelled containers for the specified oil.
Fill with the pump stopped, up to the centre of the sight glass, and do not overfill.
Clean or replace breathers and renew sealing washers as needed.

oil-sight-glass.summary: The oil sight glass is a window in the side of the bearing housing that shows the oil level and gives a first view of oil condition.
oil-sight-glass.function: It lets the operator set the oil level when filling and check it on every round without opening the housing. It also gives a first indication of oil condition, such as cloudiness or a milky appearance from water, darkening or visible particles. SKF states that a sight glass or window is needed to set the oil-bath level visually.
oil-sight-glass.operatingPrinciple: The window communicates with the sump, so the oil behind it stands at the same level as the oil around the bearings. With the pump stopped, the correct level is the design level, usually about the centre of the lowest rolling element, shown by a reference mark or the centre of a bull's-eye window. While the pump runs, the observed level fluctuates slightly because oil is splashed and held up on rotating parts, so the level should be set and judged at standstill.
oil-sight-glass.construction: It is commonly a round bull's-eye window with a reflector and centre mark, screwed into a boss at oil-level height; tubular gauges are also used. One manufacturer specifies that the oil level must lie within the 6 mm centre hole of its sight-glass reflector, which corresponds to plus or minus 3 mm from the centre when no oil slinger is fitted. Some housings combine the sight glass with a constant-level oiler that tops up oil lost in service.

materials.family: Glass window in a metal body
materials.why: Clear, scratch-resistant and chemically resistant to lubricating oils.
materials.limitations: Brittle; can crack under impact or thermal shock.

materials.family: Transparent polymer window in a metal or polymer body
materials.why: More resistant to impact than glass.
materials.limitations: May discolour or craze with age, heat or some oils, making the level hard to read; confirm temperature and oil compatibility with the maker.
materials.typicalService: Moderate temperatures and locations where impact is a risk.

failureModes.cause: Reading while running, dirty or discoloured window, wrong reference mark after a component change.
failureModes.signs: Overheating from wrong level despite apparently correct readings.

failureModes.cause: Impact, thermal shock, over-tightening or ageing seal.
failureModes.signs: Oil weeping around the glass, falling level.

failureModes.cause: Opaque or dirty window.
failureModes.signs: Water or sludge discovered only at oil change.

inspection: Check the level at standstill and compare it with the reference mark.
Look at oil colour and clarity through the window on every round.
Check for leaks and cracks around the window.
maintenance: Clean the window so that level and condition can be seen.
Replace leaking, cracked or opaque sight glasses with the OEM part so that the level reference stays correct.
Where a constant-level oiler is fitted, keep its bottle filled and its setting as the OEM specifies.

bearing-housing-drain.summary: The bearing housing drain plug closes a tapped connection at the lowest point of the oil sump used to drain the oil and take samples.
bearing-housing-drain.function: It allows the complete oil charge, together with settled water and sediment, to be removed at an oil change or before dismantling. It provides a point from which an oil sample can be taken for condition analysis. In service it must seal reliably, because a slow leak at the drain can lower the oil level unnoticed between rounds.
bearing-housing-drain.operatingPrinciple: Water and heavier particles settle to the bottom of the sump, so draining from the lowest point removes them with the oil. The drained oil is a diagnostic sample: water, metal particles or darkening indicate a seal, contamination or bearing problem that should be traced before refilling, and one pump manufacturer recommends periodically sending drained oil for analysis and correcting the cause if it is contaminated. The plug seals with a sealing washer, O-ring or thread sealant, depending on design.
bearing-housing-drain.construction: It is a threaded plug, sometimes replaced by a valve or sampling fitting, in a boss at the bottom of the housing. Some designs also have a drain connection in the bearing frame (adapter). The boss is positioned so that the housing can be drained completely with the pump in its installed position.

materials.family: Stainless steel or brass (plugs and fittings)
materials.why: Better corrosion resistance where the pump is washed down, installed outdoors or near the sea.

failureModes.signs: Drips under the housing, falling sight-glass level.

failureModes.cause: Over-tightening a tapered plug in a cast housing.
failureModes.signs: Persistent weeping, visible crack.

failureModes.cause: Infrequent draining or sampling.
failureModes.signs: Sludge and water found only at overhaul.

Renew the sealing washer or O-ring and tighten to the OEM torque.
Refill through the fill point to the centre of the sight glass.

coupling-assembly.summary: The coupling assembly is a flexible disc-pack spacer coupling, enclosed by a guard, that transmits torque from the motor shaft to the pump shaft while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement.
coupling-assembly.function: It transmits the driving torque between two separately supported shafts without slip. It tolerates small residual misalignment and axial movement from thermal growth by flexing its disc packs, which limits the forces imposed on both machines. Its removable spacer leaves a gap between the shaft ends so that the pump rotating assembly can be withdrawn without moving the motor, and its guard protects people from the rotating parts.
coupling-assembly.operatingPrinciple: Torque passes from the motor shaft through a key into the motor hub, through bolts into the first disc pack, across the spacer, through the second disc pack into the pump hub and through the shaft key into the pump shaft. The thin stainless steel discs are stiff in torsion but flexible out of their plane: angular misalignment makes them flex back and forth once per revolution, while an axial displacement deflects them by a steady amount. With two flexing planes separated by the spacer, a parallel offset is taken up as a small angle at each disc pack. This flexing produces reaction forces and moments on the shafts and alternating stress in the discs, so the service life of the coupling depends heavily on how well the shafts are aligned.
coupling-assembly.construction: The coupling consists of a pump hub and a motor hub keyed to their shafts, two laminated disc packs, a removable spacer and the fitted bolts that join them. The disc packs are bolted alternately to the hub flange and the spacer flange around a bolt circle. The distance between shaft ends (DBSE) is set to suit the spacer length, and the whole coupling is enclosed by a fixed guard. Bolt counts, disc profiles and balance quality are specific to each coupling maker.

materials.family: Carbon or alloy steel (coupling hubs and spacer)
materials.why: High strength and stiffness to carry torque and bolt loads; machinable to accurate bores, keyways and spigots.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection in wet or aggressive atmospheres; hub material and heat treatment are chosen by the coupling maker for the torque rating.

materials.family: Austenitic stainless steel spring sheet (disc packs)
materials.why: Thin laminations combine high strength with good fatigue endurance and corrosion resistance; one coupling maker states its disc packs are made from AISI 301 stainless steel for these reasons.
materials.limitations: Fatigue life falls rapidly with excessive misalignment or axial displacement; check compatibility for chloride-laden or otherwise aggressive atmospheres with the coupling maker.
materials.typicalService: Metallic flexible-element couplings in industrial and process pumps.

failureModes.cause: Excessive angular or parallel misalignment, or axial displacement from a wrong shaft-end distance.
failureModes.signs: Cracked or broken outer discs, rising 1x and 2x vibration, noise.

failureModes.cause: Shock loads, locked rotor or blockage of the pump.
failureModes.signs: Buckled or cracked disc links, sheared keys, deformed bolts.

failureModes.cause: Incorrect fit, worn key or keyway, loose set screws.
failureModes.signs: Red-brown fretting debris, hub moved on shaft, vibration.

failureModes.cause: Spacer bent or reassembled out of its match marks, missing balance hardware.
failureModes.signs: Increased 1x vibration after coupling work.

inspection: Confirm the guard is fitted and fastened before every start.
At planned shutdowns, inspect disc packs for cracks or distortion and check bolt tightness, as the coupling maker recommends.
Check alignment after any work on pump, motor, piping or baseplate, and whenever deterioration is suspected.
Trend vibration at both machines; changes at 1x and 2x running speed, or in axial vibration, suggest alignment or coupling problems.
maintenance: Align pump and motor to the OEM tolerance with dial indicators or a laser system after correcting soft foot.
Replace disc packs and hardware with the coupling maker parts and tighten bolts to the specified torque.
Identify and correct the cause of any coupling failure before fitting new parts.
Refit the guard immediately after work and before the drive is energised.

keyConcepts.title: Power transmission path: motor to impeller
keyConcepts.body: The motor converts electrical power into mechanical power at its shaft, and the coupling carries this power as torque at shaft speed. Power, torque and speed are linked by P = T*omega, with omega = 2*pi*n/60 for a speed n in r/min, so T = 60*P/(2*pi*n). As an illustrative calculation only, 15 kW at 1450 r/min gives T = 60*15000/(2*pi*1450), about 99 N*m. The torque path is: rotor and motor shaft, motor key, motor coupling hub, first disc pack, spacer, second disc pack, pump coupling hub, pump shaft key, pump shaft, impeller key and impeller. The pump bearings support the shaft but do not transmit the driving torque; only their friction adds a small loss. At the impeller, shaft power becomes hydraulic power P_h = rho*g*Q*H, and the pump efficiency is eta = P_h/P. Every element of the chain must be sized for the maximum torque it can see; KSB notes that coupling loading by torque shocks is calculated from the maximum torque, such as starting torque.

keyConcepts.title: What a flexible coupling does
keyConcepts.body: KSB describes flexible shaft couplings as slip-free connections that can partially compensate axial, radial and angular misalignment and shock loads. They are needed because two machines on a baseplate cannot be aligned perfectly in practice and their relative position changes in service: shafts grow with temperature, baseplate and piping deflect under load, and rotors move within their bearing clearances. A rigid coupling would turn every small misalignment into large bending loads on both shafts and bearings. In a metallic disc coupling, flexibility comes from thin stainless steel discs that bend elastically, with no sliding contact and therefore no lubrication. A flexible coupling is not a substitute for alignment: the flexing discs generate restoring forces and moments that load both machines, and KSB notes that the service life of flexible elements depends heavily on the misalignment they must compensate. John Crane explains that the misalignment limits quoted for a coupling allow for dynamic conditions and recommends that installed misalignment be no more than 10 percent of the maximum allowable value, with allowance for expected thermal movements.

keyConcepts.title: Parallel, angular and axial misalignment
keyConcepts.body: Misalignment describes how far the two shaft centrelines deviate from one common straight line at the coupling. Parallel (offset, radial) misalignment means the centrelines are parallel but displaced, vertically, horizontally or both. Angular misalignment means the centrelines meet at an angle, so the gap between the coupling faces differs around the circumference. Axial misalignment means the distance between the shaft ends differs from the specified value, which stretches or compresses the disc packs and adds axial force to the thrust bearings. In practice all three occur together and are measured in two planes, vertical and horizontal. In a spacer coupling with two flexing planes a distance L apart, a parallel offset delta is accommodated by an angle of roughly delta/L at each disc pack, while an angular misalignment is shared between the two packs. Vibration analysis gives clues: SKF notes that angular misalignment causes axial vibration at running speed and parallel misalignment radial vibration at two or three times running speed.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment practice in general terms
keyConcepts.body: Alignment starts with a sound installation: the baseplate is level and grouted, the machines sit flat, and soft foot is checked and corrected before any alignment readings are taken (John Crane). The distance between shaft ends is set to the coupling drawing. KSB describes checking a flexible coupling with a straightedge and feeler gauge; Fluke describes dial indicators as more accurate than feeler gauges or straightedges, and laser systems are also widely used. With dial indicators, the rim-and-face method uses one indicator on the hub rim for offset and one on the face for angularity, while the reverse-indicator (reverse periphery) method, which John Crane recommends, reads the rims of both hubs. Laser systems measure the same quantities electronically and calculate the corrections. Vertical corrections are made with shims under the motor feet and horizontal corrections by moving the motor. Allowance is made for indicator bracket sag and for thermal growth of hot or cold machines, as the pump maker specifies. Alignment is checked again after the piping is connected and the bolts are tightened, and tolerances come from the pump or coupling maker; one pump manufacturer, for example, recommends no more than 0.05 mm parallel and 0.0005 mm/mm angular misalignment for its ANSI pump range.

keyConcepts.title: How the spacer enables back-pull-out maintenance
keyConcepts.body: In back-pull-out construction the rotating assembly (bearing frame, shaft, shaft seal, casing cover and impeller) can be pulled out of the casing towards the motor while the casing stays bolted to the suction and discharge piping. That movement needs free axial space between the pump shaft end and the motor shaft end. A spacer coupling provides it: once the guard and the spacer, with its disc packs, are removed, the gap between the two hubs is long enough for the pump shaft and hub to be withdrawn. KSB explains that with a spacer the motor can remain on the foundation and its power cables can stay connected while the rotating assembly is removed. Because the motor is not moved, its position on its shims is preserved, so only a check and a small correction of alignment are usually needed after reassembly instead of a complete realignment. The spacer length, and therefore the distance between shaft ends, is chosen so that the specific pump can be dismantled this way.

keyConcepts.title: Why coupling guards are necessary
keyConcepts.body: A rotating coupling and the exposed shaft ends are entanglement and contact hazards: clothing, hair, gloves or cleaning rags can be caught by bolt heads, keyways and flanges, and fingers can be crushed or cut. Machinery-safety rules in many jurisdictions therefore require these parts to be guarded. In the United States, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.219 covers mechanical power-transmission apparatus: among other things it requires exposed horizontal shafting within seven feet of the floor or working platform to be enclosed, and shaft couplings to be constructed so that they present no hazard from bolts, nuts, set screws or revolving surfaces. ISO 14120 sets general requirements for the design and construction of fixed and movable guards that protect people from mechanical hazards, and other jurisdictions have their own machinery-safety regulations. One pump manufacturer describes its guards as intended to prevent hands, fingers or other body parts from reaching the hazard over, under, around or through the guard, states that the pump must never run without the guard, that the guard is not a step, and that no standard guard can fully contain a disintegrating coupling. In potentially explosive atmospheres that manufacturer requires non-sparking guards for some equipment categories.

pump-coupling-hub.summary: The pump coupling hub is the flanged hub keyed to the pump shaft extension that receives torque from the coupling disc pack.
pump-coupling-hub.function: It transmits the full drive torque from the disc pack to the pump shaft through the shaft key and the fit. It locates the coupling axially on the pump shaft and provides the flange to which the disc pack is bolted. Its position sets one end of the distance between shaft ends that the spacer must bridge.
pump-coupling-hub.operatingPrinciple: Torque passes from the disc-pack bolts into the hub flange and from the hub bore to the shaft through the key flanks and by friction in the fit. A light interference fit, which one coupling maker recommends for most applications, prevents relative movement and fretting under torque fluctuations and vibration, whereas a clearance fit relies on the key and on set screws for axial location. Run-out of the hub face or bore relative to the shaft causes unbalance and apparent misalignment.
pump-coupling-hub.construction: It is a machined steel hub with a bore and keyway to suit the pump shaft, a flange drilled for the disc-pack bolts and, in some designs, set screws or a shaft-end retaining nut. One coupling maker notes that the hub is usually installed with its face flush with the shaft end. Interference-fit hubs are heated for fitting, evenly in an oil bath or oven; that maker prohibits spot heating and gives a maximum hub temperature of 250 °C.

materials.family: Carbon or alloy steel (coupling hubs and spacer)
materials.why: High strength and stiffness to carry torque and bolt loads; machinable to accurate bores, keyways and spigots.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection in wet or aggressive atmospheres; hub material and heat treatment are chosen by the coupling maker for the torque rating.

materials.why: Higher strength after heat treatment allows smaller hubs for a given torque.
materials.limitations: More expensive; heating for fitting must stay within the coupling maker limits to preserve properties.

failureModes.cause: Loose fit, worn key, vibration or torque fluctuation.
failureModes.signs: Red-brown oxide at the hub end, key loose in keyway, hub movable on shaft.

failureModes.cause: Clearance fit with loose set screws or missing retaining nut.
failureModes.signs: Changed distance between shaft ends, disc packs visibly bowed.

failureModes.cause: Excessive interference or over-heating during fitting, overload.
failureModes.signs: Crack running from the keyway, hub loose.

inspection: Check hub fit, key and set screws whenever the coupling is opened.
Measure hub face and rim run-out after fitting where the OEM gives limits.
Check the distance between shaft ends against the coupling drawing.
maintenance: Remove hubs with a puller acting on the hub, never by hammering.
Clean bore and shaft, measure the fit, and heat interference hubs evenly within the coupling maker limit.
Respect the key convention used for balancing (normally half-key) when fitting a new hub.

coupling-flex-elements.summary: The flexible elements are two packs of thin stainless steel discs that connect the hubs to the spacer, transmit torque and flex to accommodate misalignment and axial movement.
coupling-flex-elements.function: They transmit torque between the hub flanges and the spacer without slip or backlash. By bending elastically they accommodate angular misalignment at each pack, parallel offset across the two packs, and limited axial movement from thermal growth. They need no lubrication.
coupling-flex-elements.operatingPrinciple: Each pack is bolted alternately to a hub flange and a spacer flange around a bolt circle; a coupling-industry article explains that torque is transmitted in tension through half of the links (the disc segments between adjacent bolt holes), while the other links are in compression and are generally not counted on. The thin laminations are stiff in their own plane but flexible out of plane: angular misalignment bends the discs back and forth once per revolution and produces alternating stress, while an axial displacement adds a steady bending stress. Fatigue life falls as misalignment and axial displacement increase, which is why one coupling maker recommends installing with no more than 10 percent of the maximum allowable misalignment.
coupling-flex-elements.construction: Each pack is a stack of thin stainless steel discs, often unitised, clamped by fitted drive bolts; one maker uses drive-bolt assemblies with washers, overload collars and locknuts. Disc outlines vary between straight-sided, scalloped and profiled shapes to balance torque capacity, flexibility and edge stresses. One coupling maker states that its disc packs are made from AISI 301 stainless steel for strength, fatigue endurance and environmental resistance.

materials.family: Austenitic stainless steel spring sheet (disc packs)
materials.why: Thin laminations combine high strength with good fatigue endurance and corrosion resistance; one coupling maker states its disc packs are made from AISI 301 stainless steel for these reasons.
materials.limitations: Fatigue life falls rapidly with excessive misalignment or axial displacement; check compatibility for chloride-laden or otherwise aggressive atmospheres with the coupling maker.
materials.typicalService: Metallic flexible-element couplings in industrial and process pumps.

materials.family: High-strength steel fasteners (drive bolts and locknuts)
materials.why: Carry the clamping force that holds the discs and transmits torque between the flanges.
materials.limitations: Must be the coupling maker hardware tightened to the specified torque; reused locknuts may lose their locking ability.

failureModes.cause: Excessive misalignment or axial displacement over many cycles.
failureModes.signs: Cracks starting at bolt holes or disc edges, broken outer discs, vibration.

failureModes.cause: Torque shock, locked rotor, pump seizure.
failureModes.signs: Buckled or cracked disc links, deformed bolts.

failureModes.cause: Loose drive bolts or torsional oscillation.
failureModes.signs: Wear marks and debris around the bolt holes.

failureModes.cause: Aggressive atmosphere or chemical splash.
failureModes.signs: Pitting on disc surfaces, reduced fatigue life.

Check drive bolts for tightness.

maintenance: Replace damaged disc packs as complete units and, where the maker requires, in pairs with new hardware.

Recheck alignment after replacing disc packs.

coupling-spacer.summary: The coupling spacer is the removable centre section that bridges the gap between the pump and motor hubs.
coupling-spacer.function: It transmits torque between the two disc packs across the distance between shaft ends. When removed it leaves enough axial space to withdraw the back-pull-out unit or to work on the seal and bearings without moving the motor. It also separates the two flexing planes, so that a parallel offset can be accommodated by small angles at the disc packs.
coupling-spacer.operatingPrinciple: With two flexing planes a distance L apart, a parallel offset delta between the shafts is taken up as an angle of roughly delta/L at each disc pack, so a longer spacer turns a given offset into a smaller angle and lower disc stress. KSB notes that with a spacer coupling the motor can stay on the foundation while the rotating assembly is removed, because taking out the spacer sideways gives sufficient axial clearance. Disc spacer couplings are typically designed so that the spacer unit can be lifted out radially between the hub flanges without moving either machine; one maker supplies compression bolts that compress the unit slightly for fitting and removal.
coupling-spacer.construction: It is a tubular or flanged steel piece with flanges for the disc packs. In many designs it is supplied with the disc packs as a factory-assembled, balanced transmission unit; one maker supplies the spacer, two disc packs and guard rings in this way. Its length is chosen to match the specified distance between shaft ends.

materials.family: Carbon or alloy steel (coupling hubs and spacer)
materials.why: High strength and stiffness to carry torque and bolt loads; machinable to accurate bores, keyways and spigots.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection in wet or aggressive atmospheres; hub material and heat treatment are chosen by the coupling maker for the torque rating.

materials.why: Higher strength and stiffness for heavily loaded or long spacers.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; balance must be maintained after any repair.

failureModes.cause: Spacer bent by dropping, reassembled out of its match marks or missing balance parts.
failureModes.signs: Higher 1x vibration after coupling work.

failureModes.mode: Wrong length for the shaft gap
failureModes.cause: Incorrect distance between shaft ends after machine movement or a replaced hub.
failureModes.signs: Disc packs visibly stretched or compressed, axial load on bearings.

failureModes.cause: Rough handling during removal.
failureModes.signs: Difficult assembly, run-out, vibration.

Measure the distance between shaft ends against the coupling drawing.
Compare vibration before and after coupling work.
maintenance: Support the spacer during removal and installation so that it cannot fall, as the coupling maker instructs.
Refit with flanges aligned to their match marks and tighten bolts evenly to the specified torque.
Store a removed spacer clean and protected.

motor-coupling-hub.summary: The motor coupling hub is the flanged hub keyed to the motor shaft extension that passes the motor torque into the coupling disc pack.
motor-coupling-hub.function: It transmits the full motor torque from the motor shaft into the first disc pack. It locates the coupling axially on the motor shaft and sets the motor-side end of the distance between shaft ends. Together with the coupling key it forms part of the balanced motor-coupling assembly.
motor-coupling-hub.operatingPrinciple: Torque passes from the motor shaft into the hub through the key flanks and the friction of the fit, and from the hub flange into the disc pack through the drive bolts. Hammer blows or levering forces would pass through the motor bearings and can damage them, and ABB states that coupling halves must never be fitted by hammering or removed by levering against the motor body. Motors are commonly balanced with a half key (ABB standard practice), so the hub must be balanced and fitted to the same key convention to avoid unbalance.
motor-coupling-hub.construction: It is a machined steel hub with a bore and keyway matching the motor shaft extension, a flange drilled for the disc-pack bolts, and set screws or another axial locking device. Its axial position is chosen so that the gap between the hub faces matches the coupling drawing. Interference-fit hubs are heated evenly for fitting within the coupling maker temperature limit.

materials.family: Carbon or alloy steel (coupling hubs and spacer)
materials.why: High strength and stiffness to carry torque and bolt loads; machinable to accurate bores, keyways and spigots.
materials.limitations: Needs corrosion protection in wet or aggressive atmospheres; hub material and heat treatment are chosen by the coupling maker for the torque rating.

materials.why: Higher strength after heat treatment allows smaller hubs for a given torque.
materials.limitations: More expensive; heating for fitting must stay within the coupling maker limits to preserve properties.

failureModes.signs: Noise and vibration from the motor bearings soon after coupling work.

failureModes.cause: Loose fit, worn key or loose set screws.
failureModes.signs: Fretting debris, hub movement, vibration.

failureModes.cause: Hub balanced with a different key convention from the motor.
failureModes.signs: Higher 1x vibration at the motor after a hub change.

Use the half-key convention marked on the motor shaft when balancing and fitting the hub.
Recheck alignment after refitting the hub.

coupling-key.summary: The coupling key is the parallel key that locks the motor coupling hub to the motor shaft and transmits torque between them.
coupling-key.function: It transmits torque positively between motor shaft and hub, in addition to any friction from an interference fit. It fixes the angular position of the hub on the shaft. It also influences the balance of the motor-coupling assembly, which is why the balancing convention for keys must be respected.
coupling-key.operatingPrinciple: Torque is carried by bearing pressure on the key flanks and by shear across the key at the shaft-hub interface; with an interference fit part of the torque is also carried by friction in the fit. One coupling maker specifies that the key should be a tight sliding fit in the keyway with a small clearance at its top. Because keys and keyways are asymmetric masses, ISO 21940-32 specifies a half-key convention for balancing the individual components of a keyed rotor assembly, and marking of the components, so that separately balanced motor and coupling combine correctly; ABB states that its motors are balanced with a half key and that the shaft is marked to show this.
coupling-key.construction: It is a rectangular parallel key of key steel, sized to the keyway of the motor shaft extension and of a length that suits the hub. The keyway dimensions are given on the motor dimension drawing. A key that projects beyond the hub, or that is shorter than the balancing assumption, changes the balance of the assembly.

materials.why: Strong, inexpensive and readily machined to a precise sliding fit.
materials.limitations: Corrodes in wet environments, which can seize the hub on the shaft.

materials.why: Used where corrosion could seize the key, such as wash-down or marine environments.
materials.limitations: Lower strength in some grades; key size and material must suit the transmitted torque as specified by the motor or coupling maker.

failureModes.cause: Torque overload, such as a seized pump or a severe start.
failureModes.signs: Hub turns on the shaft, sheared key, damaged keyway.

failureModes.cause: Loose fit or vibration.
failureModes.signs: Rounded key edges, fretting debris, play between hub and shaft.

failureModes.cause: Full key used where half-key balancing was assumed, or an over-long key.
failureModes.signs: Raised 1x vibration after reassembly.

inspection: Check the key fit and the keyway edges whenever the hub is removed.
Confirm the key length and the balancing convention marked on the motor shaft.
Check that the key cannot move axially out of the keyway.
maintenance: Replace worn or deformed keys with a new key of the specified material and dimensions.
Deburr the keyway and hub before assembly.
Use the half-key convention consistently when balancing hubs.

coupling-guard.summary: The coupling guard is a fixed cover that encloses the coupling and exposed shaft ends between pump and motor to prevent contact with the rotating parts.
coupling-guard.function: It prevents hands, fingers, clothing or tools from reaching the rotating coupling, its bolts and the exposed shaft ends. It is a safety device required by machinery-safety rules in many jurisdictions and must be in place whenever the drive can be energised. It is not designed to contain a disintegrating coupling.
coupling-guard.operatingPrinciple: The guard protects by enclosure and distance: one pump manufacturer describes it as intended to prevent body parts from reaching the hazard over, under, around or through the guard. It is fixed so that it cannot be dislodged in operation and it must not touch the rotating parts. In potentially explosive atmospheres contact between guard and rotating parts could create sparks, so that manufacturer requires a non-sparking guard for some equipment categories.
coupling-guard.construction: In this model it is a removable sheet-metal guard spanning from the bearing frame to the motor and fastened to the baseplate. Variants include hinged clam-shell guards, perforated or mesh guards that allow inspection and transparent polymer guards. One manufacturer describes its standard guard as hinged at the top and removable by loosening a foot bolt.

materials.family: Painted or galvanised carbon steel sheet or mesh
materials.why: Strong, inexpensive and easy to form into a rigid enclosure.
materials.limitations: Corrodes if the coating is damaged; can create sparks if it contacts rotating steel parts.

materials.why: Required by some manufacturers for equipment in potentially explosive atmospheres.
materials.limitations: Material must be selected for the hazardous-area category under the applicable explosion-protection rules.

materials.why: Light and corrosion-free; transparent versions allow the coupling to be observed without removing the guard.
materials.limitations: Lower stiffness and temperature limits than steel; can be cracked by impact.
materials.typicalService: Chemical plants and locations where corrosion is a concern.

failureModes.cause: Removed for alignment or maintenance and not replaced.
failureModes.signs: Exposed rotating parts; serious injury risk.

failureModes.cause: Deformed guard, wrong fitting or moved motor.
failureModes.signs: Scraping noise, marks on guard or hub, sparks.

failureModes.cause: Vibration, corrosion, missing fasteners.
failureModes.signs: Rattling guard, guard displaced.

inspection: Confirm the guard is fitted and fastened before every start.
Check that it does not touch any rotating part and has no enlarged openings or damage.
Check fixings and coating condition during routine rounds.
maintenance: Refit the guard immediately after alignment or coupling work, before the drive is energised.
Repair or replace damaged guards; do not modify openings.
Do not use the guard as a step or support.

electric-motor.summary: The electric motor is a foot-mounted, totally enclosed fan-cooled (TEFC) three-phase squirrel-cage induction motor that converts electrical energy into the shaft torque that drives the pump.
electric-motor.function: It supplies the mechanical power required by the pump at an almost constant speed set by the supply frequency and the number of poles. Its enclosure protects windings and bearings from dust and water, and its shaft-mounted fan cools it. Its feet, bolted to the baseplate on shims, are also the movable element used to align the motor shaft to the pump shaft.
electric-motor.operatingPrinciple: Three-phase current in the stator winding creates a magnetic field that rotates at synchronous speed. The field induces currents in the short-circuited bars of the rotor cage, and the interaction of these currents with the field produces torque. The rotor runs slightly slower than the field, and this slip increases with load so that the motor develops the torque the pump demands. Losses in winding, core and rotor appear as heat, which the external fan carries away by blowing air over the finned frame.
electric-motor.construction: The stator, a laminated magnetic-steel core with a three-phase winding, is fixed inside a finned frame with feet. The rotor, a laminated core with die-cast aluminium bars and end rings, is fixed on the shaft, which runs in rolling bearings held in the drive-end and non-drive-end shields. A fan on the non-drive-end shaft extension, enclosed by a fan cover, blows air over the frame, and a terminal box on the frame contains the winding and earth terminals. Frame size, degree of protection (IP code), cooling method (IC code), insulation class and efficiency class are stated on the rating plate and data sheet.

materials.family: Cast iron (motor frame, end shields, feet)
materials.why: Rigid, robust and good at damping; ABB catalogues list cast iron feet and bearing shields on larger aluminium-frame motors and separate cast iron motor ranges.
materials.limitations: Heavier than aluminium; brittle if struck.
materials.typicalService: Industrial and process motors, larger frame sizes, harsh environments.

materials.family: Aluminium alloy (motor frame, end shields, small terminal boxes)
materials.why: Light, good thermal conductivity and corrosion resistance; one ABB range uses a corrosion-resistant aluminium alloy with low copper content for frame, bearing shields and feet.
materials.limitations: Lower stiffness and strength than cast iron; threads and feet can be damaged by over-tightening or impact.
materials.typicalService: General-purpose motors in smaller and medium frame sizes.

materials.why: Thin insulated laminations carry the alternating magnetic flux with low eddy-current loss; WEG describes stator and rotor cores built of magnetic steel plates with the same characteristics.
materials.limitations: Core losses rise if laminations are damaged, shorted together or overheated during repair.
materials.typicalService: Stator and rotor cores of all induction motors.

materials.family: Enamelled copper wire with impregnating varnish (winding insulation system)
materials.why: Copper gives low resistance; the enamel, slot insulation and varnish form the insulation system, whose thermal class sets the permissible winding temperature (ABB catalogue example: copper, polyester varnish, insulation class F).
materials.limitations: Insulation ages with temperature, moisture, contamination and voltage stress; WEG notes that running 8 to 10 °C above the rated class temperature can halve motor life.

failureModes.cause: Thermal ageing from overload, frequent starts or poor cooling; moisture; voltage stress.
failureModes.signs: Protective trips, falling insulation resistance, burnt smell, earth or phase faults.

failureModes.cause: Lubrication problems, contamination, misalignment, excessive coupling loads, or bearing currents in converter-fed motors.
failureModes.signs: Noise, rising vibration and bearing temperature.

failureModes.cause: Blocked fan inlet or dirty fins, overload, single phasing, high ambient temperature, low speed on a converter without extra cooling.
failureModes.signs: High frame temperature, thermistor trips, discoloured paint.

failureModes.cause: Supply phases connected in the wrong sequence.
failureModes.signs: Pump delivers little, rotation opposite to the casing arrow.

failureModes.cause: Misalignment, soft foot, unbalance or a weak base.
failureModes.signs: High vibration at 1x or 2x running speed.

inspection: Inspect the motor at regular intervals; ABB states at least once a year, with the frequency depending on, for example, ambient humidity and local weather, and regular checking and cleaning of the ventilation in dusty environments.
Check that cooling air flows freely, fins and fan cover are clean, and nothing radiates extra heat onto the motor.
Check bearing condition by listening, vibration measurement and temperature, and check connections and mounting bolts.
Measure winding insulation resistance before commissioning and whenever dampness is suspected, as the motor maker instructs.
maintenance: Keep the motor clean and the ventilation unobstructed.
Regrease or replace bearings as the rating plate and manual specify, using the same bearing type and seal quality as the originals.
Where condensation drain plugs are fitted, open them periodically with the motor stopped and safe.
Recheck alignment after any work on the motor or its mounting.

keyConcepts.title: How an induction motor produces torque
keyConcepts.body: The stator carries three sets of coils displaced by 120 electrical degrees around the bore. Fed with three currents that are 120 degrees apart in time, they produce a resultant magnetic field of roughly constant strength that rotates around the air gap. Its speed is the synchronous speed n_s = 120*f/p in r/min, where f is the supply frequency in Hz and p the number of poles; a 4-pole motor on 50 Hz therefore has n_s = 1500 r/min. If the rotor turned at exactly n_s its bars would not cut the field, no current would be induced and no torque produced. In operation the rotor lags the field by the slip s = (n_s - n)/n_s. The relative motion induces voltages and large currents in the short-circuited rotor bars, and the force on these current-carrying bars in the magnetic field produces torque. When the pump load rises, the speed falls slightly, slip and rotor current increase, and torque rises until it matches the load. Nidec gives slip at rated load of power induction motors as about 2 to 3 percent (larger for small single-phase motors); on that basis a 4-pole 50 Hz motor would run at roughly 1455 to 1470 r/min at rated load, and the rating plate gives the actual rated speed.

keyConcepts.title: Stator versus rotor
keyConcepts.body: The stator is the stationary part: a stack of thin magnetic-steel laminations with slots that hold the three-phase copper winding, pressed into the frame. Laminating the core limits eddy-current losses from the alternating flux. The winding insulation system (wire enamel, slot insulation and impregnating varnish) has a thermal class, for example class F (155 °C) in the IEC 60085 classification quoted by WEG, and WEG notes that operating 8 to 10 °C above the rated class temperature can halve motor life because insulation ages with temperature. The rotor is the rotating part: a laminated core with axial conductor bars, usually die-cast aluminium, joined at both ends by short-circuit rings to form the cage, with no electrical connection to the supply. It is fixed on the shaft, which transmits the torque to the coupling and runs in the motor bearings. The narrow air gap between stator bore and rotor must stay uniform, which depends on the bearings and end shields keeping the rotor centred.

keyConcepts.title: TEFC cooling path (IC 411)
keyConcepts.body: In a totally enclosed motor the internal air does not exchange with the surroundings, which keeps dust and water out of the winding space. Heat from winding, core and rotor losses flows by conduction and internal air circulation to the frame. Outside, a fan on the non-drive-end shaft extension draws ambient air through the grille of the fan cover and blows it along the cooling fins of the frame; the fins enlarge the cooling area, and WEG stresses that the air must be directed over the entire circumference of the frame to be useful. In the IEC 60034-6 cooling code this method is IC 411. Following the ABB explanation of the code, 4 means frame-surface cooled, the first 1 means the internal air is circulated by the machine itself, and the second 1 means the external air is moved by the machine itself, here by the shaft-mounted fan. Consequences for users: the fan inlet needs free space, fins must be kept clean, and on a variable-frequency drive the fan slows with the shaft, so cooling falls at low speed (ABB).

keyConcepts.title: Terminal box and connections
keyConcepts.body: The terminal box is where the supply cable is connected to the winding. ABB states that a standard single-speed motor normally has six winding terminals and at least one earth terminal, which allows the winding to be connected in star or delta and supports direct-on-line or star-delta starting; the box may also contain terminals for thermistors, anti-condensation heaters or other auxiliaries. The rated voltage and connection on the rating plate must match the supply before the links are fitted. Cable glands and blanking elements must have at least the degree of protection of the box, and the box seals must sit correctly in their grooves, otherwise water can reach the winding; the IP code for rotating machines is classified in IEC 60034-5. The box must never be opened while energised, and ABB warns that voltage may be present inside it at standstill when heating elements or winding heating are connected. The phase sequence connected here also sets the direction of rotation.

keyConcepts.title: Checking direction of rotation before coupling
keyConcepts.body: A centrifugal pump must turn in the direction marked by the arrow on its casing; KSB defines clockwise or counter-clockwise as seen looking at the pump shaft from the drive, and one ANSI pump manufacturer specifies clockwise rotation viewed from the motor end. A three-phase motor runs in either direction depending on phase sequence, so rotation is checked after the electrical connection and before the coupling spacer is fitted. With the spacer removed and people clear of the shaft ends, the motor is started briefly and its rotation compared with the arrow; interchanging any two supply phases reverses it (ABB). The check is made uncoupled because reverse rotation can damage some pumps: that manufacturer, whose impellers screw onto the shaft, warns that incorrect rotation even for a short time can unscrew or dislodge the impeller and damage casing, shaft and shaft seal, and it warns against checking rotation with the coupling fitted because of the risk of severe contact between rotating and stationary parts. Motors with unidirectional fans must also run in the direction of the arrow on the motor, otherwise cooling is reduced.

motor-frame.summary: The motor frame is the finned outer housing that carries the stator, supports the end shields and bearings, and stands on the baseplate by its feet.
motor-frame.function: It holds the stator core and, through the end shields, keeps the rotor centred in the stator bore. Its feet transmit the motor weight, reaction torque and coupling forces to the baseplate and are the adjustment points used for alignment. Its external fins, together with the fan, dissipate the motor losses to the ambient air.
motor-frame.operatingPrinciple: The reaction to the torque delivered to the pump acts on the stator and is carried by the frame and feet into the baseplate. Heat produced inside flows through the core into the frame and is removed by air blown along the fins, so frame temperature depends on load, ambient temperature and cleanliness of the fins. A frame that does not sit evenly on all its feet (soft foot) is distorted when its hold-down bolts are tightened, which can shift the shaft and must be corrected before alignment.
motor-frame.construction: It is a cast iron or aluminium alloy body with integral or bolted feet and longitudinal cooling fins, machined to receive the stator core and the spigots of the end shields. It carries lifting lugs for the motor alone; ABB warns that lugs on auxiliaries or terminal boxes must not be used to lift the motor. Condensation drain holes with plugs may be provided at the lowest points, and ABB instructs that they face downwards in the mounted position.

materials.family: Cast iron (motor frame, end shields, feet)
materials.why: Rigid, robust and good at damping; ABB catalogues list cast iron feet and bearing shields on larger aluminium-frame motors and separate cast iron motor ranges.
materials.limitations: Heavier than aluminium; brittle if struck.
materials.typicalService: Industrial and process motors, larger frame sizes, harsh environments.

materials.family: Aluminium alloy (motor frame, end shields, small terminal boxes)
materials.why: Light, good thermal conductivity and corrosion resistance; one ABB range uses a corrosion-resistant aluminium alloy with low copper content for frame, bearing shields and feet.
materials.limitations: Lower stiffness and strength than cast iron; threads and feet can be damaged by over-tightening or impact.
materials.typicalService: General-purpose motors in smaller and medium frame sizes.

failureModes.cause: Uneven pads, dirty or bent shims, twisted base.
failureModes.signs: Alignment readings that change when one foot bolt is loosened, vibration.

failureModes.cause: Fins clogged with dirt or covered, insufficient free space at the fan inlet.
failureModes.signs: Higher frame temperature at normal load.

failureModes.cause: Bolting onto an uneven base, impact, excessive pipe-induced base distortion.
failureModes.signs: Visible cracks, movement of the motor, changed alignment.

failureModes.cause: Humid environment with blocked or closed drain holes.
failureModes.signs: Water at drains, falling insulation resistance.

inspection: Keep fins and the area around the motor clean and free of objects that obstruct airflow.
Check foot bolts, shims and soft foot before alignment and after any disturbance.
Check that drain holes face downwards and are not blocked.
maintenance: Clean the frame surface and fins regularly, especially in dusty areas.
Correct soft foot with clean shims before aligning.
Touch up damaged paint to prevent corrosion.

motor-stator.summary: The stator is the stationary electromagnetic part of the motor: a laminated steel core whose slots carry the three-phase winding that creates the rotating magnetic field.
motor-stator.function: It converts the three-phase supply into a rotating magnetic field that drives the rotor. With the frame it forms the stationary member that reacts the motor torque. Its winding insulation separates the live conductors from the earthed core and largely determines motor life.
motor-stator.operatingPrinciple: Three coil groups displaced by 120 degrees and fed with three-phase currents produce a resultant field rotating at n_s = 120*f/p. The laminated core concentrates the magnetic flux across the air gap with low eddy-current loss. Current in the winding produces resistive (I^2*R) losses and the alternating flux produces core losses; both heat the stator, and the winding temperature must stay within the limit of the insulation thermal class.
motor-stator.construction: It is a stack of thin magnetic-steel laminations punched with slots and pressed into the frame. Coils of enamelled copper wire are inserted in the slots with slot insulation, connected in the required pole arrangement and brought out to the terminal box. The winding is impregnated with varnish or resin, which WEG notes improves heat transfer by eliminating voids, and temperature sensors such as thermistors may be built in.

materials.why: Thin insulated laminations carry the alternating magnetic flux with low eddy-current loss; WEG describes stator and rotor cores built of magnetic steel plates with the same characteristics.
materials.limitations: Core losses rise if laminations are damaged, shorted together or overheated during repair.
materials.typicalService: Stator and rotor cores of all induction motors.

materials.family: Enamelled copper wire with impregnating varnish (winding insulation system)
materials.why: Copper gives low resistance; the enamel, slot insulation and varnish form the insulation system, whose thermal class sets the permissible winding temperature (ABB catalogue example: copper, polyester varnish, insulation class F).
materials.limitations: Insulation ages with temperature, moisture, contamination and voltage stress; WEG notes that running 8 to 10 °C above the rated class temperature can halve motor life.

materials.family: Insulating films and laminates (slot and phase insulation)
materials.why: Separate the winding from the core and the phases from each other; WEG describes aramid- and polyester-based films for this purpose.
materials.limitations: Must match the thermal class of the insulation system; damaged by overheating and mechanical abrasion.

failureModes.cause: Running above the class temperature through overload, poor cooling or frequent starts.
failureModes.signs: Gradual fall in insulation resistance, finally a winding fault.

failureModes.cause: Condensation, water ingress or conductive dust.
failureModes.signs: Low insulation resistance after standstill, earth faults.

failureModes.cause: Loss of one supply phase.
failureModes.signs: Rapid overheating of the remaining phases, protective trip.

failureModes.cause: Badly worn bearings letting the rotor touch the stator bore.
failureModes.signs: Rub marks on the stator bore, noise, winding failure.

inspection: Measure insulation resistance before commissioning and when dampness is suspected, following the motor maker procedure.
Monitor winding temperature through thermistors or other sensors where fitted.
Check that the three phase currents are balanced in operation.
maintenance: Keep the motor dry; use anti-condensation heaters where fitted during standstill.
Provide motor protection suitable for the duty, including thermal protection of the winding.
Have rewinds carried out by a qualified repairer to the original specification.

motor-rotor.summary: The rotor is the rotating electromagnetic part of the motor: a laminated core with a short-circuited cage of conductor bars, fixed on the motor shaft.
motor-rotor.function: It carries the currents induced by the rotating stator field and converts the resulting electromagnetic forces into torque on the shaft. It has no electrical connection to the supply, which KSB notes makes squirrel-cage rotors simple, reliable and maintenance-free.
motor-rotor.operatingPrinciple: Because the rotor turns slower than the stator field, the field sweeps across the bars and induces voltages in them, and with the bars short-circuited by end rings large currents flow. The force on these current-carrying bars in the magnetic field produces torque in the direction of field rotation. Rotor bar resistance shapes the torque-speed curve: Nidec explains that low conductor impedance favours efficiency at running speed, while higher impedance increases torque at low speed. Rotor losses heat the rotor, and the rotor must be balanced so that its mass is distributed symmetrically about the axis of rotation.
motor-rotor.construction: Magnetic-steel laminations are stacked and fixed on the shaft, and aluminium is die-cast into the slots to form the bars and the two short-circuit rings in one piece (WEG). The complete rotor is balanced; ABB states that its motors are balanced with a half key in the shaft keyway as standard. ISO 21940-11 gives balancing procedures and tolerances for rotors with rigid behaviour (KSB cites it for pump rotating assemblies); the balance quality of a motor rotor is set by the motor maker.

materials.why: Thin insulated laminations carry the alternating magnetic flux with low eddy-current loss; WEG describes stator and rotor cores built of magnetic steel plates with the same characteristics.
materials.limitations: Core losses rise if laminations are damaged, shorted together or overheated during repair.
materials.typicalService: Stator and rotor cores of all induction motors.

materials.family: Die-cast aluminium (cage bars and end rings)
materials.why: Bars and end rings are cast in one operation into the lamination stack, giving a robust, economical cage (WEG, ABB catalogue).
materials.limitations: Casting porosity or cracks in bars or rings can cause local heating and torque pulsation.

failureModes.cause: Loss or shift of balance weights, deposits, damage during repair.
failureModes.signs: Vibration at 1x running speed.

failureModes.cause: Locked rotor, prolonged or frequent starts, overload.
failureModes.signs: Discoloured laminations or end rings, protective trips.

failureModes.cause: Worn bearings or damaged end shields letting the rotor move off-centre.
failureModes.signs: Rub marks, noise, rapid temperature rise.

failureModes.cause: Shaft voltages and bearing currents, particularly with converter supply.
failureModes.signs: Fluting patterns on bearing raceways, bearing noise.

inspection: Trend motor vibration at 1x running speed and compare it with the baseline.
At overhaul, inspect the rotor surface for rub marks and the end rings for discolouration or cracks.
For converter-fed motors, check that the bearing-current mitigation specified by the motor maker is in place.
maintenance: Rebalance the rotor after any repair that can change its mass distribution.
Handle the rotor so that laminations and shaft journals are not damaged during removal.
Avoid starting duties beyond those the motor maker permits.

motor-shaft.summary: The motor shaft carries the rotor, runs in the motor bearings and delivers the motor torque at its drive-end extension to the coupling hub.
motor-shaft.function: It transmits the full driving torque from the rotor to the coupling through a keyed shaft extension. It positions the rotor radially in the stator bore and axially between the bearings. At the non-drive end it also carries the cooling fan.
motor-shaft.operatingPrinciple: The shaft is loaded in torsion by the transmitted torque and in bending by the rotor weight, unbalance, magnetic pull and any radial force from the coupling. A correctly aligned flexible coupling imposes only small additional loads, whereas misalignment or a wrong shaft-end distance transfers extra radial and axial load into the motor bearings. ABB warns that coupling halves must never be fitted by hammering or removed by levering against the motor body, because the force passes through the motor bearings.
motor-shaft.construction: It is a machined steel shaft with bearing seats, a rotor seat and a cylindrical drive-end extension with a keyway. The motor is normally balanced with a half key in the keyway and the shaft is marked to show the balancing convention (ABB), which the coupling hub balance must match. One bearing usually locates the shaft axially while the other allows thermal growth; which end is which depends on the motor design.

materials.why: Good strength, toughness and machinability for torque transmission and bearing seats.
materials.limitations: The exposed extension corrodes if unprotected; keyway roots are fatigue-sensitive under bending.

materials.why: Used by motor makers for higher torque ratings or corrosive environments.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; availability depends on the motor range.

failureModes.cause: Loose hub fretting, hammering during hub fitting.
failureModes.signs: Worn keyway, burrs, raised run-out.

failureModes.mode: Fatigue cracking at the keyway or a shoulder
failureModes.cause: Cyclic bending from misalignment, excessive radial load, unbalance.
failureModes.signs: Crack at the keyway end; in extreme cases shaft fracture.

failureModes.cause: Bearing inner ring creep after bearing distress.
failureModes.signs: Loose bearing fit found at overhaul.

inspection: Measure shaft-extension run-out if the motor has been dropped, struck or overloaded.
Inspect keyway and extension whenever the coupling hub is removed.
Check bearing seats at motor overhaul.
maintenance: Fit and remove coupling hubs with proper tools or heating, never by impact.
Protect the bare shaft extension against corrosion when the coupling is removed.
Respect the half-key balancing convention marked on the shaft.

motor-end-shield-nde.summary: The non-drive-end shield closes the fan end of the motor frame and holds the non-drive-end motor bearing.
motor-end-shield-nde.function: It locates the non-drive-end bearing so that the rotor stays centred in the stator bore. It closes the frame against dust and water at the fan end and carries the shaft seal there. The fan and fan cover are mounted outboard of it.
motor-end-shield-nde.operatingPrinciple: The end shield is piloted into the frame by a machined spigot, so the bearing bores at both ends are concentric with the stator bore and the air gap stays uniform. Radial loads from rotor weight and magnetic pull pass from the bearing through the shield into the frame. When a motor is supplied from a frequency converter, ABB specifies measures against bearing currents that depend on motor power and frame size; above stated limits they include an insulated non-drive-end bearing and, for the largest motors, also a common-mode filter at the converter.
motor-end-shield-nde.construction: It is a cast iron or aluminium alloy disc with a central bearing housing, a spigot fitting into the frame and bolt holes. It may carry a grease nipple and grease outlet for regreasable bearings and a V-ring or radial seal on the shaft (ABB). For insulated arrangements ABB recommends bearings with aluminium-oxide-coated bores or ceramic rolling elements.

materials.family: Cast iron (motor frame, end shields, feet)
materials.why: Rigid, robust and good at damping; ABB catalogues list cast iron feet and bearing shields on larger aluminium-frame motors and separate cast iron motor ranges.
materials.limitations: Heavier than aluminium; brittle if struck.

failureModes.cause: Lubrication problems, contamination, excessive loads or bearing currents.
failureModes.signs: Noise, vibration, high bearing temperature at the fan end.

failureModes.cause: Outer ring creep after bearing distress.

Replace bearings with the same type and seals of the same quality as the originals (ABB).
Check the bearing seat dimensions at every bearing change.

motor-terminal-box.summary: The terminal box is the enclosure on the motor frame where the supply cables, the earth conductor and any auxiliary devices are connected to the motor.
motor-terminal-box.function: It provides a protected, insulated space to terminate the supply cables on the winding terminals. It allows the winding to be connected in star or delta to suit the supply voltage, and it contains the earth terminal and terminals for thermistors or heaters. Its seals and cable glands maintain the degree of protection of the motor.
motor-terminal-box.operatingPrinciple: The six winding ends are brought to a terminal block, where links between terminals set the star or delta connection and the phase sequence of the supply sets the direction of rotation. Cable glands clamp and seal the cables and, for converter-fed motors, ABB requires glands that give 360-degree bonding of the cable screen. The box keeps its IP rating only when its seals are seated correctly and unused entries are closed with blanking elements of at least the same IP class (ABB).
motor-terminal-box.construction: On smaller motors in one ABB range the terminal box is aluminium alloy with its lower part integrated with the stator frame, while larger sizes have a bolted deep-drawn steel box. It contains the terminal block, an earth terminal, sometimes an auxiliary terminal strip, and threaded cable entries. Terminal markings follow IEC 60034-8 in that maker catalogue.

materials.family: Aluminium alloy (motor frame, end shields, small terminal boxes)
materials.why: Light, good thermal conductivity and corrosion resistance; one ABB range uses a corrosion-resistant aluminium alloy with low copper content for frame, bearing shields and feet.
materials.limitations: Lower stiffness and strength than cast iron; threads and feet can be damaged by over-tightening or impact.
materials.typicalService: General-purpose motors in smaller and medium frame sizes.

materials.family: Deep-drawn or fabricated steel (larger terminal boxes)
materials.why: Strong, rigid enclosure for larger cables and auxiliary devices.
materials.limitations: Needs a coating system; corrodes if water is trapped inside.

failureModes.signs: Moisture or corrosion inside the box, earth faults.

failureModes.cause: Star/delta links not matching the supply voltage.
failureModes.signs: Overcurrent and trips, or low torque and overheating.

Check that unused cable entries are properly blanked.
maintenance: Isolate and lock out the supply, and any heater supply, before opening the box.
Tighten connections to the motor maker values and replace damaged lugs or seals.
Use cable glands of the correct type, size and IP rating.

motor-fan.summary: The motor fan is a small fan on the non-drive-end shaft extension that blows ambient air over the finned frame of the TEFC motor.
motor-fan.function: It provides the external cooling air flow that lets the motor carry its rated load without exceeding its temperature limits. Because it runs at motor speed, cooling is available whenever the motor runs at its rated speed.
motor-fan.operatingPrinciple: The fan draws air axially through the grille of the fan cover and discharges it outward, and the cover turns the flow along the fins over the frame. Heat transfer increases with air velocity, so fan speed and clear air paths determine the cooling capacity. WEG states that its motors have bi-directional fans unless a single direction of rotation is specified, whereas ABB instructs that a motor with a unidirectional fan must rotate in the direction of the arrow on the motor. On a variable-frequency drive the fan slows with the shaft, so ABB notes that cooling capacity is lost at low speed and a separate fan may be needed.
motor-fan.construction: It is a moulded or cast fan fixed to the shaft extension by a key, clamp or locking ring. One ABB catalogue lists glass-fibre reinforced polypropylene fans for smaller motors and fans of reinforced glass-fibre laminate, aluminium or polypropylene with a metal hub for larger sizes. A metal fan is offered as an option.

materials.why: Light, corrosion-free and economical to mould into an efficient blade shape (ABB catalogue example).
materials.limitations: Temperature and impact limits lower than metal; can become brittle with age.
materials.typicalService: Standard TEFC motors in normal environments.

motor-fan-cover.summary: The fan cover (cowl) encloses the motor fan, guards it against contact and guides the cooling air from the inlet grille over the frame fins.
motor-fan-cover.function: It prevents fingers and objects from reaching the rotating fan. It turns the fan discharge into a flow along the fins so that the air sweeps the frame surface. Its inlet grille admits ambient air while excluding larger objects.
motor-fan-cover.operatingPrinciple: Air enters through the perforated end of the cover, is accelerated by the fan and leaves through the annular gap between cover and frame, where it is directed along the fins. WEG explains that a well-designed ventilation system must direct the air over the entire circumference of the frame, otherwise a large air volume is wasted. Blocking the inlet or mounting the motor too close to a wall reduces the airflow, so ABB refers to minimum free space behind the fan cover in its catalogues and drawings.
motor-fan-cover.construction: It is a pressed sheet-steel or polymer cowl with an inlet grille, fastened to the frame or end shield with screws. One ABB catalogue lists polypropylene covers on smaller motors and sheet-steel covers on larger ones, with a metal fan cover as an option. Its openings are sized to keep fingers away from the fan.

materials.why: Strong and rigid; maintains the clearance to the fan.
materials.limitations: Can dent onto the fan if struck; corrodes if the coating is damaged.

support-structure.summary: The supporting structure (baseplate with mounting pads, levelling screws, anchor bolts, grout and concrete foundation) carries the pump set, keeps pump and motor aligned and transfers loads and vibration into the ground.
support-structure.function: It provides a common, stiff and level mounting for pump and motor so that their shafts stay aligned in service. It carries the weight of the machines, the motor reaction torque, the hydraulic forces and the forces and moments from the connected piping, and passes them to the foundation and the soil. Its mass and stiffness also limit vibration.
support-structure.operatingPrinciple: A fabricated baseplate on its own is relatively flexible; once grouted to a heavy concrete block it acts together with the foundation as one stiff body. The anchor bolts clamp baseplate, grout and foundation together, the grout adds stiffness and damping, and the mass and footprint of the foundation resist dynamic forces. Machined mounting pads provide flat seats for the machine feet, and shims under the motor feet allow the final alignment. Any deformation of this structure, whether from uneven support, poor grouting or pipe forces, appears directly as misalignment at the coupling.
support-structure.construction: In this configuration a fabricated steel baseplate with longitudinal and cross members carries machined pads for the pump feet, the bearing-frame support and the motor. It is set on levelling screws over a reinforced concrete foundation, held by anchor bolts set in sleeves, and filled and underfilled with grout through grout and vent holes. A drain rim or pan can collect leakage. Cast iron, pre-grouted, polymer and stilt- or spring-mounted bases are common alternatives.

materials.why: Weldable structural steel sections and plate allow a stiff frame with cross members, pads and drain rim to be fabricated in any size.
materials.limitations: Needs a coating system and surface preparation suited to the grout; distorts if welded without control, so pads are machined after fabrication.
materials.typicalService: Common baseplates for most horizontal pump sets.
