keyConcepts.title: Purpose of the baseplate
keyConcepts.body: The Hydraulic Institute describes a baseplate as the structure to which the pump, motor and any auxiliary equipment are mounted, whose purpose is to provide a foundation under pump and driver that maintains shaft alignment between them. HI lists its functional requirements: it must survive transport, be installable with minimum difficulty, allow initial mounting and alignment, allow final alignment, control spillage, and allow removal and reinstallation of the equipment. An absolutely rigid baseplate is not necessary, but it must not be permanently deformed once the equipment is mounted. In a grouted design the baseplate is only part of the structure: its cross members are shaped as L, T or I sections to lock into the grout, and the installed stiffness and damping come from the combination of baseplate, grout and foundation. The baseplate must also cope with piping forces, and KSB notes that once pump and drive are aligned they should be protected against the effects of piping forces and moments.

keyConcepts.title: Foundation stiffness and mass
keyConcepts.body: KSB states that the foundation of a stationary centrifugal pump must absorb the forces and torques transmitted to it without shifting, and that its strength and vibration behaviour are decisive for reliable operation. Mass helps because a heavy block moves less under a given dynamic force, and a wide, shallow block resists rocking better than a tall, narrow one; ACI 351.3R warns that a foundation made only as wide as the machine footprint tends to rock more, and that an OEM foundation outline is only a guide to minimum size. Rules of thumb exist: one pump manufacturer recommends a concrete foundation mass of three times that of pump, motor and base, and a pump-industry author reports manufacturers encouraging three to five times. These are starting points only; for large or critical machines a structural engineer designs the foundation, checking soil support, natural frequencies relative to running speed and vibration amplitudes. New concrete must also cure adequately before the baseplate is grouted.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment depends on the support
keyConcepts.body: Shaft alignment is only as stable as the structure beneath it. Before alignment the baseplate is levelled in both directions, referencing machined coplanar mounting surfaces where they exist, and anchor bolts are tightened without twisting the base (one manufacturer example). Each machine must sit flat on all its feet; John Crane instructs that soft foot be checked and corrected before alignment starts, because a foot that does not bear evenly distorts the casing or frame when bolted down. Vertical corrections are made with shims under the motor feet and horizontal corrections by moving the motor, and one manufacturer recommends minimising the number of shims, with no more than five under any foot. KSB describes coupling alignment as carried out after grouting, followed by a final check after the piping and accessories are connected. KSB also advises pinning pump and drive to the baseplate after alignment so that the set cannot shift in operation.

keyConcepts.title: Grouting: cementitious versus epoxy
keyConcepts.body: Grout fills the space between baseplate and foundation and, in grouted designs, the inside of the base frame. It spreads loads over the whole base, bonds it to the foundation and adds stiffness and damping. HI states that either cementitious or epoxy grout may be used and that the surface preparation for bonding differs between them, so the type should be agreed in advance. Cementitious machinery grouts are non-shrink hydraulic-cement products that need only mixing water; ASTM C1107/C1107M covers packaged dry non-shrink grout for use under applied load such as under a machine. Epoxy grouts are resin-based systems; one industry author notes that most companies have chosen epoxy over the last decades because it yields superior results in most cases, while cementitious grout is less expensive. Curing, especially of epoxy, depends on ambient temperature, and grout can pull the base out of level as it shrinks, so level is checked during curing. After curing the grout is inspected for voids, which are repaired.

keyConcepts.title: Anchor bolts and levelling
keyConcepts.body: Anchor (foundation) bolts are cast into the concrete, often inside sleeves that allow some movement of the bolt (one manufacturer example); the sleeve must not fill with grout, and one author fills it with dry sand for that reason. Their purpose is not only to hold the base down but to pull foundation, grout and baseplate together into one monolithic mass. Before grouting, the base is levelled with levelling (jack) screws, or with shims and wedges, checking both longitudinal and lateral level. One author recommends that jack screws bear on small metal plates, preferably stainless steel, rather than directly on the concrete. Practice differs on sequence: one pump manufacturer tightens the anchor bolts after levelling and before grouting, KSB states that foundation bolts should be tightened only after the grout has set, and one author applies some bolt tension during grouting to stop the base floating. After the grout cures, jack screws, shims and wedges are removed so that the grout carries the base; one manufacturer warns that if left they could rust, swell and distort the baseplate. Follow the OEM instructions.

keyConcepts.title: Effect of pipe strain
keyConcepts.body: Pipe strain is the force and moment that connected piping imposes on the pump nozzles. HI identifies three sources: mechanical strain from flanges forced together and from the weight of pipe and liquid, hydraulic pressure reaction forces (for example at flexible joints without tie rods), and thermal expansion or contraction of the piping. Because the casing is bolted to the baseplate and coupled to the motor, these loads deform casing and base and move the pump shaft relative to the motor shaft. The consequences include coupling misalignment, vibration, premature seal and bearing failure, internal rubbing and, in extreme cases, failure of nozzles, couplings or mountings. KSB notes that permissible nozzle loads are therefore limited by codes such as the EUROPUMP guideline, API 610 and ISO 5199, and that a grouted baseplate allows higher loads than an ungrouted one; HI publishes ANSI/HI 9.6.2 on assessing applied nozzle loads. Good practice is to support piping independently, bring flanges together without force, connect piping only after the base is grouted, and then recheck alignment to confirm that no significant pipe load has been introduced.

baseplate.summary: The baseplate is the fabricated steel frame on which the pump, the bearing-frame support and the motor are mounted, providing a common reference for alignment.
baseplate.function: It holds pump and motor in their aligned positions and transfers their weight, torque reaction and piping loads to the grout and foundation. It carries the mounting pads, the anchor-bolt holes and the levelling screws. Its rim and drain collect drips and leakage, one of the baseplate functions listed by HI.
baseplate.operatingPrinciple: Loads from the machine feet pass through the pads into the longitudinal members and, through the grout locked around the cross members, into the foundation. Before grouting a fabricated base is relatively flexible and can twist if levelled or bolted unevenly; after grouting it acts together with the foundation. HI states that closed baseplate designs need grout and vent holes so that grout can be placed inside the base, and venting lets displaced air escape so that no voids remain.
baseplate.construction: It is welded from steel channels, beams or plate, with cross members shaped to lock into the grout, machined mounting pads, anchor-bolt holes, levelling-screw bosses, lifting points, grout and vent holes, and often a drain rim and connection. One practitioner notes that manufacturers usually prepare the underside only for transit corrosion protection, so surface preparation for grouting has to be specified separately. Grout makers advise the preparation and paint for their grout, and excessive paint thickness can cause epoxy grout to pull the paint off the steel.

mounting-pads.summary: Mounting pads are the machined, raised seats on the baseplate on which the feet of the pump, the bearing-frame support and the motor are bolted.
mounting-pads.function: They provide flat, coplanar seats at defined heights so that the machines can be aligned with a minimum of shims. They carry the drilled or tapped holes for the hold-down bolts. The motor pads leave room for the shims used for vertical alignment.
mounting-pads.operatingPrinciple: Machine feet must sit flat and fully supported; if a pad is out of plane or a foot does not bear evenly (soft foot), tightening the hold-down bolt bends the casing or frame and changes the shaft position. Machined coplanar pads therefore also serve as the reference surfaces for levelling the baseplate during installation (one manufacturer example). Shims between pad and foot give fine height adjustment for alignment, and that manufacturer recommends minimising the number of shims in a pack, with no more than five under any foot.
mounting-pads.construction: They are steel blocks or plates welded to the baseplate members and machined, usually after welding, so that all pads of one machine lie in a common plane. Hold-down holes are drilled or tapped in them. Clearance in the motor foot holes lets the motor be moved horizontally during alignment, sometimes with horizontal jacking screws.

materials.limitations: Needs a coating system and surface preparation suited to the grout; distorts if welded without control, so pads are machined after fabrication.

levelling-screws.summary: Levelling screws are jacking screws threaded through the baseplate that support it at the correct height and level on the foundation before grouting.
levelling-screws.function: They allow the baseplate to be raised, lowered and levelled precisely in both directions before grout is placed. They hold the base in position while the grout is poured and cures. After the grout has cured they are removed so that the grout carries the base.
levelling-screws.operatingPrinciple: Turning a screw in its threaded boss jacks the baseplate up or lets it down at that point, so a set of screws around the base allows level and flatness to be adjusted without shims. If the screws were left bearing after grouting, the base would rest on a few hard points instead of the full grout area. One pump manufacturer warns that jack screws, shims or wedges left in place can rust, swell and distort the baseplate.
levelling-screws.construction: They are threaded bolts in welded nuts or bosses on the baseplate, often placed near the anchor bolts. An industry author recommends placing small metal plates (pucks), preferably stainless steel, under the screw points so they do not dig into the concrete, and coating the screws with grease so they can be removed after curing. The holes left by the screws are then filled with grout or liquid epoxy.

materials.why: Strong and cheap; a grease coating allows removal from the cured grout.
materials.limitations: Corrode and can swell if left in the grout.

materials.why: Spread the screw load on the concrete and do not corrode, as one industry author recommends.
materials.limitations: Must be bedded on sound, prepared concrete.

failureModes.cause: Not removed after grouting.
failureModes.signs: Hard spots, cracked grout, corrosion and distortion over time.

failureModes.cause: No bearing plate under the screw.
failureModes.signs: Level changes during adjustment, imprecise levelling.

failureModes.cause: No release coating, corrosion.
failureModes.signs: Screws cannot be removed after curing.

inspection: Check level in both directions before grouting.
Confirm the screws are coated and bear on plates before pouring.
After curing, confirm the screws have been removed and the holes filled.
maintenance: Remove the screws after the grout has cured and fill the voids.
Keep the screws for re-levelling if the base is ever re-grouted.
Protect the threaded bosses against corrosion.

anchor-bolts.summary: Anchor (foundation) bolts are steel bolts embedded in the concrete foundation that clamp the baseplate, grout and foundation together.
anchor-bolts.function: They hold the baseplate down against overturning moments, shear and vibration forces. When tightened they clamp baseplate, grout and foundation into one monolithic mass, so that loads are transferred through the grout in compression rather than by bending of the bolts.
anchor-bolts.operatingPrinciple: Tightening the nut stretches the bolt and creates a clamping force between baseplate and foundation; as long as the clamping force exceeds the dynamic forces, the joint does not slip or open. Bolts are often installed in sleeves so that they can be moved slightly to suit the baseplate holes, and the sleeve must be kept free of grout (Elsey). ACI 351.3R describes a cycle in which cracking and loosening of anchors increase vibratory forces, which further damage the foundation, and notes that higher clamping force transfers vibratory forces more efficiently into the foundation.
anchor-bolts.construction: They are headed, hooked or bent steel rods cast into the foundation, typically in sleeves, or anchors installed later in existing concrete, with nuts and washers above the baseplate. Their size, embedment, material and tightening procedure are set by the foundation designer and the OEM drawings. ASTM F1554 specifies steel anchor bolts in three strength grades for anchoring structural supports to concrete foundations.

materials.family: Carbon or high-strength low-alloy steel anchor bolts
materials.why: Standardised anchor bolts for anchoring structural supports to concrete, available in three yield-strength grades and with zinc coating where required.
materials.limitations: Uncoated carbon steel corrodes where water collects in sleeves or at the grout line; grade and coating must suit the design loads and environment.
materials.typicalService: Machinery and structural anchorage in concrete.

materials.why: Among its repair techniques for deteriorated dynamic-equipment foundations, ACI 351.3R lists upgrading anchor bolts from lower-strength steel to higher-strength alloy steel (its example is ASTM A193/A193M Grade B7) so that the increased clamping force transfers vibratory forces more efficiently into the foundation.
materials.limitations: Selection, tightening and embedment must be engineered; higher strength alone does not compensate for poor concrete or grout.
materials.typicalService: Heavily loaded or vibrating machine foundations.

failureModes.cause: Vibration, grout creep or insufficient initial tension.
failureModes.signs: Nut can be turned by hand, movement of the base, fretting marks.

failureModes.cause: Water collecting in sleeves or at the base.
failureModes.signs: Rust at the nut and grout line, loss of section.

failureModes.signs: Radial cracks in grout or concrete near the bolt.

maintenance: Retighten only by the procedure given by the foundation designer or OEM, then recheck alignment.
Protect exposed threads and nuts against corrosion.
Replace corroded or damaged bolts through an engineered repair.

grout.summary: Grout is the cementitious or epoxy filling placed between the baseplate and the concrete foundation that bonds them and supports the baseplate over its full area.
grout.function: It provides continuous, uniform support under the baseplate instead of support at a few points. It bonds the baseplate to the foundation, adding stiffness and damping and helping the structure resist pipe forces and vibration. In grouted designs it also fills the inside of the base frame so that the cross members are locked in.
grout.operatingPrinciple: Grout is placed as a flowable material that fills the gap under and inside the baseplate and then hardens. To work it must fill completely without voids, keep its volume while hardening, and bond to both the prepared concrete and the prepared steel. Once cured it carries the clamping force of the anchor bolts and the dynamic loads of the machines.
grout.construction: It is placed in strong, liquid-tight forms around the baseplate and poured from one side, from a head box above the base, so that air escapes from the other side, using a one-pour or two-pour method (Elsey). The concrete surface must be sound, with the weak surface layer (laitance) chipped away, and the baseplate underside must be prepared and coated as the grout maker specifies. Grout type, thickness and edge details follow the grout maker and the OEM drawings.

materials.why: Packaged hydraulic-cement grout that needs only mixing water; ASTM C1107/C1107M covers non-shrink grout of this type intended for use under applied load, such as under a machine, where a change in height below the initial placement height is to be avoided. One industry author notes that it is less expensive than epoxy.
materials.limitations: Bond to steel and resistance to some chemicals and oils are generally lower than for epoxy grouts (check the grout maker data); curing must be protected from heat, cold and rain.

materials.why: Resin-based grout that one industry author reports most companies have chosen over recent decades because it yields superior results in most cases.
materials.limitations: Higher cost; curing depends strongly on temperature; surface preparation and paint thickness are critical to avoid delamination.
materials.typicalService: Process and critical pumps, high vibration or chemically aggressive locations.

failureModes.cause: Insufficient venting, poor flow or too little grout.
failureModes.signs: Hollow areas, baseplate deck vibration.

failureModes.cause: Poor surface preparation, paint too thick, contamination.
failureModes.signs: Separation at the grout-steel interface, movement under load.

failureModes.cause: Shrinkage, thermal cycling, dynamic loads or a weak foundation.
failureModes.signs: Visible cracks, especially near anchor bolts and corners.

failureModes.cause: Extreme temperature or rain during curing.
failureModes.signs: Low strength, surface defects, base pulled out of level.

inspection: After curing, check for voids under the base and repair them (one manufacturer instruction).
Inspect grout edges and areas around anchor bolts for cracks periodically.
Treat a rise in baseplate or foundation vibration as a reason to inspect the grout.
maintenance: Repair voids and cracks with materials and methods approved by the grout maker.
Protect grout from leaking oil and process liquids.
Plan re-grouting if the base has broken loose from the grout, then re-level and realign.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

Material options are common families listed for education, not recommendations. For wetted pump parts, selection is driven by temperature, pH, chloride content, solids content, pressure, erosion/abrasion and cavitation; drive-end parts are normally not wetted, so the governing factors are temperature, the surrounding atmosphere (humidity, splash or leakage of the pumped liquid, which brings its pH and chlorides), dust and solids, mechanical load and vibration. Final selection must be confirmed with the pump, bearing, coupling or motor manufacturer (OEM) for the actual service conditions.
Standards are cited for scope and relevance only; no conformity with any standard is claimed.

Statements attributed to a named manufacturer describe that product range only and are cited as examples of practice, not as general requirements.

foundation.summary: The concrete foundation is the reinforced concrete block that supports the grouted baseplate and transmits all static and dynamic loads of the pump set to the ground.
foundation.function: It provides a stable, stiff and heavy support that keeps the pump set level and aligned throughout its service life. It absorbs the forces and torques from pump, drive and piping without shifting and limits vibration. Where required it also isolates the machine from the surrounding floor or structure.
foundation.operatingPrinciple: The foundation adds mass and footprint to the machine support: a heavier block moves less under the same dynamic force, and a wider block resists rocking. Its stiffness and natural frequencies, together with the soil or piles beneath it, determine how it responds to unbalance and other periodic forces; KSB refers to high-frequency-tuned and low-frequency-tuned pump foundations. Deterioration is progressive: ACI 351.3R describes how cracking and loosened anchors increase vibratory forces, which further damage the foundation, so early repair is warranted.
foundation.construction: It is a cast-in-place reinforced concrete block on prepared soil or piles, with anchor bolts and sleeves cast in at the positions on the baseplate drawing. Its top surface is roughened, or the laitance is chipped away before grouting, so the grout can bond, and new concrete must cure before grouting, for a time that depends on the mix and conditions. KSB notes that small and medium pump sets with moderate piping loads can be installed without a special foundation when the baseplate is rigid enough to prevent distortion.

materials.why: Provides mass, stiffness and durability at low cost and can be cast to any shape around anchor bolts.
materials.limitations: Cracks under excessive dynamic loads or poor design; must cure fully before grouting; reinforcement corrodes if cracks admit water.
materials.typicalService: Foundations for all grouted pump sets.

materials.why: ACI 351.3R mentions polymer-modified concrete for repairing degraded machine foundations because of its higher strength.
materials.limitations: Repairs must be engineered and compatible with the existing concrete.

failureModes.cause: Dynamic loads, shrinkage, inadequate reinforcement or poor design.
failureModes.signs: Visible cracks, rising vibration, loosening anchor bolts.

failureModes.cause: Inadequate soil support or soil changes.
failureModes.signs: Baseplate out of level, repeated alignment drift.

failureModes.cause: Natural frequency of the foundation system close to running speed.
failureModes.signs: High vibration that changes strongly with speed.

failureModes.cause: Foundation too narrow or too tall for the machine.
failureModes.signs: High horizontal vibration at the top of the foundation.

inspection: Inspect for cracks, spalling and settlement during routine inspections.
Check the baseplate level when alignment drifts repeatedly.
Measure foundation vibration when machine vibration rises.
maintenance: Have cracks and deterioration assessed and repaired early, under the direction of a structural engineer.
Keep drainage working so that water and leakage do not collect around the foundation.
Re-level and realign after foundation repairs.
assumptions: Generic educational configuration, not a specific manufacturer design; proportions shown in the 3D model are illustrative and must not be read as real dimensions.

curves.title: Illustrative example - not manufacturer data
curves.disclaimer: Educational example values generated from simplified relationships. Not test data for any real pump and must not be used for equipment selection.
curves.source: Generated in code from the simplified relations listed under the assumptions (no measurement, no catalogue data). Plausible orders of magnitude only.
assumptions: Generic single-stage, single-suction end-suction pump with a radial impeller, constant speed 2900 rpm (a typical 2-pole motor speed on a 50 Hz supply) and a nominal 200 mm impeller diameter. It does not represent any real product.
Liquid: clean water at about 20 °C, density 998 kg/m³ (approximate). g = 9.80665 m/s².
Head: H = H0 − a·Q² with H0 = 56 m (shut-off) and a = 0.0032 m/(m³/h)², giving H = 48 m at the assumed best-efficiency flow of 50 m³/h. Real H–Q curves are not exact parabolas.

Efficiency: η = η_BEP·[2(Q/Q_BEP) − (Q/Q_BEP)²] with η_BEP = 0.70 (a plausible order of magnitude for this size, not a reference value). This symmetric parabola is zero at shut-off and at 2·Q_BEP; real efficiency curves are usually flatter to the right of BEP.

Shaft power: P = ρ g Q H / η, so the power column is consistent with the head and efficiency columns by construction (values rounded to 1 W). At Q = 0 the formula is 0/0 and its limit ρ g H0 Q_BEP / (2 η_BEP) ≈ 5.4 kW is used; real shut-off power comes from disc-friction, leakage and recirculation losses that this simple model does not represent.

NPSHr: NPSHr = 1.5 m + 2.0 m·(Q/Q_BEP)², listed from 10 m³/h upwards and meant to stand for NPSH3 (3 % head drop). Real NPSHr curves often rise again at low flow because of recirculation; that is not modelled.

Operating regions: preferred 70–120 % and allowable 40–130 % of BEP flow are ASSUMED for illustration. For a real pump these limits are stated by the manufacturer (see e.g. Hydraulic Institute ANSI/HI 9.6.3, Guideline for Operating Regions).
Rated point (45 m³/h, on the curve) is a hypothetical example duty point, not a rating.
Runout: the curve ends at 75 m³/h (1.5 × Q_BEP), chosen for illustration.

Plausibility check only: tip speed u2 = π·D·N/60 ≈ 30.4 m/s, head coefficient ψ = 2gH/u2² ≈ 1.0 at BEP and specific speed n_q ≈ 19 (rpm, m³/s, m), orders of magnitude commonly seen for small radial impellers.
